word_study.significance: In biblical law, mishpat is the official legal process. Job uses courtroom language to describe his situation: God has brought him not just into crisis but into a formal judgment scene. The verb 'bring' suggests coercion—Job is dragged before the bar.

word_study.meaning: With you; alongside you; in your presence. The preposition im means 'with' in the sense of 'before' or 'in the company of.' This indicates not just judgment but confrontation—Job is brought face to face with God as judge.
word_study.significance: The phrase emphasizes the asymmetry: Job must stand before his maker and answer. There is nowhere else to stand; this is the only court that matters. The 'with you' language appears elsewhere when the righteous stand before God (Psalm 41:12), but here it carries accusation.

cross_references.connection: "Thou puttest my feet also in the stocks, and lookest narrowly unto all my paths." This earlier verse establishes the surveillance complaint that Job now escalates—God's watchfulness has become a form of bondage.

"Hast thou eyes of flesh? or seest thou as man seeth? Are thy days as the days of man?" Job poses a similar accusation: God's judgment standards are applied to humans as if God were human, ignoring the vast difference in nature and lifespan.

"Now we know that what things soever the law saith, it saith to them who are under the law: that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God." Paul echoes Job's accusatory tone but reframes it: the law's purpose is precisely to render all humanity accountable before God, not to ignore human limitation.

"O LORD, thou hast searched me, and known me. Thou knowest my downsitting and mine uprising, thou understandest my thought afar off." The psalmist celebrates the same divine omniscience and surveillance that Job finds horrifying—a contrasting perspective on God's attention.

"For God shall bring every work into judgment, with every secret thing, whether it be good, or whether it be evil." This verse affirms exactly what Job protests: God will judge all human deeds. The perspective differs (resigned acceptance rather than indignant protest), but the basic claim is identical.

commentary.historical_context: Ancient Near Eastern royal inscriptions and wisdom texts often depicted gods as all-seeing judges who examine human conduct. The metaphor of the god's opened eyes was a standard expression of divine awareness and judgment. However, Job's twist is distinctive: he grants the reality of God's surveillance but questions its justice when applied to beings of such limited duration. In ancient legal contexts, a judge's scrutiny (looking narrowly into a case) was expected and necessary; Job inverts this—the scrupulousness of God's examination of a creature with 'few days' is disproportionate to the object being examined. The courtroom imagery would have been visceral for an ancient audience familiar with legal proceedings before local elders or royal judges.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 12:15 explains the divine perspective Job protests against: 'And it shall come to pass that when all are raised from the dead, that all shall know what has been done unto them.' The Book of Mormon affirms that God's judgment will eventually make sense to all creatures, not because they are made less temporary, but because resurrection and exaltation transform the stakes of judgment.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:111-112 speaks of the celestial kingdom as a place where God's presence becomes not surveillance but communion: 'Where God and Christ are the judge of all... And they shall be gods, because they have no end; therefore shall they be from everlasting to everlasting.' The Restoration's answer to Job is that judgment in God's presence, properly understood, is not a torment but an invitation to become eternal.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple judgment scene presents the soul standing before God to answer for deeds, yet within the covenant framework where mercy and grace temper judgment. Job protests the bare fact of judgment; the temple contextualizes it within a redemptive process. The soul stands before God, yes, but not alone—Christ stands as advocate and mediator.

commentary.christological_typology: Job stands accused before God and finds no mediator; Christ's role as mediator begins precisely here—standing between human transience and divine judgment. In 1 Timothy 2:5, Paul describes Christ as "the one mediator between God and men." Job's dilemma is: how can a creature of a few days answer to an eternal God? The Atonement supplies the answer: through Christ's infinite sacrifice, the temporal creature becomes able to stand before the eternal judge without being crushed. Job asks, "Why bring me into judgment?" Christ answers, "Because through me, that judgment becomes redemptive, not destructive."
commentary.application: Job 14:3 speaks to the modern experience of feeling judged—by God, by conscience, by society—with a weight that seems disproportionate to one's actual significance or staying power. The verse validates the complaint: if you are mortal and limited, relentless scrutiny becomes a form of injustice. Yet the verse also invites reflection on what kind of judgment we seek or resist. Do we want God to ignore us? Or do we want to be judged mercifully, with consideration for our constraints? The application: bring your complaint about divine judgment to God honestly, as Job does, rather than pretending it doesn't sting. The honesty itself becomes part of the covenant dialogue.

text_kjv: Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? not one.

commentary.narrative:
Job shifts from accusation to a deeper philosophical point: the impossibility of achieving the moral purity that might justify God's judgment. This verse does not confess specific, personal sin (Job has consistently denied particular wrongdoing); rather, it articulates a universal human condition of moral compromise. The formulation "Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean?"—posed as a rhetorical question with the answer "not one"—expresses a logical necessity: if humans themselves are born into uncleanness (as verse 1 established), then nothing they produce can be clean.

The TCR rendering makes the logical structure more apparent: "Who can bring something clean from what is unclean? No one." This is not a statement about individual defilement but about a cosmic principle. If the source is unclean, the product must be unclean. The question echoes Platonic and Near Eastern concepts of moral causation: like produces like. Importantly, Job is not claiming that humans are uniquely evil or that God is justified in this condition; he is claiming that the standard God applies (absolute purity) is impossible to meet given the terms of human existence. This verse anticipates Paul's argument in Romans 3:23 ("all have sinned") and Romans 5:12 ("as by one man sin entered into the world"), though Paul will eventually frame a solution that Job cannot see.

word_study.meaning: Who can give/make/bring forth. The question mi ('who') expects the answer 'no one' (lo echad). Yitten is the causative form, emphasizing bringing forth or producing as an active achievement.
word_study.significance: The rhetorical question implies impossibility—not merely that no one has achieved it, but that it cannot be achieved. The use of yitten (to give/make) emphasizes agency: it's not about what one receives but what one produces or creates.

word_study.meaning: Clean, pure, undefiled. In Hebrew Scripture, tahor has both physical and moral/spiritual connotations. Tahor can mean ritually clean (permitted to approach the tabernacle) or morally pure (innocent, righteous). The term is often paired with its opposite, tame (unclean, defiled).
word_study.significance: Job uses the loaded language of purity laws: if you are born tame (unclean), you cannot produce tahor (cleanness). The use of purity language connects individual moral status to the broader covenant vocabulary of Israel's law. Job is not merely describing human imperfection but invoking the language of ritual and moral status.

word_study.meaning: Unclean, defiled, impure. Tame is the opposite of tahor and can refer to ritual defilement (contact with corpses, diseased conditions) or moral corruption. The term describes things and people separated from the holy.
word_study.significance: By using tame, Job invokes the whole apparatus of Israel's purity laws—the entire system that maintains the distinction between the holy and the unholy. His argument: humans are born on the unholy side of that boundary and cannot cross it through their own effort.

word_study.meaning: Not one, not even one, not a single one. The emphatic negation with echad (one) makes the claim universal and absolute. No exception exists, no one person escapes this condition.
word_study.significance: The phrase echoes verse 1's "adam yelud ishah" (every human born of woman) and confirms the universal scope. Echad (one) appears in the Shema ('Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God is one'), establishing that God alone is unified, complete, wholly other. Humans are not even one in purity; only God is one in perfection.

cross_references.connection: "What is man, that he should be clean? and he which is born of a woman, that he should be righteous?" Eliphaz quotes this verse back to Job as if it were Job's own confession of guilt, but Job intends it as a statement about the impossible standard, not a plea of personal guilt.

"For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God." Paul makes a similar claim of universal moral inadequacy, but unlike Job, Paul frames it within the redemptive logic of justification through Christ.

"Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me." David echoes Job's language of being born into an unclean state, though David frames it as personal confession rather than cosmic principle.

"If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins." John acknowledges the universality of human moral compromise that Job states but offers confession and forgiveness as the remedy.

"Thou hast set our iniquities before thee, our secret sins in the light of thy countenance." The psalmist acknowledges that even hidden sins are known to God, implying the impossibility of hidden cleanness.

commentary.historical_context: Job's formulation draws on both Mesopotamian wisdom tradition and the purity laws of Israel. Babylonian wisdom texts grapple with the problem of human limitation and moral imperfection, often concluding that humans cannot meet the standards of the gods. The Hebrew purity laws created a complex system for determining ritual cleanness—but these laws addressed external conditions (corpses, leprosy, bodily discharges), not moral nature. Job's move is to extend the logic: if even ritual cleanliness requires careful management and can be compromised, what hope is there for moral cleanness, which is internal and originates from one's very birth? The question "Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean?" suggests a problem of causation: contamination flows from source to product. In the ancient world, this operated both magically (contact with unclean things makes one unclean) and morally (parents of a certain moral character produce children of that character).

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 3:19 directly addresses this Jobian dilemma: 'For the natural man is an enemy to God, and has been from the fall of Adam, and will be, forever and ever, unless he yields to the enticings of the Holy Ghost, and putteth off the natural man and becometh a saint.' The Book of Mormon acknowledges the unclean source (the natural man) but identifies a mechanism for producing cleanness (yielding to the Spirit and the Atonement). Job sees the problem; Mormon scripture reveals the solution.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:34-35 speaks of the mechanism of purity through the Atonement: 'Wherefore, I the Lord God will send forth flies upon the face of the earth, which shall eat their flesh, and shall cause them to sting because of their sins... And it shall come to pass that those who die in me shall not taste of death, for it shall be sweet unto them.' The Restoration teaches that from the unclean (sinful death), God brings forth the clean (resurrection in Christ). Job's paradox is resolved not by denying the uncleanness but by divine transformation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the endowment, the individual is presented in their natural unclean state (Adam and Eve in the Garden, then in the lone and dreary world), yet the temple ceremony shows how, through covenant and divine instruction, the unclean can be made fit to approach God. The purity language of the temple (washing, anointing) directly addresses the paradox Job articulates—the gap between the unclean source and the clean requirement—and shows it bridged through ordinance and covenant.

commentary.christological_typology: Job's statement—that nothing clean can come from an unclean source—is reversed in Christ's incarnation and ministry. Christ is the clean thing that emerges from unclean origins: born of Mary (a mortal, therefore unclean in Job's terms), yet entirely pure and undefiled (Hebrews 7:26). Moreover, Christ's sacrifice transforms the impossible principle Job articulates: his infinite cleanness becomes available to the unclean through faith. Christ is the answer to the rhetorical question: he alone brings infinite cleanness from finite uncleanness. He is the one exception to "not one"—the one who can, through grace, make unclean things clean.
commentary.application: Job 14:4 offers modern readers permission to hold two truths simultaneously: the acknowledgment of inherent limitation ("I am born into imperfection") and the refusal to accept that limitation as a reason for despair or self-rejection. The verse can become a tool of grace rather than condemnation. Instead of reading it as "You are hopelessly unclean," read it as "The expectation of moral perfection arising from your own effort is impossible—and that impossibility is not your personal failure but the structure of the fallen condition itself." This can free people from the tyranny of perfectionism and open them to seeking help beyond themselves—divine help. The verse also invites reflection on how you judge others: if no one can bring cleanness from uncleanness, on what basis do you hold others to standards of perfection?

text_kjv: Seeing his days are determined, the number of his months are with thee, thou hast appointed his bounds that he cannot pass;

commentary.narrative:
Job now pivots from the general human condition (verses 1-4) to God's role in limiting that condition. The verse builds a crescendo of divine determinism through three parallel statements: days are determined, months are numbered, bounds are set. The TCR rendering clarifies the structure: "Since his days are determined, / the number of his months is with you. / You have set his limit, and he cannot pass it." Each statement narrows the focus from abstract principle to concrete barrier. This is not a complaint about God's foreknowledge (Job doesn't argue that God couldn't know in advance); rather, it is an observation that God actively fixes and controls the boundaries of human life.

Importantly, Job presents this as an established fact that should inform God's judgment. The "Seeing" (or "Since") that opens the verse introduces a logical condition: *given* that God has already set a fixed term for human life, *therefore* it would be incongruous for God to apply judgment as if humans had unlimited time and capacity for moral growth. The fixed boundary (chuqqav, statute or decree) is not something humans can transgress—it is absolute and inescapable. This echoes the earlier observation that humans are "few of days." Now Job suggests that this limitation is not merely circumstantial but divinely ordained. The theological implication: if God predetermined the brevity, how can God hold humans strictly accountable for moral achievement within that brief span?

word_study.meaning: His days are determined, fixed, marked out, decreed. Charutsim comes from charatz, meaning 'to cut, carve, decide, determine.' The plural 'days' suggests the entire sequence is predetermined, not day by day but as a whole.
word_study.significance: The verb charutz appears in contexts of decisive action (cutting stone, carving decisions). Job uses language of permanence and fixity: the days are not flexible but carved in stone. This echoes the language of divine decree.

word_study.meaning: The number/count of his months. Mispar means 'number, count, enumeration.' Chodesh means 'month' (literally 'new,' from the lunar cycle). The phrase emphasizes accounting—each month is numbered, not left to chance.
word_study.significance: By moving from 'days' to 'months,' Job emphasizes the precision and completeness of divine accounting. God doesn't just know the rough lifespan; God counts the months. The particularity suggests omniscience applied to each individual.

word_study.meaning: With you; in your keeping, possession, or knowledge. The preposition 'im' establishes that the count is not autonomous or external—it is held in God's hand.
word_study.significance: The phrase suggests both knowledge and custody: the months are not only known but held, controlled, guarded by God. They rest in divine possession.

word_study.meaning: His statute/bound/decree you have made. Chuqqav is 'his statute, his law, his boundary, his decreed limit.' The root chaqaq means 'to engrave, carve, decree.' Asita means 'you have made, established, created.'
word_study.significance: The use of chuqqav (statute) elevates the boundary from mere fact to law—it is not just that humans die but that death is decreed as law, engraved and established. The same word appears in contexts of God's eternal laws (Isaiah 40:28). Job is suggesting that mortality is a statute as fundamental as gravity.

word_study.meaning: And he cannot pass, transgress, cross over. The verb abar means 'to cross, pass over, transgress.' The negation is absolute: the boundary is not merely difficult but impossible to cross.
word_study.significance: The same verb appears in legal contexts (you cannot transgress the law) and geographical ones (you cannot cross this river). Job uses the language of law and geography: the boundary of death is as fixed as a river or a statute.

cross_references.connection: "LORD, make me to know mine end, and the measure of my days, what it is; that I may know how frail I am." The psalmist asks for awareness of God's predetermined boundary, finding in that limitation a reason for humility rather than resentment.

"Thou hidest thy face, they are troubled: thou takest away their breath, they die, and return to their dust." Like Job, the psalmist acknowledges that God actively determines the end of human life; the breath is taken, not merely released.

"To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven: A time to be born, and a time to die." Qoheleth affirms the predetermined timing of life and death, finding in this pattern evidence of divine order.
"And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment." The New Testament echoes Job's language of divine appointment and the fixedness of mortality as a universal statute.

"Is there not an appointed time to man upon earth? are not his days also like the days of an hireling?" Job returns to the theme of divine appointment of lifespan, comparing life to the fixed contract of a hired laborer.

commentary.historical_context: The concept of a fixed lifespan, divinely determined, was widespread in ancient Near Eastern thought. Egyptian texts reference the "Ren" or 'years determined' by Thoth. Mesopotamian texts speak of the gods' decisions regarding human span. However, these texts typically frame predetermination as decreed by the divine council in advance—part of the cosmic order. Job's move is to make this predetermined boundary into an argument against divine judgment: if the term is short and the boundary unpassable, why hold humans strictly accountable? This reflects a sophisticated theological problem that runs through both ancient wisdom and biblical thought.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 2:21-25 explains the predetermination of mortality differently than Job: 'And the days of the children of men were prolonged, according to the will of God; and they began to multiply and to spread forth upon the face of the earth... And they would have had no children; wherefore they would have remained in a state of innocence, having no joy, for they knew no misery.' The Book of Mormon frames the predetermined boundary (mortality) not as arbitrary constraint but as part of the divine plan for exaltation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:39 speaks of the predetermined nature of judgment and reward: 'That by him, and through him, and of him, the heavens and all their hosts were made; and the inhabitants thereof are begotten sons and daughters unto God.' While not directly addressing lifespan, the revelation frames predetermination within a context of exaltation. The boundary Job complains about is temporary and part of a larger trajectory.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment presents the human lifespan as a progression through set stages (the garden, the fall, mortality, the spirit world, exaltation). Job complains about the fixed boundaries of mortality; the temple shows those boundaries as part of a larger, predetermined economy of salvation where each phase has meaning.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's life presents a unique relationship to the predetermined boundary that Job describes. Christ's days and months were determined (he lived an average lifespan of about 33 years), yet he transcended the boundary through resurrection. His predetermined lifespan was not a constraint but a fulfillment: he lived exactly as long as necessary to accomplish the Atonement. In this way, Christ embodies the paradox Job cannot resolve: the finite and predetermined can become infinite through divine purpose. Christ's statement in John 10:17-18—"No man taketh it [my life] from me, but I lay it down of myself"—suggests active participation in the predetermined boundary rather than passive subjection to it.
commentary.application: Job 14:5 can function as both a humbling and liberating statement. The modern tendency is to try to extend lifespan indefinitely through technology and health optimization, as if the boundary were not fixed. Job's verse invites acceptance: your lifespan is determined, numbered, and bounded. This need not be depressing—it can be clarifying. It frees you from the burden of indefinite self-improvement and the fear of cosmic waste ("I haven't done enough"). Within a fixed span, the question becomes: what is the quality of engagement with the time given? The verse also invites theological reflection: if your days are determined by God, do you trust that determination? Or are you spending your few days in anxiety about extending them?

text_kjv: Turn from him, that he may rest, till he shall accomplish, as an hireling, his day.

commentary.narrative:
Job's petition reaches its climax: a plea for God to look away and grant respite. After establishing the human condition (verses 1-2), the disproportionality of judgment (verse 3), the impossibility of cleanness (verse 4), and God's predetermined boundaries on life (verse 5), Job asks for the one mercy he can imagine: inattention. The TCR rendering—"Look away from him so he can rest, / until he finishes his day like a hired worker"—captures the poignancy: Job asks not for removal of the boundary (death is inevitable) but for freedom from scrutiny while living.

The "hired worker" (sakhir) comparison returns Job to the labor metaphor of 7:1-2. A hired laborer's relationship to their employer is transactional and time-limited: the worker completes their shift, receives payment, and is done. Job asks for a similar arrangement with God: surveillance off, contracted time fulfilled, and life complete. The plea suggests that the burden of living under divine gaze—combined with the brevity of days and the impossibility of achieving cleanness—makes ordinary life impossible. The irony is profound: if God truly reduced attention, would that be merciful? Or would it be abandonment? Job cannot see a third way—only the binary of intense judgment or merciful indifference.

word_study.meaning: Look away from, gaze elsewhere, remove your eyes from. The verb shaa'ah means 'to gaze, look, regard.' The preposition min means 'from.' The imperative form addresses God directly.
word_study.significance: This echoes the surveillance complaint from 13:27. Job asks for the reversal of 'opened eyes' (14:3)—he wants those eyes pointed elsewhere. The verb shaa'ah appears in contexts of attention and intention: to look away requires an act of will, not mere indifference.

word_study.meaning: And let him cease, let him rest, let him be quiet. The verb chadal means 'to cease, stop, rest, desist.' The cohortative form (yechdal) expresses a wish or hope.
word_study.significance: The word chadal appears in contexts of ending labor (Nehemiah 6:9, 'the work was done... and my hands rested'). Job seeks not rest in death but rest from examination while living—the ability to simply exist without being scrutinized.

word_study.meaning: Enjoys, accomplishes, completes his day. The verb ratsah can mean 'to be pleased, pleased, to accomplish, to accept.' The noun yom means 'day,' but in the context of labor, it means 'day's work.'
word_study.significance: The verb ratsah carries a sense of satisfaction or completion: the hired worker finishes the shift, the work is accepted, and the day is done. Job asks for this ordinary completion, not vindication or exoneration.

word_study.meaning: Like a hired worker, day laborer, employee. Sakhir is one hired for wages, typically by the day. The comparison is to the lowest level of economic relationship: transactional, temporary, bounded.
word_study.significance: The sakhir (hired worker) comparison appears in Job 7:1-2 and recurs here. It emphasizes the temporary nature of the relationship—not familial or covenantal but contractual. Once the shift ends, the relationship is complete. Job wishes to relate to God like a laborer to an employer: do the work, get paid, leave.

cross_references.connection: "Is there not an appointed time to man upon earth? are not his days also like the days of an hireling? As a servant earnestly desireth the shadow... so am I made to possess months of vanity." This passage introduces the hired worker metaphor and establishes the longing for the day's end that returns here.

"Thou puttest my feet also in the stocks, and lookest narrowly unto all my paths; though I am like a rotten thing that consumeth, as a garment that is moth eaten." The surveillance complaint that Job now asks God to reverse is established in these verses.

"Six days thou shalt do thy work, and on the seventh day thou shalt rest: that thine ox and thine ass may rest, and the son of thy handmaid, and the stranger, may be refreshed." God's own law mandates rest even for hired workers and servants—a principle Job invokes in asking for respite.

"For the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder, which went out early in the morning to hire labourers into his vineyard." Christ's parable reframes the hired worker relationship in terms of divine generosity, not mere transaction—suggesting a more hopeful answer to Job's hired worker comparison.

"And if ye call on the Father, who without respect of persons judgeth according to every man's work, pass the time of your sojourning here in fear." Peter acknowledges that believers live under God's judgment during their 'sojourning,' a temporary work-like existence, yet frames it within fear and respect rather than resentment.

commentary.historical_context: The hired worker (sakhir) in ancient Levantine society was among the most vulnerable and least protected laborers. Biblical law makes special provision for the sakhir's wages (Deuteronomy 24:14-15) because they had no other security. By comparing human life to a sakhir's day, Job evokes both the harsh reality of precarious labor and the legal principle that even the vulnerable deserve fair treatment—they complete their work, receive their compensation, and are released. The image would have resonated with an agrarian audience familiar with day laborers hired for harvest or construction. The comparison to God as an exacting employer is striking: it removes the familial or covenantal language that usually characterizes the God-Israel relationship and replaces it with pure transaction.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Jacob 5, the allegory of the olive tree, uses similar agricultural labor imagery (tending, pruning, harvesting) but frames God's attention as not burdensome but redemptive—the Lord of the vineyard works tirelessly not to torment but to save. Where Job sees divine scrutiny as crushing, the Book of Mormon sees it as salvific.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:7-8 addresses the divine relationship differently than Job's hired worker model: 'My son, peace be unto thy soul; thine adversity and thine afflictions shall be but a small moment; And then, if thou endure it well, God shall exalt thee on high; thou shalt triumph over all thy foes.' The Restoration reframes the period of examination not as burdensome scrutiny to be escaped but as a trial that leads to exaltation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple work requires the individual to 'work' through the covenant ceremony, receiving keys and understanding at each stage. Unlike Job's hired worker who simply endures and leaves, the temple participant actively engages with divine instruction and receives exaltation as the outcome. The scrutiny Job fears becomes partnership in the temple model.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's statement in Matthew 11:28—"Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest"—directly answers Job's prayer for rest from labor and scrutiny. Where Job sees no solution but divine indifference, Christ offers active redemption: the burden itself is transformed through grace. Moreover, Christ's incarnation involves a voluntary taking-on of the hired worker's position: in Philippians 2:7, Paul describes Christ as taking "the form of a servant" (doulos, a stronger term than sakhir but similar in meaning). Christ experiences labor and limitation, but uniquely, he transcends it through resurrection. Christ is the answer to Job: the one who both identifies with the hired worker's condition and breaks its boundaries.
commentary.application: Job 14:6 names the longing for relief from scrutiny that many people feel in relationship to authority (God, parents, employers, society). The verse validates the exhaustion of constant evaluation and the human need for space to simply live without being watched and judged. Yet the verse also exposes the limitations of Job's solution: if God truly looked away, would that be rest or abandonment? Modern application invites considering: what kind of divine attention would feel like grace rather than burden? The verse might lead to prayer not for God to look away but for God's gaze to transform—from judgment to compassion, from surveillance to presence. The hired worker metaphor also invites reflection on how you relate to God: as a laborer meeting a quota, or as a covenanted partner invited into larger purposes?

text_kjv: For there is hope of a tree, if it be cut down, that it will sprout again, and that the tender branch thereof will not cease.

commentary.narrative: Job pivots from the universality of human suffering to a startling observation: a tree has what humans lack—hope. The Hebrew word תִּקְוָה (tiqvah) anchors this verse and the entire chapter. Tiqvah is not mere optimism; it is a cord, a binding to the future, something stretched between present and what is to come. A tree, when felled, has this cord intact. Its biology guarantees renewal. The wood is cut, the stump remains, and from that apparently dead wood, new shoots emerge. Job is not being poetic here—he is being rigorously observational. Many Mediterranean and Near Eastern trees (oaks, pines, terebinths) exhibit exactly this regenerative capacity. The shock of the verse lies in its theological implication: the non-sentient tree, lacking reason, speech, and moral agency, possesses a future that conscious, worshiping humanity does not.

word_study.meaning: A cord stretched tight; that which binds one to the future; expectation grounded in something real and binding. The root sense is 'to bind' or 'stretch.' In Job's usage, tiqvah is not subjective feeling but objective fact—the tree is bound by its biology to regeneration.
word_study.significance: This is the hinge-word of Job 14. Job grants tiqvah to the tree but systematically denies it to humans (verses 10-12). Yet in verses 13-15, Job will contradict himself, imagining tiqvah for himself if God would but remember him. The tension between what he argues (no hope for humans) and what he desperately wishes (that God would give him hope) is the tragic core of the chapter.

word_study.meaning: To change, exchange, renew, put forth new growth. Describes the replacement of the old with the new. In this context, the tree does not merely survive—it is transformed and renewed.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that yachalif is both a botanical fact and a theological statement. What was destroyed is exchanged for what is new. The verb carries hope not as feeling but as biological process.

word_study.meaning: That which suckles or draws nourishment; tender new growth dependent on the mother plant (or stump). The word pictures intimate biological nurture—the young shoot drawing life from the old stump.
word_study.significance: Yoneqet emphasizes not just growth but sustained life-giving connection. The new shoots do not spring up independent; they are fed by the old root system. This paradoxically strengthens Job's point: the tree's future depends on what is beneath the ground, on what is hidden and invisible.

cross_references.connection: A shoot shall come forth from the stem of Jesse—a messianic prophecy using the exact image Job employs of a tree cut down yet sprouting anew. The later tradition reads Isaiah's 'Branch' in light of Job's tree.

The righteous person is like a tree planted by water, yielding fruit in season—the inverse of Job's image. Where the psalmist sees the tree as metaphor for human blessing, Job sees the tree as proof that humans lack the tree's advantage.

There is a time to plant and a time to pluck up what is planted—wisdom's acknowledgment of seasons and cycles that Job's tree metaphor invokes. The tree's hope rests on cycles; humans break the cycle at death.

Alma uses the tree and seed as an extended metaphor for faith that grows and bears fruit. Where Job sees the tree's hope as biological and human hope as absent, Alma reclaims the tree image as emblem of spiritual growth grounded in testimony.

commentary.historical_context: The ancient Near Eastern world knew well the regenerative capacity of certain trees. The terebinth (turpentine tree) and oak were common in the Levantine landscape, and both exhibit the sprouting-from-stump behavior Job describes. This is not mystical observation but practical knowledge any farmer or shepherd would possess. The tree metaphor would have resonated with readers familiar with coppicing—the intentional cutting of trees to encourage new growth, a practice used for fuel and timber management. Job's use of the tree is therefore scientifically accurate in its observation while theologically devastating in its implication: what nature grants freely to vegetation, the Creator denies to the human who bears His image.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma's extended botanical sermon in Alma 32 directly engages this imagery. Alma invites listeners to experiment upon the word as upon a seed planted in the heart—ground from which hope will grow. Where Job's tree is mute evidence of hope denied to humans, Alma's tree becomes a teaching tool for spiritual growth and the hope that comes through faith in Christ.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 88:25-29 teaches that all things are bound together by the law that sustains them. Job's tree operates within that law; it is bound to its future growth by the natural law God ordained. The tragedy is that Job sees humans as exempt from that binding law—released from it at death.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The tree of life appears in temple symbolism and in the vision granted to Lehi (1 Nephi 11). That tree's fruit heals and sustains; it is rooted in the water of life. Job's naturalistic tree, bound by mere biology, is implicitly compared with the transcendent tree of life that offers what mortal trees cannot: eternal sustenance and hope beyond the grave.

commentary.christological_typology: The tree cut down yet sprouting anew prefigures Christ's descent into death and subsequent resurrection. Where Job sees only the finality of human death, the Restoration reveals that the very image he uses—death that is not final, cutting that leads to greater growth—is the pattern of redemption. Christ is the Tree cut down who brings forth new life not merely for Himself but for all humanity. The tree's hope, denied to humans in Job's logic, is restored through the Atonement.
commentary.application: Job's argument here is intellectually honest and emotionally devastating. When suffering is intense, we feel the force of his observation: trees persist; humans vanish. But the verse invites us to ask what Job will not yet ask—what if the same God who granted the tree its resilience has a different plan for humans? The later scriptures answer: resurrection, judgment, and eternal life. For modern covenant members, this verse challenges us to hold two truths: (1) mortality is real and its sting is not minimized, and (2) we are not abandoned to the tree's fate. We are invited to receive a hope not rooted in biology but in covenant, in the binding God makes with us through Christ.

text_kjv: Though the root thereof wax old in the earth, and the stock thereof die in the ground;

commentary.narrative: Job intensifies the metaphor by imagining the worst possible scenario for the tree. The root grows old—ancient, exhausted, seemingly spent—buried deep in the earth. The stock (giz'a, the stump or main trunk) dies completely. It is not merely damaged or dormant; it dies. And it dies in the dust, the ground itself. The point is to remove every reason for hope by describing complete, utter death. The tree in verse 7 offered obvious hope because it had recently been cut down; the wood was still relatively fresh. But what if decades pass? What if the tree is so buried, so rotted, so aged that it seems impossible that anything could emerge? This verse extends the metaphor to its breaking point. The tree becomes a test case: if even in these extremes—old root, dead stump, buried in dust—something can emerge, then the tree's hope transcends all rational expectation. Job is building suspense. He is asking: can anything return from this?

word_study.meaning: To become old, to age, to grow senile or decrepit. Describes the process of aging and deterioration over time.
word_study.significance: The verb suggests not just age but weakness accompanying age. An old root has lost its vigor. The wood is brittle. Time itself seems to work against the tree's renewal.

word_study.meaning: The stump or main trunk of a tree, especially the part remaining after the tree has been felled or after years of decay. In this context, the visible, lifeless evidence of the tree's existence.
word_study.significance: The giz'a represents what remains—not the living tree but its corpse, so to speak. By verse 9, this dead stump will become the source of resurrection. The apparent contradiction is the crux of Job's argument about human death.

word_study.meaning: Dust, soil, earth; the substance of human mortality. Humans are formed from afar, and to afar they return. The term carries theological weight in the creation account.
word_study.significance: Job uses afar here to place the tree's death in the same realm as human death. Both tree and human are bound to the earth; both return to dust. Yet the tree's fate differs from the human's, which is Job's disturbing conclusion.

cross_references.connection: Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return—the human condition stated at the Fall. Job's image of the tree buried in dust invokes this fundamental reality of mortality.

The dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it—wisdom's acknowledgment that death is return to the earth. Job's tree lies in the dust; humans return to dust; the parallel frames the contrast.
Thou turnest man to destruction; again thou sayest, Come again, ye children of men—a prayer that acknowledges human fragility and the brevity of human life, themes Job will develop in verses 10-12.

The Book of Mormon speaks of death as the separation of body and spirit, and the body returning to its natural elements. This verse recalls that fundamental doctrine of mortality which Job experiences as absolute finality.

commentary.historical_context: Ancient observers would have known that buried, aged wood was not dead in the way that fire consumes it or rot completely destroys it. The wood hardens, becomes dense, loses moisture—but the cellular structure remains capable of response to water. In arid regions like the ancient Near East, a tree could remain dormant for years until rain came. Shepherds and farmers would have observed that even apparently dead stumps, if water reached them through an underground source (as happens in limestone regions where water percolates below), could produce shoots. Job's botanical knowledge is sophisticated. He is not describing miracle but observed natural resilience that he finds theologically troubling when compared to human fate.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 15:12-14 discusses the tree of life and the path to it, using botanical imagery to teach spiritual truth. Where Job's tree seems to offer a temporal hope that humans lack, Nephite teaching reclaims botanical metaphor to speak of the eternal tree whose fruit gives life to those who partake.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 29:24-25 speaks of the death of bodies and their resurrection—a doctrine that reverses Job's despair. The body returns to dust, but it is not lost. The covenant of resurrection means that death is not final for the covenant people, just as it is not final for Job's tree.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches the plan of salvation, which includes resurrection and exaltation. The tree buried in dust, seemingly dead, yet capable of resurrection, becomes a type of the human being who must pass through the grave but is promised resurrection through covenant.

commentary.christological_typology: The stump buried in dust awaiting resurrection prefigures Christ's burial in the tomb and His three-day resurrection. The 'death' described in verses 8 is not final; it is the prerequisite for the renewal described in verse 9. Christ's death in the earth is the condition for His resurrection and the resurrection of all humanity.
commentary.application: Verse 8 asks us to contemplate death in its most extreme form—not sudden death but slow decay, burial, the passage of time that seems to erase all traces. Modern members facing long-term grief or loss know this verse's power. The loss feels permanent, final, impossible to recover from. But the verse does not end here. Job's logic is built on the assumption that the tree, despite all evidence, will recover. For us, the Resurrection is not biological accident but covenant promise. We face death with the knowledge that God has made a binding commitment (tiqvah) to raise us up.

text_kjv: Yet through the scent of water it will bud, and bring forth boughs like a plant.

commentary.narrative: The reversal is absolute. The dead stump, buried in dust, aged beyond recovery, is not only alive but conscious in a profound sense: it can smell water. The phrase 'at the scent of water' (me-reach mayim) is extraordinary. The tree does not require water actually present; it responds to the mere scent of approaching moisture. This speaks to a latent aliveness that transcends all visible appearance. The stump has been dead to all observation, yet beneath the ground, in the wood itself, the capacity to detect, to respond, to awaken remains intact. The verbs shift to vitality: yafriach (it will bud, blossom, flourish) and ve-asah qatsir kemo nata (it will produce new branches like a freshly planted tree). The comparison is striking—the ancient stump will be indistinguishable from a young plant. Not merely recovering but appearing as if new-born. This is resurrection language. The tree does not merely survive; it is reborn. And the trigger is water—the biblical symbol of life, Spirit, and covenant. Yet Job is describing this as a natural phenomenon, a fact observable in the material world. This is the crux of his argument: nature itself proves that apparent death is not final—for trees. But not for humans.

word_study.meaning: Scent, smell, odor—the sensory perception of something distant or not yet visible. In Hebrew, reach can also mean 'smell' in the sense of 'perceive' or 'sense intuitively.'
word_study.significance: The tree perceives water before the water arrives. This suggests a sensitivity, an awareness, a responsiveness that exceeds the merely mechanical. The tree is not merely reacting to stimulus already present; it is responding prophetically, as it were, to what is coming. The Covenant Rendering captures this: 'at the scent of water' implies the tree's readiness, its attunement to what approaches.

word_study.meaning: To bud, blossom, break into flower; to flourish and produce. Describes the exuberant emergence of life and growth.
word_study.significance: The verb is active, vigorous, exuberant—not merely survival but flourishing. The dead stump does not merely send up weak shoots; it blooms, flowers, manifests full vitality.

word_study.meaning: Harvest, or by extension, branches or produce gathered from a tree. The literal sense is that which is reaped or cut; the extended sense is the productive output of the tree.
word_study.significance: The tree will not only live again; it will be productive, bearing the fruit and branches that mark a living, fruitful tree. The parallel 'like a young plant' emphasizes that this is not merely recovery but renewal—the old stump becomes functionally identical to a sapling.

word_study.meaning: A plant, sapling, or young planting—literally, that which is planted and is still in its youth and vigor.
word_study.significance: The comparison is miraculous. The ancient stump, buried in dust, will appear as a nata—a young plant bursting with the vigor of new life. This is not repair but transformation. The old becomes young again.

cross_references.connection: The living water Jesus offers to the Samaritan woman becomes a spring welling up to eternal life. Job's tree responds to water with biological renewal; the Gospel offers spiritual renewal through the living water of Christ.

The Lord shall guide thee continually, and satisfy thy soul in drought, and make fat thy bones; and thou shalt be like a watered garden—a promise that inverts Job's separation of human from tree. The righteous human becomes like the watered garden, the flourishing tree.

The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree, grow like a cedar in Lebanon—the human who trusts in God manifests the tree's vitality and longevity. The psalmist claims for humans the very hope Job denies them.
Nephi's vision shows the tree of life, whose fruit is white, pure, and desirable—the resurrected, renewed life offered through Christ, the antitype of Job's naturally renewed tree.

The word, nourished by faith like a plant nourished by water, grows into a tree whose fruit is sweet and desirable—Alma's spiritual botanizing directly addresses and reverses Job's despair by showing that humans can bear spiritual fruit if they receive the living water of the word.

commentary.historical_context: The scent of water would be recognizable to ancient Near Eastern peoples living in semi-arid regions. A human can smell rain approaching; animals can sense it; plants respond to changes in humidity and soil moisture even before water is visibly present. Roots deep in the earth would respond first, drawing up moisture before the surface shows any sign of water. The ancients, observing this, would understand that the apparently dead stump possessed hidden responsiveness. The image is precise: the latent life beneath the surface exceeds what the eye can perceive. This is observable fact used for theological argument.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 12:10-11 teaches that the light of Christ 'enlighteneth every man that cometh into the world.' Like the tree sensing water from afar, humans possess an inner light, an attunement to truth, that Job denies. The Book of Mormon reclaims for humans the sensitivity and responsiveness that Job grants only to trees.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 88:6-12 speaks of light and truth emanating from God, by which all things are sustained and governed. The tree's response to water reflects this cosmic law of responsiveness. Humans, made in God's image, possess this responsiveness infinitely more than the tree.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The waters of the baptismal font represent the cleansing and life-giving power of covenant. Just as the tree responds to the scent of water, the covenant member responds to the waters of baptism, which are the token of the water of life administered through the Atonement.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the water of life. The tree's responsiveness to water—its capacity to perceive, respond, and be renewed—images forth humanity's capacity to perceive Christ and to be renewed through covenant with Him. Where Job sees only the tree's biological renewal, the Gospel reveals the tree's renewal as a type of spiritual resurrection through Christ.
commentary.application: For modern members, verse 9 offers both challenge and comfort. The challenge: Job describes the tree as possessing a sensitivity, an attunement, a responsiveness that humans in his view lack. Are we, made in God's image, less attuned to the source of life than a tree stump? The comfort: Latter-day revelation tells us we are not. We possess the gift of the Holy Ghost, the still small voice, the ability to sense the presence of God, the living water of the Atonement. We are invited to be like the tree—to sense where the water is, to grow toward it, to be renewed by it. This requires sensitivity, attunement, and trust that renewal is possible even when outward appearance suggests final death.

text_kjv: But man dieth, and wasteth away: yea, man giveth up the ghost, and where is he?

commentary.narrative: The pivot is devastating. Ve-gever yamut va-yechelash—but a strong man dies and is weakened, lies down powerless. The Hebrew word gever (strong man, warrior) is chosen deliberately. Not a weak person, not someone already fragile, but a man in his strength, in his prime. And he dies. He becomes weak. The sequential verbs describe a process: death, then deterioration, then the final release of the spirit. Va-yigva adam ve-ayyo—and a human expires, and where is he? The question hangs in silence. There is no answer because there is no one to answer. The person is not merely absent; the question itself becomes meaningless. 'Where is he?' cannot be answered because he is nowhere. He is not in any place. He does not persist. This verse articulates the nothingness that death, to Job, represents. The contrast with verse 9 could not be starker. The tree, after death, blooms like a fresh plant. The human, after death, ceases to exist, and the question 'where is he?' receives no answer. Job is not being hyperbolic. He is stating what appears to him to be an observed fact: humans disappear at death in a way that trees do not.

word_study.term_english: strong man, warrior, person of strength
word_study.meaning: A strong man, a man in his prime, a warrior or mighty one. Contrasts with 'ish (man) or 'adam (human). Gever emphasizes strength, power, and vital force.
word_study.significance: Job's choice of gever rather than simply 'ish is crucial. The strongest, most powerful human still dies. There is no hierarchy of human worth that protects the strong from death. The very word that should denote resilience becomes the subject of inevitable death.

word_study.meaning: To die, to cease living, to depart from life. In the qal form, it is simple statement of fact.
word_study.significance: The verb is not softened or metaphorized. Death is death. The tree dies; the human dies. Yet the consequences differ utterly.

word_study.term_english: wastes away, is weakened, lies powerless
word_study.meaning: To be weak, to become faint, to lose strength, to languish or pine away.
word_study.significance: The verb describes a process of deterioration—strength ebbing, vigor fading. The strong man becomes weak. The process is not instantaneous but involves diminishment and loss.

word_study.term_english: gives up the ghost, expires, breathes his last
word_study.meaning: To expire, to breathe one's last, to perish, to die (often of a difficult or painful death).
word_study.significance: The verb emphasizes the moment of death, the final severance. It often carries connotations of struggle or difficulty. The expiration is not passive but an event, a final breath.

word_study.meaning: And where is he? The interrogative 'ayyo (where?) combined with the third-person masculine singular 'o (he). The question expects no answer.
word_study.significance: This is not a rhetorical question expecting a hopeful answer. It is a question that receives only silence. The human person is gone—not transformed, not sleeping, not waiting for renewal, but absent. 'Where is he?' means 'He is nowhere.' This is the void that death, to Job, represents.

cross_references.connection: And the Lord God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life—the creation of the human is the infusion of life-breath (neshamah). Job's image of death as the cessation of that breath reverses the creative act.
O spare me, that I may recover strength, before I go hence and am no more—the psalmist's prayer echoes Job's question: before I am no more, let me recover. Death means being 'no more.'

It is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment—New Testament doctrine that accepts death as universal but promises what comes after. Job sees only the 'once to die' without the resurrection.

And then shall the spirits of the dead be led away into a state of happiness, which is paradise...or into outer darkness—the Book of Mormon answers Job's question 'Where is he?' with the doctrine of the spirit world and the persistence of identity beyond death.

The vision of the redemption of the dead reveals that the spirits of righteous humans who die remain conscious, engaged, and active in the work of the Lord—a direct answer to Job's 'where is he?' The person persists; he is not nowhere.

commentary.historical_context: Job's observation reflects the ancient world's struggle to find evidence of human persistence beyond death. Unlike the tree, which sends visible shoots, the dead human leaves no such evidence. The grave is sealed; the corpse decays; there is no return. Ancient Israelite thought (especially in the older strata of biblical religion) lacked the clear doctrine of resurrection that later Judaism would develop. Sheol was conceived as a place of shade and forgetfulness, not as a destination of conscious existence. Job is thinking within the older paradigm where death is final, where the grave is the end. His question 'Where is he?' reflects a genuine perplexity: the dead are gone, and there is no visible mechanism for their return.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 9:6-10 states that when the body has returned to dust and the spirit has departed to the world of spirits, the body can exist no more except through the resurrection of Christ. Job asks 'where is he?'; the Book of Mormon answers: 'The spirit departs to the world of spirits, which is a state of rest and peace' (Alma 40:12). The person is not nowhere but in a conscious state awaiting resurrection.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 45:41-42 teaches that Christ will come in glory and all the dead will hear His voice and come forth—their graves will be opened, and they will answer. The question 'where is he?' will be answered when the voice of the Son of God calls forth the dead.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches the plan of salvation, which includes resurrection and eternal life. The dead who have received temple ordinances are bound to the eternal family unit through the sealing power. They are not nowhere; they are sealed to those who remain, and they await the resurrection and the fulfillment of covenant.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's death on the cross was followed by the same apparent finality Job describes. The disciples asked in essence, 'Where is He?' when His body lay in the tomb. Yet Christ's resurrection is the answer to Job's question. Christ is the first fruits of the resurrection, proving that death is not the end, that the human person can return even from the grave, and that 'where is he?' receives an answer: 'He is risen.'
commentary.application: This verse expresses the existential terror of death with devastating clarity. When we have lost someone—a parent, a spouse, a child—we feel the force of Job's question. 'Where is he? Where is she?' The person we loved seems to have vanished, and there is no visible mechanism for their return, no scent of water awakening them, no new shoots emerging. Modern Latter-day Saints hold the answer that Job lacked: the Atonement promises resurrection and reunion. Our loved ones are not nowhere. They are in the spirit world, conscious and aware, waiting for the resurrection and the redemption of their bodies. We are sealed to them by priesthood authority. But the verse invites us to feel the rawness of Job's loss, to acknowledge that mortality is not minimized or softened by doctrine, and to recognize that our faith in resurrection is meaningful precisely because death is as final as Job describes it—until Christ answers and the tomb is opened.

text_kjv: As the waters fail from the sea, and the flood decayeth and drieth up:

commentary.narrative: Job shifts from human death to cosmic comparison. If the sea itself could lose its waters, if a river could dry up completely—then in that same impossible way, the dead remain dead. The comparison operates through hyperbole: the sea losing its water is nearly unthinkable, yet Job uses it as a measure of how long the dead remain dead. Azelu mayim minni yam—waters depart from the sea. Ve-nahar yecherav ve-yavesh—and a river dries up and is gone. The parallelism presents two scales: the vastness of the sea and the flow of a river. Both are sources of life, abundance, continuity. Both are made to disappear in this comparison. The idea is that just as these elemental forces of nature would have to reverse—the sea would have to empty, the river would have to cease—so the dead would have to reverse their condition. The comparison sets up the final statement of verse 12: until the heavens are no more, the dead will not awake. It is a way of saying 'never' while preserving a theoretical exception at the absolute end of time. Job is being rhetorical, but the rhetoric carries devastating force: death is as permanent as the permanence of water sources that sustain all life.

word_study.meaning: To go, to depart, to pass away, to be gone. Describes movement away, departure, disappearance.
word_study.significance: The verb suggests not exhaustion but departure—the waters do not diminish gradually but go away, cease to exist in their place. They are gone, departed.

word_study.meaning: Water, waters, liquid. In biblical thought, mayim is fundamental to life, fertility, and divine provision.
word_study.significance: The choice of water as the comparison element is theologically significant. Water sustains all life. The removal of water is the removal of the condition for life. Job uses water, the source of life, as the measure of the permanence of death.

word_study.meaning: To dry up, to become desolate, to be ruined. Often used of rivers, fields, or lands losing their water and fertility.
word_study.significance: The verb yachriv describes not merely the absence of water but the desolation that follows. The land becomes a wasteland. Applied metaphorically to the dead, it suggests a final desolation—the complete absence of the vitality that life represents.

word_study.meaning: To be dry, to be withered, to perish, to wither away. Can describe both the drying of water and the withering of vegetation.
word_study.significance: The parallel to yachriv emphasizes totality: the river dries up (yachriv) and is gone (yavesh). No trace remains. The land is dead and desolate. This is the finality Job ascribes to human death.

cross_references.connection: Art thou not it which hath dried the sea, made the waters of the great deep a way for the ransomed to pass over?—Isaiah invokes the image of the sea drying up as an act of divine power in the past, suggesting resurrection and redemption. Job uses the same image to describe permanence; Isaiah uses it to describe divine intervention.

The floods have lifted up, O Lord...mightier than the noise of many waters, mightier than the mighty waves of the sea—the psalmist celebrates the permanence and power of the Lord over against the waters. Job ironically uses the permanence of waters as evidence against human permanence.

And I saw a new heaven and a new earth: for the first heaven and the first earth were passed away; and there was no more sea—in the ultimate restoration, the sea itself will be no more. Job's comparison (until the heavens are no more, the dead remain dead) points toward this final transformation.

All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field...but the word of our God shall stand for ever—the contrast between human transience (grass withering, flowers fading) and divine permanence. Job makes the opposite comparison: human transience exceeds that of water sources.

commentary.historical_context: The ancient Near Eastern world knew water sources as the markers of life and civilization. The Nile, the Euphrates, the Jordan—these rivers defined the limits of human habitation and fertility. The sea, though mysterious and dangerous, was known to be constant and vast. The image of the sea losing its waters would have seemed to ancient audiences as nearly apocalyptic—the reversal of the cosmic order. Job invokes the permanence and vastness of water sources to measure the permanence of death. His comparison would have resonated with audiences who understood water as both the source of life and the marker of the boundaries between the living and the dead (rivers often served as boundaries between lands of the living and lands of the dead in ancient cosmologies).

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 12:16-17 teaches that the sea shall bring forth its dead and the dry land its dead, and they shall be judged—the Book of Mormon echoes Job's imagery of water and dryness but transforms it through doctrine. The sea and the land do return their dead, but through resurrection and judgment, not through natural processes.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 29:23-24 teaches that the earth shall pass away, and every corruptible thing shall be consumed, and every immortal thing shall be quickened and remain. Job's comparison of the drying up of the sea as a measure of eternity points toward the final transformation when the earth itself will be renewed, and the dead will be raised.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The baptismal font in the temple rests upon twelve oxen, representing the twelve tribes, and is filled with water—symbolic of the waters of life and resurrection. Job's image of water sources is redeemed in temple symbolism, where water becomes the sign of covenant, cleansing, and the promise of eternal life.

commentary.christological_typology: The drying up of waters, which Job uses to describe final death, is inverted in the Gospel. Christ is the living water, and through Him the waters of life flow to all who believe. The comparison suggests that just as water is permanent and essential to life, so Christ is the permanent source of life, and through Him, resurrection is assured. Where Job sees only the permanence of natural law leading to death, the Gospel reveals a more permanent law—the law of resurrection through Christ.
commentary.application: Job's use of water sources as the measure of permanence reveals his despair's sophistication. He is not making an emotional argument; he is appealing to the most fundamental realities of nature—the constancy of seas and rivers, the necessity of water for life, the unthinkable reversal it would take for them to disappear. When we face profound loss, we might feel similarly: that the dead are as 'gone' as water departing from the sea, that their return is as impossible as the permanent drying up of every water source on earth. Yet Latter-day revelation teaches that what seems impossible by natural law—the resurrection of the dead—is accomplished by grace through Christ. Our faith in resurrection is not naive optimism but a trust that divine law transcends natural law, and that Christ has already overcome death, making the impossible actual.

text_kjv: So man lieth down, and riseth not: till the heavens be no more, they shall not awake, nor be raised out of their sleep.

commentary.narrative: Job's argument reaches its conclusion. Ve-ish shakhav ve-lo yaqum—and a man lies down and does not rise. The finality is stated without qualification or hope. The verb shakhav ('to lie down,' 'to sleep') becomes the governing metaphor for death. And then the temporal limit: ad bilti shamayim—until the heavens are no more. As long as the sky exists, as long as the cosmos continues, the dead will not awaken. Lo yaqitsu—they will not awake. Lo ye'oru mi-shenatam—they will not be roused from their sleep. The parallelism is stark: awake/rouse, sleep/sleep. Death is sleep without waking, slumber from which no morning comes. The metaphor is simultaneously gentle (sleep) and terrifying (eternal sleep). The passage of time is irrelevant. A hundred years, a thousand years, ten thousand ages—nothing changes. The dead remain dead. The phrase 'until the heavens are no more' is theologically ambiguous. Later interpreters would read in it a hidden hope: if the heavens pass away, perhaps then the dead awake. But in Job's context, this is not hope; it is rhetorical excess. 'Until the heavens are no more' means 'forever,' because the heavens are eternal. Job is denying resurrection and reducing hope for the dead to meaninglessness. Yet in the Restoration, we find that the heavens do not remain unchanged forever. The earth itself will be renewed, transformed into a terrestrial or celestial sphere, and the dead will be raised. Job's very image—the passing away of the heavens—becomes the sign of the resurrection.

word_study.meaning: To lie down, to sleep, to recline, to rest. Can denote literal sleep or the sleep of death, or sexual relations. Here, it means the final lying down of death.
word_study.significance: The verb governs the entire image. Death is presented as sleep—which is comforting but also deceptive, because this sleep has no waking. The metaphor of death as sleep appears throughout the Bible and becomes a Christian commonplace, but Job darkens it by denying the resurrection that would be the waking.

word_study.meaning: To rise, to stand up, to awake, to arise. Often used of resurrection in later biblical literature.
word_study.significance: The denial is explicit: ve-lo yaqum ('and he does not rise'). The verb that will later mean resurrection is here explicitly denied. Job is not merely saying the dead are absent; he is saying they do not experience the rising/awakening that resurrection would entail.

word_study.meaning: To awake, to wake up, to be roused from sleep. Implies transition from sleep to wakefulness.
word_study.significance: The verb is explicitly about transition, about the breaking of sleep. Job denies this transition will happen. The dead will remain asleep, unroused, unchanged.

word_study.meaning: To awake, to wake up, to stir, to rouse. Often means to rouse to action or consciousness.
word_study.significance: The parallel to yaqits emphasizes totality. Not only will they not awake; they will not be roused. No force, no event, no intervention will disturb their sleep until the heavens pass away.

word_study.meaning: Until, up to, as far as. Marks a temporal limit or boundary.
word_study.significance: The 'ad' is the crux of the ambiguity. 'Until the heavens are no more'—this could mean 'forever' or it could leave open the possibility that when the heavens do pass away, something changes. Job intends forever; later tradition reads it as leaving hope.

cross_references.connection: But Christ is risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept...for as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive. Paul directly contradicts Job's denial: the dead do awake, through Christ.

For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so them also which sleep in Jesus will God bring with him...and the dead in Christ shall rise first. This is the answer to Job's question: the sleepers will awake through the power of Christ.

And many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt. Late-period Judaism directly addresses Job's despair, proclaiming that those who sleep in dust shall awake.

The Book of Mormon teaches that the spirit of man is removed to a state of rest and peace, awaiting the resurrection when the soul and body are reunited. Job's 'sleep' is reinterpreted as a state of waiting and rest, not as unconscious oblivion.

The vision of the degrees of glory reveals that the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God and shall come forth—they that have done good unto the resurrection of life. Job's denial of resurrection is answered by the revelation that Christ's voice awakens the dead.

The heavens shall pass away with a great noise, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat, and the earth also and the works that are therein shall be burned up...nevertheless we, according to his promise, look for new heavens and a new earth. The heavens do pass away, and when they do, resurrection follows—exactly the reversal of Job's logic.

commentary.historical_context: The language of sleep for death was common in the ancient Near East. Egyptian tomb inscriptions speak of eternal sleep; Homer describes death as sleep without waking. The metaphor is both comforting (suggesting peace rather than conscious torment) and terrifying (suggesting absence and finality). Job's use of the metaphor, combined with his denial of awakening, represents one of the deepest expressions of despair in ancient literature. He is not declaring that death is the end because resurrection seems impossible; he is declaring that the dead will not rise as a fact about the nature of death and time. The phrase 'until the heavens are no more' invokes the permanence of the cosmic order. In ancient thought, the heavens were eternal, unchanging, the marker of time's continuity. To say 'until the heavens are no more' is to say 'forever,' because the heavens are understood as permanent.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 9:6-13 teaches that Christ comes in the fulness of time to bring about the resurrection and redemption of the dead. The dead are not left sleeping; through Christ, they awake. 'This is the plan of salvation unto all men, by reason of the atonement of Christ' (2 Nephi 9:12). The entire plan of salvation is the answer to Job's despair.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 29:26-27 teaches that the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God and shall come forth—they who have done good unto the resurrection of life and they who have done evil unto the resurrection of damnation. Death is not eternal sleep; it is a temporary state from which all shall awake through the power of Christ. Doctrine and Covenants 84:100 promises that at the resurrection, the mortal body is quickened and made alive—the sleep ends.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment teaches the plan of salvation, including the resurrection and eternal life made possible through Christ's Atonement. The temple veil represents the veil between mortality and eternity; through the sealing ordinances, families are bound together beyond the veil. Death is not the final separation; the sealed dead remain part of the family unit and await resurrection and exaltation.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's resurrection is the answer to Job's denied awakening. Christ rose on the third day, the firstfruits of them that slept. His resurrection is not merely His own triumph; it is the guarantee of the resurrection of all humanity. Where Job sees sleep without waking, Christ is the one who awakens from the dead and raises all who believe in Him. The 'passing away of the heavens' that Job uses as a measure of eternity becomes, in Revelation 21, the sign of the new creation and the resurrection. Job's very image is inverted: the heavens do pass away, and when they do, the dead are raised and the righteous inherit a renewed earth and new heavens.
commentary.application: This final verse of Job's argument is perhaps the most devastating. Job reduces the human person to 'he lies down'—undignified, passive, asleep. And he will not rise. Not because he is unworthy, not because God has abandoned him, but because that is the nature of death itself. He will sleep, and he will not awake, until the impossible occurs (the heavens vanishing), which means never. For modern members, this verse invites us into the depth of Job's despair so that we might understand what our faith means. We do not have an answer that minimizes death or pretends it is not what it is. We have something more: the testimony that Christ has risen, that He is the power by which the dead are raised, and that through covenant, we are connected to His resurrection. When we lose someone, we can sit with Job in the recognition that death is real, that the dead do lie down and do not rise by their own power. But we can also testify that Christ is risen, and that through Him, the sleeping dead shall awake. This is not false comfort; it is the comfort of the Atonement, purchased at infinite cost and offered freely to all.

text_kjv: O that thou wouldest hide me in the grave, that thou wouldest keep me secret, until thy wrath be past, that thou wouldest appoint me a set time, and remember me!

commentary.narrative:
Job shifts from asking whether death leads to resurrection (verse 12) to expressing an audacious wish: if he must die, could God hide him in Sheol as a temporary refuge? The phrasing "O that thou wouldest" (mi yitten, literally "who would give") indicates Job knows this is not a promise but an impossible longing. Critically, Job reimagines the underworld not as Hades-like torment but as asylum—a place where divine wrath cannot penetrate. This is theologically radical: Sheol becomes not punishment but protection. Job's desperation has evolved into a kind of prayer, albeit one framed as wishful thinking rather than confident petition.

The progression in this verse is significant: hide (protect), conceal (hide until anger passes), appoint a time (give him a future), and remember (restore him to relationship). Each verb stacks another layer of hope onto an impossible situation. Job is essentially negotiating with God: "If you're angry with me now, couldn't you simply hide me until it passes? Set a date. Then remember me." The verb "remember" (yizkhereni) carries covenant weight in Hebrew—to be remembered by God is to be restored to relationship, to be brought back into the narrative of the living. Job is asking for remembrance after death, which borders on resurrection faith, though he frames it as mere wishful thinking.

word_study.meaning: to hide, conceal, store up, preserve in secret. The root suggests protection and preservation, not merely hiding. Related to the noun tzipun (treasure, what is hidden and kept safe).
word_study.significance: Job uses language of preservation rather than mere concealment. Sheol becomes a sanctuary where God's anger cannot reach—a revolutionary reimagining of the underworld as protective rather than punitive. The TCR translation emphasizes this nuance: 'hide me' connotes safe-keeping.

word_study.meaning: a fixed statute, appointed time, prescribed limit, ordinance. The word carries the sense of something decreed and immutable—a divine appointment or boundary that cannot be moved.
word_study.significance: Job asks God to set a choq for his resurrection—a scheduled return to life. This is not arbitrary; it is a formal divine decree. The term suggests that resurrection, if it comes, would not be random grace but a constituted appointment, almost legal in its formality. In Latter-day Saint understanding, this echoes the concept of a set time for resurrection.

word_study.meaning: to remember, to bring to mind, to act on behalf of someone. In covenant language, 'to remember' means to maintain relationship and fulfill promises. The object of divine remembrance is chosen, preserved, and restored.
word_study.significance: This is the climactic verb. In Hebrew biblical theology, God's remembrance is transformative—it signals restoration and renewal. Job's ultimate hope rests not on his own power but on God's decision to remember him. This foreshadows New Testament concepts of resurrection through divine remembrance and presages LDS teaching about God knowing and remembering each soul.

word_study.meaning: anger, wrath, nostril (the nostril being the seat of anger or breath in Semitic physiology). The term emphasizes emotion and presence—anger that is present but can pass away.
word_study.significance: Job treats God's wrath as temporary and subject to expiration. This is a bold theological move: he frames divine justice as anger that burns and burns out, rather than eternal condemnation. It suggests a God whose emotional state can change, and whose justice is not eternal punishment but temporary correction.

cross_references.connection: Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me. Job's prayer for God to remember him echoes the psalmist's confidence in divine remembrance even in abandonment.
