commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern judicial systems, accountability worked through multiple channels: divine judgment (understood through fate, omens, or divine decree), legal proceedings (before judges or elders at the gate), and social shame (community pressure and ostracism). Job's complaint acknowledges that the first channel (divine retribution) is obviously not operating as his friends claim, and he now points out that the third channel (social accountability) is also failing—the wicked are too powerful to be shamed. Ancient Near Eastern wisdom assumed that the community's moral oversight was a real check on wickedness. Job's observation that this too fails is particularly corrosive to that worldview.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 41 teaches that 'wickedness never was happiness,' and that justice and mercy operate to bring souls to their proper state. Yet Job would ask: where is this in life? The Nephite prophets also confront the mystery of why the wicked sometimes prosper (see Helaman 6:35), acknowledging Job's real observational problem.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 64:10 states 'I, the Lord, will forgive whom I will forgive, but of you it is required to forgive all men'—placing the burden of judgment and retribution on the Lord, not on human agents. Job's friends assumed humans and God working together would enforce justice; the Restoration clarifies that only God can fully repay.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that justice and mercy operate through covenant, not through social power. Job's wicked man has no covenant relationship with God and receives no confrontation from the community precisely because his power is unconverted—it is not held in trust under covenant. The absence of both divine and social accountability springs from his standing outside the covenant community.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the one who will ultimately declare the wicked's way to their face and repay them for what they have done (see Revelation 20:12-13). Job's rhetorical question—'Who shall declare...? Who shall repay?'—finds its answer in Christ as judge. The fact that no earthly agent confronts the wicked in Job's day points to the necessity of a divine judge who alone can see all ways and render perfect recompense.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse challenges the assumption that visible earthly success and lack of social accountability indicate divine approval. Many who prosper by wickedness never face public confrontation. The lesson is not to assume that visible justice will come to the wicked in this life, and therefore not to base our faith in God's justice on whether we see it operating immediately around us. Rather, we trust in a judgment that transcends social visibility. Additionally, the verse reminds us that our responsibility is not to wait for social pressure to stop wickedness, but to speak truth—gently, with love, but clearly—to those whose conduct is wrong. The community's silence in Job's observation is a moral failure.

text_kjv: Yet shall he be brought to the grave, and shall remain in the tomb.

commentary.narrative: The cruelty of Job's argument deepens. Not only does the wicked man escape confrontation in life, but he escapes it in death as well—and even receives honor. The Hebrew text (as clarified by the Covenant Rendering) suggests that the wicked man is brought to his grave in a proper funeral procession, with his burial mound tended and guarded. This is not the horror of a forgotten grave or an unburied corpse. The wicked man dies peacefully and is buried with dignity. In the context of Job's argument, this is devastating because it contradicts any sense of poetic justice or divine repayment.
commentary.narrative_continuation: In the ancient Near Eastern worldview, a proper burial was essential—an improper death (dying shamefully, being left unburied, having one's grave desecrated) was a curse and a sign of divine disfavor. Job's friends would have expected the wicked man to die badly, to be buried hastily or shamefully, to have his name and memory blotted out. Instead, Job says, he is given a hero's funeral. The 'watch' kept over his burial mound suggests ongoing veneration or at least maintenance—his memory is preserved, his grave honored. The verb yishoqod ("watches" or "keeps watch") carries the sense of dedicated vigilance. Someone cares for his grave. This is the opposite of what retributive justice would predict.

word_study.meaning: to the graves/tombs he is carried. The verb yuval (נשא in sense of bearing, carrying) suggests a formal, ceremonial procession. The plural qevarot (graves) may indicate either multiple graves (as in a family tomb) or be a poetic plural emphasizing the finality of the grave.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's 'carried to his tomb in honor' captures the ceremonial dignity here. This is not a shameful death or hasty burial, but a formal, respectable funeral—the kind that would have been given to a person of status and wealth. For Job's argument, this undermines any expectation of visible punishment.

word_study.meaning: to keep watch, stand guard, keep vigil, remain on watch. The root shaqad conveys vigilant attention and dedication. It appears in Jeremiah 1:12 ('I will hasten my word to perform it') with overtones of watchfulness.
word_study.significance: Job's use of this term is ironic. Someone keeps watch over the wicked man's grave—perhaps his heirs, perhaps the community, perhaps out of fear or respect. The point is that his burial mound is not abandoned but tended. In a world where the graves of the righteous might be neglected or desecrated, the wicked man's grave is kept under watch. This is another reversal of expected justice.

word_study.meaning: heap, mound, stack. In the context of burial, it refers to the mound or tumulus raised over a grave, serving as a visible monument. The term emphasizes visibility and permanence.
word_study.significance: The gadish is not a modest, hidden grave, but a visible monument. Its 'mound' keeps the grave visible and commemorable. This contradicts any notion that the wicked man's memory will be blotted out. Instead, his grave is a landmark.

cross_references.connection: The Preacher observes a similar perplexity: 'I saw the wicked buried, who had come and gone from the place of the holy, and they were forgotten in the city where they had so done.' Ecclesiastes shares Job's observation that the wicked can die and be buried with apparent normalcy.

Abraham is 'gathered to his people' and 'buried...by Isaac and Ishmael his sons.' A proper burial among one's people is presented as a blessing. Job points out that the wicked receive even this apparent blessing.
Samuel is 'gathered together unto his people, and buried in Ramah, even in his house.' Samuel's burial is honorable. Job suggests that the wicked receive similar honor.

The Lord promises that the righteous will be 'brought out of obscurity and out of darkness.' Job's point is that the wicked do not remain in obscurity—their graves are visible, their memory preserved.

commentary.historical_context: Burial practices in the ancient Near East varied, but proper burial with a tomb or grave monument was a sign of honor and social status. The wealthy could afford elaborate tombs, and families maintained burial sites across generations. An "improper" death—sudden, violent, far from home, or followed by an unmarked grave—was considered a curse and a sign of divine disfavor. The powerful wicked man of verse 32 is not receiving an improper death; he is receiving the death of the honored. This would have struck ancient readers as a profound injustice, undermining their confidence in divine retribution. The 'watch' kept over his mound suggests not just a family inheritance of his grave, but ongoing social recognition of his importance.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon emphasizes that the wicked will face judgment, yet also acknowledges that in mortality, the wicked sometimes flourish and die in apparent peace. Mormon's commentary on the cycles of righteousness and wickedness among the Nephites confirms Job's observation that material prosperity and peaceful death are not reliable indicators of divine favor.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 75:5 teaches that 'the wicked shall be redeemed out of hell by the resurrection, after the thousand years of the reign of Christ.' The Doctrine and Covenants clarifies that while the wicked may die peacefully on earth, a fuller judgment awaits them after resurrection. Job's earthly confusion about the wicked man's honor is resolved only by understanding post-mortal justice.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that death and the grave are not the end of judgment—they are a transition to a more penetrating accounting before God. The wicked man's honored burial on earth is a pale thing compared to the judgment seat of God. The temple endowment sequence moves from the earthly to the celestial, revealing what mortals cannot see.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ descended into hell and rose from the grave, ensuring that death and the grave cannot hide anyone from divine justice. The fact that the wicked man is 'brought to the grave' while Christ rose from it points to the ultimate reversal: Christ's resurrection proves that death is not the end of accountability. Those who die peacefully in wickedness will face the same risen Christ in judgment.
commentary.application: This verse is a sobering reminder that visible earthly justice—proper funerals, honored memory, financial success—are not reliable measures of divine approval or condemnation. We must resist the temptation to assume that because someone wicked prospers, God either does not exist or does not care. We must also resist the temptation to assume that because someone righteous suffers, God has abandoned them. Our confidence must rest not in visible earthly outcomes but in faith in Christ's judgment, which transcends death and the grave. For those who have lost loved ones to injustice, this verse acknowledges the reality that earthly justice sometimes fails—but it points us forward to a judgment that cannot be evaded.

text_kjv: The clods of the valley shall be sweet unto him, and every man shall draw after him, as there are innumerable before him.

commentary.narrative: Job now universalizes his argument, moving from the particular case of the wicked man to the human condition itself. The image of clods of earth being 'sweet' (pleasant, gentle) to the wicked man in death is remarkable—it inverts the typical ancient Near Eastern imagery of the grave as harsh, dark, and terrible. Instead of experiencing the grave as a place of punishment and suffering, Job says the wicked man simply dies gently, and even the earth that covers him is pleasant. This poetic inversion is crucial: Job is saying that even in death, the wicked man experiences no apparent retribution.
commentary.narrative_continuation: The second part of the verse shifts to a broader observation: 'All humanity follows in his path; those who went before him are beyond counting.' This is Job's most devastating point. Everyone dies. Countless multitudes have preceded the wicked man into the grave. And countless multitudes will follow him. The grave is the great leveler—death makes no distinction between the righteous and the wicked, between the honored and the shamed. All humanity shares this path. In this vision, death is not a punishment for the wicked man; it is simply part of the human condition, shared equally by all. If his death is supposed to be his recompense, then so is every human's death—a notion that contradicts any special judgment for the wicked.

word_study.meaning: sweet, pleasant, lovely. The root mataq conveys both literal sweetness and metaphorical pleasantness or agreeableness. In Hebrew poetry, 'sweet' often describes something desirable or comforting.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering captures the surprise here: 'The clods of the valley lie gently on him.' The grave is not presented as harsh punishment but as gentle rest. This is a radical inversion of typical judgment imagery. For the wicked man to experience the grave as 'sweet' contradicts the expectation that death should be bitter or bitter for him.

word_study.meaning: clods, lumps of earth, dirt. The term emphasizes the physical substance of soil—the raw material of the grave. 'Clods of the valley' suggests both the location of the burial (in a valley, not a palace) and the simple earthiness of human mortality.
word_study.significance: Even the raw earth that covers the wicked man is not harsh to him. Job is using the most basic image of burial—the dirt that fills the grave—to make his point. There is no torture, no torment, just the gentle weight of earth.

word_study.meaning: to draw, pull, drag, follow. The root meshakh conveys being drawn along a path, pulled toward a destination. In this context, it means all humanity is drawn toward the grave.
word_study.significance: Everyone is 'drawn' toward death—not by choice, but by necessity. The image suggests an inexorable force pulling all people in the same direction. The wicked man is not uniquely or specially drawn; he joins the universal procession.

word_study.meaning: before, in front of, in the presence of. Combined with 'no number' (ein mispar), it means 'an uncountable multitude who preceded him.'
word_study.significance: Job emphasizes the vastness of human mortality stretching back through time. Countless generations have already died. The wicked man is joining an endless procession of the dead. This sense of historical continuity undercuts any notion that his death is a special or particular judgment.

cross_references.connection: The Preacher similarly observes: 'The wise man's eyes are in his head; but the fool walketh in darkness: and I myself perceived also that one event happeneth to them all...As the fool dieth, so dieth also the wise man.' Both Job and Ecclesiastes confront the universal leveling of death.

The Psalmist cries: 'Remember how short my time is: wherefore hast thou made all men in vain? What man is he that liveth, and shall not see death?' The universal fact of human mortality that Job cites here is a cause of lamentation in the Psalms.

The New Testament affirms: 'And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment.' Job observes the universal appointment of death; Hebrews adds that death is followed by judgment—the very thing Job's friends promise but Job questions.

Alma teaches that 'the spirits of all men, as soon as they are departed from this mortal body...are taken home to that God who gave them life. And then shall it come to pass, that the spirits of those who are righteous are received into a state of happiness.' The Book of Mormon affirms post-mortal judgment, addressing Job's concern that death itself provides no visible recompense.

commentary.historical_context: The ancient Near Eastern worldview understood the grave as the place of Sheol or the Netherworld—a shadowy, weak realm where the dead existed in a diminished state. It was not typically conceived as a place of active torture (that concept develops later), but as a place of separation from life, light, and the presence of God. However, the idea that the grave might be 'sweet' or pleasant would have struck ancient readers as odd. The grave was generally viewed with apprehension. Job's inversion—suggesting that the wicked man experiences his grave as gentle rest—challenges the entire framework of poetic justice. Additionally, the observation that countless multitudes have preceded the wicked man into death reflects a sense of historical consciousness common in wisdom literature, which often meditates on the brevity of human life against the vastness of time.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 3:26-27 teaches that the wicked 'are cast out and consigned to an awful view of their own guilt and abominations.' Yet Job observes that in mortality, the wicked experience no such 'awful view'—they experience apparent peace. The Book of Mormon distinguishes between mortal experience and post-mortal awareness, which helps resolve Job's puzzle.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76 provides extensive imagery of post-mortal realms—the celestial kingdom, the terrestrial kingdom, the telestial kingdom, and outer darkness. Job's observation that death itself does not distinguish between the righteous and wicked points to the truth that the real differentiation comes after resurrection and judgment before God, not at the moment of death.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment teaches that the veil between mortality and post-mortality is penetrable only through covenant. The wicked man who has no covenantal relationship with God experiences death as mere sleep; the righteous who have made covenants understand death as a transition within a larger plan. Job sees only the sleeping; the temple reveals the awakening.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the resurrection and the life (John 11:25)—he breaks the universal pattern of death that Job describes. While all humanity 'follows in his path' to the grave, Christ alone exits the grave with power and authority, proving that death is not the final equalizer. His resurrection declares that there is a judgment that distinguishes between righteousness and wickedness, between those who are in covenant with him and those who are not. Job sees the universality of death; the New Testament reveals that Christ transcends it for the sake of those who believe in him.
commentary.application: This verse can be both deeply humbling and ultimately hopeful for modern covenant members. The humbling part: we are not exempt from mortality. We too will be drawn toward the grave as all humanity is drawn. Our riches, our status, our achievements do not exempt us from death. But the hopeful part, in light of the Restoration, is that our covenant relationship with God through Christ means that our death is not simply the end. We die as all humans do, but we die in covenant, expecting a resurrection and a judgment that will vindicate the righteous and condemn the wicked. Job's observation that the grave levels all people should teach us not to trust in earthly distinctions, but to place our hope in heavenly judgment and Christ's resurrection.

text_kjv: How then comfort ye me in vain, seeing in your answers there remaineth falsehood?

commentary.narrative: Job now delivers his devastating conclusion. After three rounds of arguments, he dismisses his friends' comfort as not merely inadequate but utterly false. The verse is structured as a final accusation: your comfort is vain (hollow, empty, insubstantial), and your answers leave nothing but falsehood. Job characterizes what his friends have said as hevel (vapor, breath, emptiness)—using the very word that will later define the book of Ecclesiastes and its vision of meaninglessness. Their words are as insubstantial as exhaled breath; they dissipate as soon as they are spoken. The friends have offered theology—a carefully reasoned doctrine of retribution—but Job has shown through evidence and argument that this theology cannot survive contact with reality.
commentary.narrative_continuation: Crucially, Job uses the word ma'al (treachery, covenant breach, unfaithfulness) to describe the character of their answers. This is not a casual insult; ma'al is a covenant term. By using it, Job elevates the problem from 'your arguments are weak' to 'your arguments constitute a breach of faith.' The friends came to comfort Job in his suffering (see Job 2:11), which was a righteous impulse. But instead of listening (as verse 2 suggests they did on the first day), they launched into speeches defending God's justice and implying that Job must have sinned. This was a betrayal of the covenant of friendship, a failure of the trust implied by their presence at his side. Job's final word is not that the friends are stupid, but that they are unfaithful—they have broken the covenant of compassion by substituting ideology for empathy.

word_study.meaning: comfort me with emptiness/breath/vapor. The root nacham conveys consolation, comfort, reassurance. Havel is the signature word of Ecclesiastes—it literally means 'breath' or 'vapor,' but metaphorically it means emptiness, insubstantiality, futility, and the transitory nature of all things.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering captures this: 'So how can you comfort me with empty breath?' Your words of comfort evaporate as soon as they are spoken. They have no substance, no staying power, no real power to console. Job is saying that the friends' attempted comfort is not merely wrong; it is fundamentally insubstantial. It cannot bear the weight of his suffering.

word_study.meaning: your answers, your responses, your replies. The root teshuva (turning) can mean both a response and a repentance or return. Here it simply means the words the friends have spoken in their speeches.
word_study.significance: Job is evaluating their entire argumentative enterprise. What remains of their answers, after he has exposed their flaws through observation and counterargument, is only ma'al—treachery and falsehood. Their attempts at theodicy have collapsed.

word_study.meaning: to remain, be left, be left over, survive. The sense is what is left standing after everything else has been stripped away.
word_study.significance: Job is saying that after all the arguing, after all the friends' elaborate theological positions have been challenged and undermined, only falsehood and betrayal remain. Their arguments do not survive scrutiny. This is a thorough rhetorical and logical victory for Job.

word_study.meaning: treachery, unfaithfulness, breach of faith, trespass, guilt. The root 'al conveys going beyond bounds, transgressing. Ma'al specifically denotes a breach of covenant or a violation of trust. It is used for unfaithfulness within relationships bound by covenant.
word_study.significance: This is the most cutting word in the verse. Job does not merely say the friends' answers are 'false' (sheqer), but that they constitute 'treachery.' They have violated the covenant of compassion that should exist between suffering person and comforter. By insisting on a theodicy that requires Job to have sinned, the friends have broken faith with Job in his moment of need. The use of ma'al elevates this from a theological dispute to a relational betrayal.

cross_references.connection: The friends initially 'sat down with [Job] upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great.' This was faithful covenant behavior. But once they began to speak, they broke that covenant of silence and compassion.
Proverbs teaches that 'there are precious treasures and oil in the dwelling of the wise.' But the friends' words are not treasures; they are vapor. True wisdom is valuable; their words are worthless.

The Preacher opens: 'Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher; vanity of vanities; all is vanity.' Job uses the same word (hevel) to describe his friends' comfort. Like Ecclesiastes, Job wrestles with the apparent meaninglessness that human explanation cannot resolve.

Isaiah promises: 'The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.' The friends' words are like grass that withers; they cannot stand under scrutiny. Only God's word has staying power.

The Lord teaches: 'reproving betimes with sharpness, when moved upon by the Holy Ghost; and then showing forth afterwards an increase of love toward him whom thou hast reproved, that he may know that thy faithfulness is stronger than the cords of death.' The friends have reproved Job without the increase of love. They have not kept faith.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern wisdom literature, the function of a comforter (nacham) was both to console the suffering and to help the sufferer understand their place within the cosmic order. The assumption was that understanding (theodicy) would bring comfort—that if someone understood why they were suffering, the suffering would become bearable. The friends fulfill one role (they show up, they sit with him), but fail at the deepest level: they offer an understanding (you must have sinned) that does not fit the reality (Job knows he has not sinned in proportion to his suffering). Job's charge of ma'al (covenant breach) suggests that the covenant of friendship and comfort requires not intellectual certainty, but emotional honesty. The friends cannot say 'I do not know why you suffer; let us suffer together and wait for God's answer.' Instead, they defend God's justice in a way that implicitly condemns Job. This violates the basic covenant of human solidarity.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mosiah 27, Alma the younger is struck dumb by an angel and falls into a comatose state. His father Alma does not argue about Alma's guilt; instead, he prays. The difference between Alma's father and Job's friends is that Alma's father does not insist on theological explanations—he simply prays and trusts God. The friends fail to do what Alma's father does: they exchange prayer and trust for argument and condemnation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 38:24-25 teaches: 'Let him that is among you without sin first cast a stone at her...And now, verily I say unto you, I, the Lord, will make a way for their escape.' The Lord explicitly warns against the kind of judgment the friends make—condemning the sufferer to justify God. Only the Lord may judge; human comforters must extend mercy.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches covenant relationships of mutual care and sustaining. The covenant of marriage, of fellowship in the priesthood, of discipleship in Christ—all these involve sustaining one another through difficulty. The friends' failure is a failure to sustain Job in his covenant relationship with God. Instead of helping him maintain faith despite suffering, they undermine his faith by implying he has broken covenant.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the ultimate 'comforter' (paraclete—one called alongside) who sustains us in suffering without offering false explanations. Christ does not explain to us why we suffer; he suffers with us and promises redemption through suffering. The friends offer explanation (theodicy); Christ offers presence and redemption. Christ is faithful (trustworthy, true to covenant) in a way the friends are not. He does not breach the covenant of compassion by insisting on human guilt; instead, he bears our guilt himself.
commentary.application: Job's final words are a warning and a teaching for modern Latter-day Saints. When someone we love is suffering, our first responsibility is faithfulness to the covenant of compassion, not intellectual defense of God's justice. The suffering person does not need our theodicy; they need our presence, our listening, our refusal to condemn them. Secondly, we must be willing to acknowledge that some suffering resists explanation—that God's ways are truly higher than our ways—and that faith can exist in the midst of mystery. Third, we must recognize that offering false comfort (reassurance that is not grounded in real understanding or hope) is a form of treachery. It is better to sit in silence with the suffering than to speak falsehood. Finally, Job's use of the covenant term ma'al teaches that there are covenants we make simply by being human, by entering into relationships of care. Breaking those covenants by substituting ideology for empathy is a serious transgression.

text_kjv: Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said,

commentary.narrative: This verse marks the third and final speech of Eliphaz the Temanite. Throughout the dialogue, Eliphaz has positioned himself as the most measured and philosophical of Job's three friends—the one who appeals to wisdom tradition and cosmic order rather than crude moralizing. The prologue to Job established that Teman was renowned for wisdom (Jeremiah 49:7 prophetically associates Teman with the counsel of the wise). Yet as this speech opens, something has shifted dramatically. Eliphaz's restraint has evaporated. The translator notes indicate that this speech "abandons his earlier restraint entirely." What we are about to read is not the careful elder but the frustrated prosecutor, willing to move from philosophical speculation directly to explicit criminal charges.
commentary.narrative_p2: The timing of Eliphaz's intervention is significant. Job has just finished his longest soliloquy (chapters 19–21), in which he proclaimed his confidence that his redeemer lives and dwelt on the prosperity of the wicked—a position that directly attacks the retributive theology Eliphaz represents. Job has also begun making declarations that cannot be ignored: he knows he is innocent, and he is willing to face God directly in judgment. For Eliphaz, this confidence in innocence is intolerable. If Job truly suffered and truly is innocent, then the entire framework of divine justice collapses. Eliphaz must therefore do what he has avoided for most of the dialogue: stop debating abstractions and start naming specific sins.
commentary.narrative_p3: The Hebrew phrase "wa-ya'an Eliphaz ha-Temani wa-yomer" ('then responded Eliphaz the Temanite and said') uses the verb 'anah, which means not merely to speak but to answer—to respond to something. Eliphaz is responding to Job's claim of innocence with an escalation. The reader who has followed the prologue knows that God himself has testified twice to Job's integrity (1:8 and 2:3, using the exact term tam—'blameless'—that Job and his friends now debate). Eliphaz's response, though he does not know this, amounts to a direct contradiction of God's own verdict.

word_study.meaning: to answer, to respond, to reply; implies responding to a charge or statement that precedes
word_study.significance: In the dialogue structure of Job, 'anah is used when speakers directly rebut what has come before. Eliphaz is not making an isolated philosophical statement but responding with escalating force to Job's declaration of innocence.

word_study.meaning: one who comes from or belongs to Teman, a region in Edom associated with wisdom tradition in the ancient Near East
word_study.significance: Teman's reputation for wisdom (referenced in Jeremiah 49:7 and Obadiah 8-9) means Eliphaz carries the weight of wisdom authority. His abandonment of measured rhetoric in this speech is therefore a profound failure of that tradition.

cross_references.connection: Eliphaz's first response, where he appeals to wisdom and personal experience. This third response shows how his confidence in the traditional framework has calcified into accusation.
Job's immediately preceding declaration of confidence in his redeemer and vindication. Eliphaz's answer is a direct rebuttal to Job's claim of innocence.
Teman's reputation for wisdom. Eliphaz embodies the wisdom tradition of the ancient Near East, yet this tradition fails to grapple with innocent suffering.
God's own assessment of Job as tam (blameless). The reader knows what Eliphaz does not: that God has already vindicated Job's integrity.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near Eastern wisdom tradition—particularly as preserved in texts like the Counsels of the Wise and Mesopotamian proverb collections—the role of the elder or wise counselor was to transmit proven knowledge about divine justice and human behavior. Teman, as an Edomite center of wisdom, would have been part of this international wisdom network. Eliphaz represents the orthodox position of this tradition: the gods (or God) maintain cosmic order through retributive justice. Suffering is punishment; righteousness is rewarded. This framework was not cynical—it was the best explanation available to ancient Near Eastern thinkers for why the world works as it does. Yet Job's experience contradicts it. Eliphaz's response is instructive: when faced with evidence that the framework fails, the defender of orthodoxy often escalates from rational argument to accusation. If the victim must be guilty (because the system is just), then we must discover the hidden crime.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains a similar dynamic in Alma 32:6-16, where Alma addresses those who have been 'compassed about by the bands of death' but refuses to condemn them as sinners. The Nephite tradition affirms that suffering does not automatically indicate sin, a principle that directly contradicts Eliphaz's framework.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:1-9 presents Joseph Smith in profound suffering while maintaining perfect integrity. The Lord's response (121:7-9) does not claim that suffering is punishment but rather affirms that 'all these things shall give thee experience, and shall be for thy good.' This inverts the retributive logic entirely—suffering is not payment for sin but educational material for growth.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant affirms that individuals can be in proper relationship with God (holy) while still experiencing profound trials. The endowment does not teach that holiness exempts one from suffering, but rather that covenant fidelity is maintained through suffering.

commentary.christological_typology: Eliphaz's accusation foreshadows the false charges brought against Christ. Just as Eliphaz looks at Job's suffering and concludes it must indicate hidden sin, the accusers of Jesus assumed His execution proved He was cursed by God (Galatians 3:13). Yet Christ, like Job, was innocent. The distinction between legal condemnation and actual guilt—central to Job's defense and to Christ's passion—is what Eliphaz cannot comprehend.
commentary.application: This verse invites us to examine how we respond when our theological frameworks encounter contradictory evidence. When someone we know to be righteous experiences devastating suffering, do we question the framework or question the person's actual righteousness? Modern members face this temptation: if someone loses a job, became ill, or experienced family dissolution, there is an impulse to attribute hidden sin. Verse 1 teaches us to recognize this moment—when we move from speculation to accusation, from philosophy to character attack—as the moment we have abandoned truth for the defense of a system.

text_kjv: Can a man be profitable unto God, as he that is wise may be profitable unto himself?

commentary.narrative: Eliphaz opens his third speech with what appears to be an irrefutable theological principle: Can a man be profitable to God? The immediate answer Eliphaz expects is no. God is transcendent, self-sufficient, and infinite. Human behavior cannot add to or diminish God's being or power. This principle is, in isolation, correct—and Eliphaz knows it. The Hebrew verb sakan ('to be of use, to be of service, to benefit') appears twice, establishing a contrast: the gaver (strong man, hero) cannot benefit God, but the maskil (the wise man, the one who acts with insight) benefits only himself.
commentary.narrative_p2: The structure of the verse is a syllogism disguised as a rhetorical question. The logic runs: (1) A man cannot profit God; (2) A wise man profits only himself; (3) Therefore, human righteousness cannot be motivated by benefiting God, and God has no reason to reward it. But here is where Eliphaz weaponizes truth. If God gains nothing from Job's piety, then God has no motive to shield Job from suffering simply because Job is pious. God must be punishing Job for something else. The conclusion is elegant and inexorable: hidden sin. Eliphaz has transformed a metaphysical truth (God's transcendence) into a justification for a causal claim (Job's hidden sin causes visible suffering).
commentary.narrative_p3: What Eliphaz does not consider—what his framework cannot accommodate—is that God might have purposes for suffering entirely unrelated to the reward-and-punishment calculus. God might permit suffering to deepen faith, to test integrity, to reveal character, or simply because a fallen world includes suffering that is not causally linked to individual sin. The book of Job is, in part, a refutation of the very principle Eliphaz begins with. God does care about human righteous—not because it profits Him, but because He is the kind of being who loves righteousness and desires relationship. Job's piety matters not because God needs it but because Job's faithfulness constitutes the content of the covenant. Eliphaz has the metaphysics right and the theology wrong.

word_study.meaning: to be of service, to be useful, to benefit, to be of advantage; in some contexts, 'to lodge' or 'to dwell,' but here clearly in the sense of pragmatic benefit
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering emphasizes that sakan connotes utilitarian value: does the man's piety give God something God did not have? The verb appears only here in Job, making this a deliberate theological statement by Eliphaz. He is asserting God's transcendent self-sufficiency.

word_study.meaning: one who acts with understanding, insight, or prudence; often used to describe wisdom or wise conduct; can also refer to a psalm or liturgical composition of instructive character
word_study.significance: The maskil is not merely intelligent but possesses practical wisdom (hokhmah paired with binah—understanding). Yet Eliphaz claims the maskil benefits only 'aleimu (upon himself). This dismissal of wisdom's social value is itself a failure of wisdom teaching.

word_study.meaning: a strong man, a mighty man, a hero; in the wisdom tradition, often connotes moral and physical strength
word_study.significance: Job is described throughout as a gaver—a person of strength and standing. Eliphaz's rhetorical question implicitly denies that Job's strength or moral stature has any value before God.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah's affirmation of God's transcendence and self-sufficiency: 'To whom then will ye liken me, or shall I be equal?' This supports Eliphaz's opening theological principle while deepening it beyond retributive calculus.

God's declaration: 'I will not reprove thee for thy sacrifices... For every beast of the forest is mine... If I were hungry, I would not tell thee.' God explicitly denies that He profits from human offerings, yet does not conclude (as Eliphaz does) that righteousness is therefore meaningless.

Elihu's echo of Eliphaz's argument: 'If thou sinnest, what doest thou against him?... Thy wickedness may hurt a man as thou art.' Yet Elihu adds nuance that Eliphaz lacks—that human sin affects human society, not God.

Isaiah 49 as cited in the Book of Mormon: the servant of the Lord labors without visible reward ('I have laboured in vain, I have spent my strength for nought'). Yet the covenant remains valid regardless of whether the work 'profits' the master.

King Benjamin teaches that God 'doth require that ye should do as I have done, or as your fathers have done, to keep the commandments of God'—not because God benefits, but because the covenant demands it. Obedience is intrinsic, not transactional.

commentary.historical_context: The ancient Near Eastern understanding of deity emphasized the transcendence and self-sufficiency of gods. Mesopotamian creation myths depict the gods as creating humanity partly to serve them—to perform temple work and offer sacrifices—because the gods cannot actually perform labor themselves. This creates a transactional relationship: humans work, the gods receive honor and sustenance, and in return protect their worshippers. Eliphaz, influenced by this wisdom tradition, assumes a similar transactional frame. Yet even within Mesopotamian thought, a parallel tradition emerges: the truly wise person recognizes that the gods' justice operates according to cosmic principle (ma'at in Egyptian thought, me in Sumerian), not according to barter. Eliphaz grasps the transcendence but not the covenantal dimension—the idea that God relates to humanity not through profit-and-loss but through promise and fidelity.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 9:20 presents a different framework: 'O how great the holiness of our God! For he knoweth all things, and there is not anything save he knows it.' Here, omniscience is paired not with transcendent indifference but with divine love. God knows all things and therefore knows Job's integrity—a knowledge that does not depend on Job's righteousness 'profiting' God.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:34-35 teaches that God 'gave unto them commandment, that they should love one another and that they should choose me, their Father; but behold, they are left to their own agency.' God does not command obedience because He profits from it but because He is establishing a relationship of love. This reframes the entire theological problem Eliphaz raises.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ceremony emphasizes that covenants are reciprocal—God promises, and the person commits to live according to divine principle. The relationship is not transactional (God gains something from our obedience; we gain something from God's blessing) but covenantal (God commits to uphold the covenant as we commit to live it). This transcends the profit-loss framework entirely.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's redemptive work cannot be understood through a profit-loss framework. Christ benefits nothing materially from His suffering; the Atonement is not a transaction but a covenant act—God's total commitment to relationship with humanity. Eliphaz's logic would suggest that if Christ suffered, He must have sinned. Yet the cross reveals that innocent suffering can be redemptive and purposeful in ways that transcend retributive economics.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members often think in transactional terms about righteousness: 'If I keep the commandments, I should be blessed; if I suffer, I must have done something wrong.' Verse 2 invites us to examine this assumption. Righteousness is not a financial transaction with God but a covenant relationship. Faithfulness may or may not result in material blessing, prosperity, or health in this life. The value of righteousness is intrinsic—it is the way of becoming like God—not instrumental (a way to obtain outcomes). When we find ourselves thinking, 'I kept the covenant, so I should be protected from this trial,' we are using Eliphaz's faulty logic. Instead, the covenant invites us to maintain fidelity precisely in uncertainty and suffering.

text_kjv: Is it any pleasure to the Almighty, that thou art righteous? or is it gain to him, that thou makest thy ways perfect?

commentary.narrative: Eliphaz drives home his opening point with a second rhetorical question, now directed at Job personally. The shift from 'a man' (v. 2) to 'you' (v. 3) personalizes the argument. Eliphaz asks: Does it give the Almighty pleasure that you are righteous? Does He profit if you make your ways blameless? The questions use the Hebrew chefets (desire, pleasure, delight) and betsa (profit, gain, advantage), echoing the sakan of verse 2 but now in explicitly emotional and transactional language. The Almighty (Shaddai) is contrasted with human righteousness (tsadaq) and human blamelessness (tamam).
commentary.narrative_p2: What makes verse 3 devastating—though Eliphaz does not realize it—is that he uses the exact language God used to describe Job in the prologue. In Job 1:8 and 2:3, God says of Job: 'Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth, a perfect [tam] and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil.' The term tam—blameless, perfect, complete—is God's own assessment of Job's integrity. Yet here Eliphaz uses the verb form tattem ('you perfect, you make blameless') to ask whether such perfection means anything to God. He has unwittingly invoked the very term God used to vindicate Job, only to argue that vindication is irrelevant.
commentary.narrative_p3: The deeper problem with Eliphaz's logic becomes apparent here. He is arguing that because God does not profit from Job's righteousness, God has no reason to value or protect it. But this inverts the actual metaphysics. If God truly is transcendent and self-sufficient, then any commandments God issues are not for God's benefit but for the covenant community's benefit. God commands 'Thou shalt not steal' not because God profits from honesty but because theft harms human society. God values righteousness not as payment but as the form of relationship He desires. By this logic, Job's righteousness is even more valuable to God precisely because it costs Job something (restraint, effort, sacrifice) while costing God nothing and therefore proving Job's genuine allegiance. Eliphaz cannot see this because he is locked within a transactional framework.

word_study.meaning: pleasure, desire, delight; that which gives satisfaction; can also mean 'will' or 'purpose'
word_study.significance: The question 'Is it chefets to the Almighty?' asks whether Job's righteousness gives God satisfaction or fulfillment. The term personalizes the transcendent God, yet in a way that undermines the question—if God is truly transcendent, does His satisfaction depend on human righteousness?

word_study.meaning: profit, gain, advantage, sometimes unjust gain or dishonest profit; in some contexts, 'to cut' or 'to divide'
word_study.significance: Betsa emphasizes material or practical advantage. The question 'Does he get betsa if you perfect your ways?' assumes a mercenary relationship—unless God gains something, He will not reward righteousness.

word_study.meaning: complete, whole, blameless, undefiled; the root tam- means 'to be whole' or 'to be complete'; tattem is the second-person verb form 'you make blameless'
word_study.significance: This is the crucial term. Job 1:1 describes Job as 'a perfect [tam] and upright man.' In 1:8, God affirms Job's integrity: 'a perfect [tam] man.' Now Eliphaz uses the verb tattem—asking whether Job's pursuit of blamelessness means anything. He is unknowingly invoking God's own judgment while denying its relevance.

word_study.meaning: the Almighty; often understood as 'God of the mountain' or 'God of the breast' (nourishing); emphasizes divine power and self-sufficiency
word_study.significance: Shaddai underscores that God is all-powerful and needs nothing. Yet the name is also used for the covenantal God who makes promises to Abraham (Genesis 17:1) and sustains His people. Eliphaz invokes the power without the covenant.

cross_references.connection: God's own description of Job: 'There is none like him in the earth, a perfect and an upright man.' Eliphaz's question implicitly denies the relevance of the very quality God affirmed.

God reiterates His assessment: 'There is none like him in the earth' and Job 'still he holdeth fast his integrity,' even after losing children, servants, and property. God clearly values Job's blamelessness, contrary to Eliphaz's argument.

The psalmist asks, 'LORD, who shall abide in thy tabernacle?' and then describes the righteous person—the tam (blameless) one. The psalm affirms that God does desire the righteous and welcomes them into His presence.
Moses teaches that God commands righteousness 'for thy good'—not God's good. This inversion directly refutes Eliphaz's assumption that God's commandments serve God's profit.

Alma teaches that Jesus will come forth 'to take upon him the transgressions of his people.' The atonement is not motivated by profit to God but by covenant love—God's freely chosen commitment to relationship.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern wisdom literature, the relationship between human conduct and divine response was understood as part of the cosmic order. However, there were two strands: the retributive strand (sin brings punishment, righteousness brings reward) and the covenantal strand (God commits to relationship regardless of fluctuating fortune). Eliphaz represents the retributive strand in its purest form, stripped of covenantal nuance. In Mesopotamian thought, the gods were understood to be dependent on human offerings and prayer—without humans, the gods would have no sustenance. This creates a transactional logic: humans serve the gods, gods protect humans in return. The Israelite covenant radically inverts this: God is self-sufficient and serves humanity through promise, not exchange. Eliphaz, despite being associated with Edom (not Israel), seems to operate within the wisdom tradition but has missed the covenantal dimension entirely.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 34:34-35 teaches that 'this life is the time for men to prepare to meet God' and warns against procrastination. Yet the logic is inverse to Eliphaz's: righteousness matters not because God profits from it but because it constitutes the soul's preparation for relationship with God. The value is spiritual, not transactional.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:41 teaches that 'the spirit and the body are the soul; and nothing is at the last, nothing is at the last, nothing is at the last, but that which is of God is of God and will remain of God.' Righteousness endures not because it profits God but because it aligns with the eternal nature of reality. God values what is good because God is good, not because God stands to gain.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the endowment, the initiate is brought before the throne of God. The transition is not earned through transaction but granted through covenant. The invitation to return to God's presence is predicated not on righteousness being profitable to God but on righteousness being the condition by which a person becomes capable of dwelling in God's presence—the ultimate good for the person, not for God.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's perfection (tamim) is not profitable to God in a transactional sense. Rather, Christ's blamelessness is the form of covenant relationship in its fullest expression. Christ does the will of His Father not to profit the Father but because perfect alignment with the Father's will constitutes perfect love. When Christ commands His disciples to 'be ye therefore perfect' (Matthew 5:48), He is not calling them to profit God but to become like God—to grow into the image of their Father.
commentary.application: Verse 3 invites a searching examination of motivation in covenant life. Do we keep the commandments to profit ourselves (seeking blessings, protection, prosperity)? Or do we keep them because righteousness is intrinsically valuable—because living in alignment with God is the good we seek? Modern Latter-day Saint culture sometimes frames obedience as transactional: 'Keep the Word of Wisdom and you will be healthy; pay tithing and you will prosper; attend the temple and your family will be strong.' These promises may be true, but they are not why the covenant is kept. The covenant is kept because we seek to become like God, to live in genuine relationship with Him, and to align ourselves with eternal truth. Verse 3 confronts us with Eliphaz's error: we cannot assume that if we are righteous, God must reward us materially or shield us from suffering. But neither should we conclude (as Eliphaz does) that righteousness is meaningless. It is supremely meaningful—precisely because it is not about profit.

text_kjv: Will he reprove thee for fear of thee? will he enter with thee into judgment?

commentary.narrative: Having established (in his mind) that God gains nothing from Job's righteousness, Eliphaz now moves to the logical consequence: God would never punish someone simply for being pious. The implied answer to both rhetorical questions is an emphatic no. Would God reprove Job for Job's piety? Absurd. Would God bring a God-fearing man into judgment? Of course not. The Hebrew ha-mi-yir'atkha yokhichekha ('is it from your fear/reverence that he reproves you?') uses the verb yir'ah (to fear, to reverence, to stand in awe of)—the very fear of God that is elsewhere identified as the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 9:10). Eliphaz is arguing that piety cannot be grounds for punishment.
commentary.narrative_p2: The second question—'Will he enter with thee into judgment?'—uses the legal language of mishpat (judgment, justice, lawsuit). To 'come with someone into judgment' is to bring them into court, to litigate against them. Eliphaz is asserting that a God-fearing person simply would not be subject to divine litigation. The logic appears airtight: if God repaid righteousness with blessing, why would He bring a righteous man into judgment? Yet here Eliphaz has made a fatal error. He is assuming that Job is being punished. He sees Job's suffering and works backward: God is bringing Job into judgment (implicitly punishing him), therefore Job must have done something to warrant it. The very premise—that suffering equals punishment—is what needs to be questioned.
commentary.narrative_p3: What Eliphaz cannot conceive is that God might have brought Job into judgment for a purpose other than punishment. In the prologue, God does indeed single out Job in a kind of 'judgment'—but not to punish him. God puts Job's integrity to the test precisely because it is genuine, and the test itself becomes the point. Job is being tried, but not tried as a defendant standing accused. He is being tested as someone whose faith God values enough to deepen. The distinction is not one that the retributive framework can accommodate. For Eliphaz, there are only two possibilities: reward or punishment. There is no category for testing, deepening, or the refinement of faith itself.

word_study.meaning: to reprove, to rebuke, to correct, to argue, to convince; in legal contexts, 'to reprove' someone of guilt
word_study.significance: The verb yakach carries both the sense of correction (a teacher reproving a student) and of legal accusation (proving someone guilty). Eliphaz assumes that if God were reproving Job, it would be for punishment—missing entirely the possibility of correction that aims at growth.

word_study.meaning: fear, reverence, awe, piety; the 'fear of the LORD' is a central concept in Hebrew wisdom, often meaning reverence, respect, or proper orientation toward God
word_study.significance: Yir'ah is what Job possesses (1:8: 'Job, that feareth God, and escheweth evil'). It is the foundation of wisdom and the mark of piety. Yet Eliphaz asks whether God would punish someone for this quality—inadvertently highlighting the absurdity of his own conclusion.

word_study.meaning: judgment, justice, law, legal case, ordinance; the execution or administration of justice; can refer to God's judgment or human legal proceedings
word_study.significance: Mishpat frames the interaction as a legal matter. To 'come into mishpat' with someone is to sue them, to take them to court. Yet the prologue uses the same language differently: God's testing of Job is a kind of judgment, but not a trial for crime.

cross_references.connection: Job says to his friends: 'Surely I would speak to the Almighty, and I desire to reason with God.' Job, contrary to Eliphaz's assumption, is willing to enter into judgment with God because he trusts his innocence.

'The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom.' This fundamental wisdom principle establishes yir'ah (fear of God) as the basis of all understanding—yet Eliphaz implies this fear is irrelevant to God.

Peter teaches that faith is 'tried' (tested) by fire, 'that the trial of your faith... might be found unto praise and honour and glory.' Testing is not punishment but a means of refining and demonstrating genuine faith.
'Whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth.' Correction is consistent with love, not with guilt. God corrects those He receives as sons, not as criminals.

The Lord tells Joseph Smith: 'If thou art called to pass through tribulation... know thou, my son, that all these things shall give thee experience, and shall be for thy good.' Testing aims at growth, not punishment.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern legal systems, judgment (mishpat) was a formal public proceeding. A person brought into mishpat faced either vindication or condemnation. The assumption that judgment equals condemnation was culturally embedded. Similarly, in the wisdom literature of the ancient Near East, the universe is imagined as a vast legal and moral order in which innocence and guilt are ultimately revealed and recompensed. To be brought 'into judgment' by the divine court meant one was accused of violating cosmic order. Eliphaz cannot imagine any other meaning. Yet Job, even in the ancient Near Eastern context, invokes a different understanding: that a person might be tested or tried by the divine in order to deepen integrity, not to punish violation.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 1:18-20, Nephi's father Lehi is 'much troubled in spirit' and brought into visionary judgment, seeing the judgment of God upon Jerusalem. Yet this is not punishment but revelation—God is not condemning Lehi but showing him something he needs to know. The judgment aims at transformation, not condemnation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:10 teaches that 'the Lord God hath spoken unto you... in judgment.' Yet the message that follows (D&C 1:11-19) is one of mercy, forgiveness, and covenant renewal. God's judgment and God's mercy are not opposites. God judges to correct and covenant, not merely to punish.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple includes a sequence of judgment and mercy. The candidate faces guardians and is tested, but not as a criminal facing trial. The sequence moves toward the throne of God, where the person is received rather than condemned. Testing confirms readiness; judgment leads to blessing.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ was brought into judgment before Pilate, yet was innocent. The cross appears to confirm the retributive logic: Jesus suffered, therefore He must be guilty. Yet the Atonement reveals a different truth—Christ's suffering is not punishment for His sin (He had none) but sacrifice for the sins of others. The form of judgment (suffering) is present, but the meaning is inverted. This parallels Job: Job is being tested in a form that looks like punishment, but the meaning is not retributive. Christ makes this inversion explicit and redemptive.
commentary.application: Verse 4 confronts us with a question: When we experience difficulty, hardship, or unexpected trial, how do we interpret it? Do we assume it must be punishment for hidden sin (Eliphaz's framework)? Do we assume our righteousness should have protected us (Eliphaz's expectation)? Or do we ask whether God might be bringing us 'into judgment' in a different sense—not as defendants but as students, testing and deepening our faith? Modern covenant members know intellectually that suffering is not always punishment. Yet emotionally and habitually, we often revert to Eliphaz's logic. Verse 4 invites us to examine this reversion and to open ourselves to the possibility that God's testing of our faith may be the deepest expression of His confidence in us, not a sign of His condemnation.

text_kjv: Is not thy wickedness great? and thine iniquities infinite?

commentary.narrative: With verse 5, Eliphaz makes the pivot from philosophical insinuation to direct accusation. The rhetorical form changes. Verses 2-4 posed questions designed to lead Job to a conclusion; verse 5 announces the conclusion as established fact. 'Is not thy wickedness great?' The Hebrew ha-lo ra'atkha rabbah ('is not your evil/wickedness great?') is phrased as a question, but the tone is now accusatory rather than exploratory. The answer Eliphaz expects is no longer implicit but demanded: yes, your wickedness is indeed great. The follow-up—'And thine iniquities infinite?'—pushes the accusation to an extreme. The Hebrew ve-ein qets la-avonotekha ('and there is no end to your iniquities') makes an extraordinary claim: Job's sins are not merely present but limitless.
commentary.narrative_p2: The escalation is stunning. Eliphaz has moved from an abstract principle (God gains nothing from human righteousness) to a specific charge (Job is wicked without end). The logical structure is now fully visible: (1) God would not punish a righteous man; (2) Job is being punished severely; (3) Therefore, Job must be guilty; (4) The severity of the punishment indicates unlimited guilt. It is a syllogism in which the middle term—Job's actual conduct—is entirely bypassed. Eliphaz has concluded what must be true from the visible suffering and has worked backward to declare it. He has constructed a closed system in which any suffering confirms guilt and any claim of innocence must mask hidden sin.
commentary.narrative_p3: The reader of the prologue knows that this is precisely backwards. God has testified to Job's integrity twice (1:8 and 2:3), describing him as tam va-yashar—perfect and upright. God is not punishing Job for hidden sin; God is testing Job's faith precisely because Job is righteous. Yet Eliphaz has eliminated the possibility of hearing or understanding this truth. He has moved to the only conclusion his framework permits: Job is guilty. The cruelty of the accusation lies in this certainty. Eliphaz is not saying, 'Perhaps you have sinned'; he is saying, 'You must have sinned; your silence about your crimes confirms it.' Job's protestations of innocence become, in Eliphaz's logic, evidence of his guilt. He is denying what must be true given the observable facts of his suffering.

word_study.meaning: wickedness, evil, harm, misfortune; in moral contexts, wickedness or wrongdoing; in other contexts, misfortune or harm befalling someone
word_study.significance: The word ra'ah carries a semantic ambiguity: it can mean 'the evil you do' or 'the evil that happens to you.' Eliphaz conflates these meanings, assuming Job's misfortune (ra'ah happening to him) must indicate ra'ah (moral evil) he has done. The Covenant Rendering renders it 'wickedness' to clarify the moral dimension Eliphaz intends.

word_study.meaning: great, much, many, abundant; can modify quality, quantity, or intensity
word_study.significance: Rabbah emphasizes magnitude. Eliphaz is not accusing Job of minor transgressions but of great, abundant wickedness. The claim is extreme and proportional to the scale of Job's suffering.

word_study.meaning: iniquity, transgression, guilt, punishment for transgression; the root avon- conveys both the act of wrongdoing and its consequences
word_study.significance: Avonat is stronger than ra'ah—it specifically means iniquity or sin with its consequent guilt and punishment. Eliphaz is not merely accusing Job of harm but of covenant violation and guilt before God.

word_study.meaning: 'there is no end,' 'no limit,' 'infinite,' 'without boundary'
word_study.significance: The phrase ein qets is hyperbolical. Job's iniquities do not merely exist; they are boundless. This language suggests that Job has committed so many sins, or such great sins, that they cannot even be numbered or contained. It is the language of cosmic transgression.

cross_references.connection: Job is introduced as 'a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil.' Eliphaz's accusation directly contradicts the narrator's own description.

God says: 'Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth, a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil?' Eliphaz accuses Job of exactly what God says Job does not do.

In his closing oath (which follows this speech), Job swears: 'I made a covenant with mine eyes; why then should I think upon a maid?'... and proceeds through detailed denials of wrongdoing. Job's own testimony, given later, refutes Eliphaz's accusations directly.

At Jesus' trial, the chief priests 'sought for false witness against Jesus.' Job's accusers, like Jesus' accusers, construct charges that do not match reality. False accusation becomes a mark of those who cannot acknowledge innocence.

The Lord teaches: 'He that seeketh to bring down Zion shall be brought down and be destroyed; for I, the Lord, have put forth my hand to exert the powers of heaven... that the bounds of the earth shall tremble before you.' God vindicates the innocent against accusers.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient legal proceedings, both in Israel and the broader ancient Near East, accusation in the presence of witnesses could be formalized into legal charges. Eliphaz's statement, if made publicly (and Job's speeches are made in the presence of all three friends), constitutes a serious charge. The language of 'infinite iniquities' echoes courtroom denunciations in which an accused person is portrayed as a habitual offender whose crimes are beyond numbering. Yet there is a critical difference: Eliphaz is making these charges based entirely on inference from Job's suffering, not on any actual knowledge of wrongdoing. In the retributive worldview that Eliphaz represents, such inference is treated as proof. The visible fact of suffering is evidence enough. However, even in ancient legal tradition, inference was not absolute proof—testimony, witnesses, and cross-examination were valued. Eliphaz offers none of these; he offers only his interpretation of the facts.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 39:5-6, Alma confronts Corianton about his transgression, but not in Eliphaz's manner. Alma names the actual sin (he took a harlot) and offers both correction and redemption. Alma does not make up charges or assume hidden sin beyond what Corianton has already revealed. The Nephite tradition rejects Eliphaz's method of accusation based on inferred guilt.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 135:3, on the martyrdom of Joseph and Hyrum Smith, declares: 'In life they were not divided, and in death they were not separated!' The revelation celebrates the innocence and integrity of the martyrs against those who sought to destroy them. The Lord's judgment affirms innocence against human accusation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple ordinances, the candidate is tested by guardians but never accused without grounds. The testing is educational, not accusatory. The form is 'Are you prepared?' not 'Confess your crimes.' The Latter-day Saint covenantal tradition rejects the assumption that testing indicates guilt.

commentary.christological_typology: Verse 5 foreshadows the charges made against Jesus before Pilate and Herod. Accusations of wickedness without end, plots to destroy Him based on false inference and distorted evidence. Yet Christ's innocence is absolute. The Atonement does not work by Jesus accepting false charges but by His bearing the genuine consequences of human sin. Job's innocence and Christ's innocence are absolute truths that no amount of external suffering or accusation can overturn.
commentary.application: Verse 5 is a warning about accusation and judgment. Eliphaz's move from philosophical reasoning to concrete accusation represents a common human temptation: when we cannot understand why something is happening, we assume guilt and construct charges accordingly. In modern life, this takes many forms: 'If you got divorced, you must have sinned.' 'If you struggle with mental illness, you must lack faith.' 'If your child has special needs, God must be punishing you.' These are Eliphaz's accusations in contemporary dress. Verse 5 invites us to notice how Eliphaz, starting from a false assumption about cause and effect, ends by making up crimes that have never been committed. The inverse is also true: when someone we know experiences suffering, the covenant invites us to refrain from Eliphaz's move. Instead, we should ask how we can support them, how we can hold space for the mystery of suffering without resolving it through false accusation. This is the covenant of charity.

text_kjv: For thou hast taken a pledge from thy brother for nought, and stripped the naked of their clothing.

commentary.narrative: Having declared Job guilty in principle (v. 5), Eliphaz now offers concrete evidence—or what he claims is evidence. This is the first of six specific charges Eliphaz will level against Job (vv. 6-9). Verse 6 contains two accusations: (1) 'Thou hast taken a pledge from thy brother for nought'—Job has seized collateral (a pledge, a security for debt) from his own kinsmen without just cause; (2) 'Stripped the naked of their clothing'—Job has taken the garments of the poor, leaving them exposed and defenseless. Both charges are violations of explicit biblical law, which creates a rhetorical problem for the reader: these are precisely the kinds of sins condemned in Deuteronomy and Leviticus, the laws of Israel. Eliphaz is accusing Job of being a covenant-breaker in the most flagrant sense.
commentary.narrative_p2: The first charge—taking a pledge from kinsmen for nothing (chinnam, 'without cause' or 'for nothing')—invokes Exodus 22:26-27 and Deuteronomy 24:12-13, which explicitly prohibit taking a poor person's outer garment as collateral. The law recognizes that for someone without property, the cloak (tallit) is both clothing and blanket—essential for survival. To seize it is to strip someone of their dignity and their ability to survive the night. Eliphaz accuses Job of precisely this inhumanity. The charge is credible in form because the law against it is well-known. Yet the prologue establishes that Job is the opposite: he is someone who 'brought food to the hungry' (31:17), who 'put on righteousness as a garment' (29:14), and who was 'eyes to the blind, and feet was I to the lame' (29:15). Job's entire character is built on compassion for the vulnerable.
commentary.narrative_p3: This is the genius and the cruelty of Eliphaz's accusation: he accuses Job of sins that are (1) serious and condemnable, (2) explicitly forbidden in Torah, (3) completely inconsistent with what the prologue tells us about Job's character. For a modern reader, Eliphaz's accusation seems almost absurd—we know it is false. But for Job, sitting in his suffering and hearing his friend declare him a heartless creditor and a thief, the accusation must have felt like a final betrayal. Everything Job has done—his integrity, his generosity, his careful ethical conduct—has been rendered invisible by the interpretive frame that Eliphaz has constructed. Job's suffering is so great that it must mean he is a criminal; therefore, the virtues he claims must be lies. The translator notes point to Job's later defense (31:19-20): 'If I have seen any perish for want of clothing, or any poor without covering; If his loins have not blessed me, and if he were not warmed with the fleece of my sheep.' Job directly denies Eliphaz's charge and invokes his actual conduct as evidence of his character.

word_study.meaning: to take as a pledge, to give as a pledge, to mortgage, to bind; the root chavol- means 'to bind' or 'to pledge'
word_study.significance: The verb tachbol refers to taking property as security for a debt. In ancient societies, this was a normal economic practice, but it was regulated by law to prevent abuse of the poor. Eliphaz uses the verb in the accusatory sense: Job has taken pledges from his own kin ('achekha'—literally 'your brothers,' meaning kinsmen or people of his own community).

word_study.meaning: for nothing, without cause, gratuitously, in vain; suggests an unjust or unnecessary taking
word_study.significance: Chinnam indicates that Job took the pledge without just grounds. In economic law, a pledge could be taken for legitimate debt, but chinnam suggests violation—taking security when no debt exists, or when the debt is not genuine. This makes the charge especially vicious: not just taking pledges, but taking them without reason.

word_study.meaning: to strip, to remove, to take off, to despoil
word_study.significance: The verb tafshit carries the sense of violent removal. Job did not merely accept clothing as collateral but actively stripped it from the poor, leaving them exposed and vulnerable. The word choice emphasizes the brutality of the alleged act.

word_study.meaning: naked, nude, bare, destitute; can refer to literal lack of clothing or metaphorical nakedness/vulnerability
word_study.significance: The plural form arummim emphasizes that this is not an isolated victim but a pattern—Job has stripped multiple people of their only protection. The term conveys both literal exposure (to cold and the elements) and metaphorical exposure (to shame and powerlessness).

cross_references.connection: 'If thou at all takest thy neighbour's raiment to pledge, thou shalt deliver it unto him by that the sun goeth down... wherein shall he sleep?' The law forbids the exact practice Eliphaz accuses Job of committing.

'When thou dost lend thy brother any thing, thou shalt not go into his house to fetch his pledge; But thou shalt stand abroad, and the man to whom thou dost lend shall bring out the pledge abroad unto thee... thou shalt surely restore to him the pledge when the sun goeth down.' Again, explicit prohibition of the practice Eliphaz charges.

Job's own description of his charity: 'Because I delivered the poor that cried, and the fatherless, and him that had none to help him... I was a father to the needy: and the cause which I knew not I searched out.' This flatly contradicts Eliphaz's accusation.

Job's oath of innocence: 'If I have withheld the poor from their desire, or have caused the eyes of the widow to fail; Or have eaten my morsel myself alone... If his loins have not blessed me, and if he were not warmed with the fleece of my sheep.' Job directly denies the charges Eliphaz makes.

'Rob not the poor, because he is poor: neither oppress the afflicted in the gate: For the LORD will plead their cause, and spoil the soul of those that spoiled them.' The wisdom tradition itself teaches compassion for the poor—a wisdom that Eliphaz, as a Temanite, should know.

'If thy brother be waxen poor, and fallen in decay with thee... thou shalt relieve him... Thou shalt not give him thy money upon usury, nor lend him thy victuals for increase.' Economic justice toward kinsmen is covenant obligation.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israelite society, debt and collateral were fundamental to economic relationships. A poor person borrowing grain or money from a wealthy creditor would offer collateral—often personal items of value or (in extreme cases) labor or land. The Torah's regulations on pledges reflect a concern for the vulnerable: a poor person who offers their outer garment as collateral might not survive the night without it. The regulations thus protect the debtor by limiting what can be taken and requiring its return by nightfall. Eliphaz's accusation—that Job has taken pledges unjustly and stripped the naked of their clothing—would have resonated powerfully in a society where such abuses were known to occur. Wealthy creditors sometimes did exploit the poor by taking excessive collateral or refusing to return pledges. Yet the law existed precisely to prevent this. Eliphaz's accusation places Job among the worst offenders: not merely a negligent creditor but a cruel exploiter. In the context of ancient Near Eastern wisdom, such conduct would disqualify a person from being called wise or righteous. It would mark him as misdirected, cruel, and under the judgment of heaven.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 4:16-17 teaches: 'And also, ye yourselves will succor those that stand in need of your succor; ye will administer of your substance unto him that standeth in need... for ye are desirous to come into the fold of God, and to be called his people.' The Nephite tradition emphasizes active compassion for the poor as the mark of covenant membership—the opposite of Eliphaz's charge against Job.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 56:16-17 condemns 'those who will not give unto the poor' and promises that such will be bound up 'until my wrath is poured out upon them.' The Lord's judgment falls on those who exploit the poor or refuse them compassion. Eliphaz's accusation invokes precisely the conduct that brings divine wrath.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenants include an oath to 'succor the weak, lift up the hands which hang down, and strengthen the feeble knees.' Covenant membership is defined partly through commitment to care for the vulnerable. Eliphaz's charge is thus not merely a legal violation but a covenant transgression.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ embodied the opposite of what Eliphaz accuses Job of: Christ gave freely, healed the sick, fed the hungry, and welcomed the outcast. When Christ was stripped of His garment (at the crucifixion), He took the place of the vulnerable ones Eliphaz accuses Job of victimizing. The Atonement is, in part, a reversal of exactly the kind of economic and social injustice Eliphaz names. Christ identifies with those stripped of their dignity and protection, and He vindicates them.
commentary.application: Verse 6 presents a particular form of false accusation: accusing someone of a specific crime that contradicts their known character. Eliphaz names concrete sins (taking pledges, stripping the poor) that would be criminal if true. Yet the prologue has established that Job is generous and compassionate. For modern covenant members, verse 6 is a warning against a specific kind of slander: making specific criminal accusations against someone based on inference from their suffering or circumstance. It also warns against assuming that if someone is suffering, they must have committed the particular sins we associate with their suffering type. If someone loses their home, do we assume they are a financial predator? If someone's business fails, do we assume they are a fraud? Eliphaz's move teaches us to resist this leap. True accusation requires evidence, not inference. And even where evidence appears to point toward guilt, the covenant calls us to maintain space for the possibility that we do not understand the full picture. The opposite of Eliphaz's approach is found in D&C 41:5: 'Wherefore, I say unto you, that ye ought to forgive one another; for he that forgiveth his brother his trespasses, and his debts, and for the kind offices which he hath done, he shall be forgiven of the Father also.' Verse 6 teaches us to be very slow to accuse and very quick to forgive.

text_kjv: Thou hast not given water to the weary to drink, and thou hast withholden bread from the hungry.

commentary.narrative: Eliphaz opens his third speech with a series of devastating accusations, none of which Job has actually committed. This verse represents the first of three fabricated charges of social cruelty. Eliphaz claims Job refused water to the exhausted and bread to the starving — the most fundamental acts of hospitality in the ancient Near East. What makes this accusation so potent is that it inverts Job's actual character. Job will later reveal in chapter 29 that he was renowned for his generosity to the vulnerable. The accusation of withholding water and bread strikes at the heart of covenant obligation: to care for those in need is not optional charity but mandatory duty rooted in Israel's law and memory of slavery.
