Eliphaz is constructing a logical narrative: if Job's suffering is so severe, he must have committed terrible sins; therefore, he must be a cruel oppressor hiding behind a facade of piety.

word_study.meaning: To be weary, exhausted, or faint; someone depleted of strength, vulnerable and dependent on others for survival. The Covenant Rendering emphasizes 'exhausted' to capture the totality of depletion.
word_study.significance: The term implies not casual tiredness but complete vulnerability. In the covenant context, the exhausted person has a legal claim on the provision of the community. To deny water to the ayef is to violate the fundamental hospitality code.

word_study.meaning: To withhold, refuse, deny, or prevent from receiving. The root carries intentionality — this is not accidental deprivation but deliberate refusal.
word_study.significance: The verb form timna (2nd person feminine singular) places direct blame on Job for active refusal. This is worse than mere negligence; it is culpable malice. The same verb appears in Deuteronomy 15:10 regarding withholding from the poor, which brings divine curse.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah describes the true fast God desires: 'Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house?' The contrast sharpens the irony — Eliphaz accuses Job of exactly what Isaiah identifies as covenant violation.

Moses commands Israelites to lend freely to the poor: 'Thou shalt surely give him...thou shalt not harden thine heart, nor shut thine hand.' Withholding from the needy brings explicit divine curse, the very logic Eliphaz is applying.
Job's own testimony: 'I was eyes to the blind, and feet was I to the lame...the cause which I knew not I searched out.' Job will later demonstrate that the accusation is exactly backwards.
The noble person 'opens thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction.' Eliphaz's standard is biblically sound; his application to Job is utterly false.

commentary.historical_context: Ancient Near Eastern hospitality law was not merely custom but covenant obligation. The dependent classes — the exhausted traveler, the hungry stranger — had legal standing. In Egypt, the wealthy's moral fitness in the afterlife was measured partly by whether they had fed the hungry. In Mesopotamia, the king's legitimacy rested on his provision for widows and orphans. Israelite law systematized this: Exodus 22:22-24 explicitly protects the widow and orphan, with a divine threat attached. To deny water and bread was not just unkindness; it was the violation of the fundamental reciprocal obligation that held society together. An ancient reader would recognize Eliphaz's charge as the most serious social crime imaginable.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon echoes this emphasis on covenant responsibility to feed the hungry. Mosiah 4:16-17 teaches that those who have are obligated to share, and denying the needy invites divine judgment. Alma 34:38-39 similarly warns against withholding from those in want. The same logic Eliphaz employs — that suffering indicates hidden sin — Job's ancient and modern readers must resist.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 38:35-36 reiterates the covenant: 'If thou lovest me thou shalt serve me and keep all my commandments...the poor shall be exalted, in that the rich are made low.' The principle is eternal: covenantal societies rest on mutual obligation to the vulnerable.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant in LDS theology includes specific responsibilities to the poor and afflicted. Modern revelation emphasizes that one cannot take upon oneself the name of Christ while refusing to clothe the naked or feed the hungry (D&C 52:40). Eliphaz's standard is actually gospel standard — his misapplication to Job is the problem.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ embodied perfect response to the hungry and exhausted. The Gospels show him multiplying bread (Matthew 14:15-21), offering living water (John 4:10-14), and identifying with the hungry, thirsty, stranger, and imprisoned (Matthew 25:35-40). The accusation Eliphaz levels at Job — refusing water and bread — is precisely what Jesus rejected in his own temptation (Matthew 4:3-4). To refuse provision to the vulnerable is to refuse the Christological obligation.
commentary.application: This verse pierces the modern tendency to spiritualize suffering as deserved punishment. Eliphaz's logic — suffering proves sin — remains seductive: we blame the poor for poverty, the sick for illness, the bereaved for loss. This verse calls us to resist that logic ruthlessly. The covenant obligation to feed the hungry and give water to the exhausted is absolute, regardless of our interpretation of their suffering. We cannot use theodicy as excuse for withholding compassion. The practical takeaway: examine whether we are using a doctrine of divine justice to justify social indifference. If we are not actively providing for the vulnerable, we risk Eliphaz's error, not Job's innocence.

text_kjv: But as for the mighty man, he had the earth; and the honourable man dwelt in it.

commentary.narrative: Eliphaz shifts his accusation from passive cruelty (refusing charity) to active oppression (land seizure). This verse suggests that Job used his power and influence to dispossess others, concentrating wealth and territory in the hands of the powerful. The 'mighty man' and 'honourable man' are two ways of describing the exploitative elite — those who seize what they want because they have the strength or status to do so. The parallelism creates a single indictment: the powerful took the land, and their privileged position allowed them to hold it. Eliphaz is painting Job as a robber baron, someone whose wealth rests on systematic dispossession of weaker neighbors. This charge is particularly insidious because it takes the visible fact (Job was wealthy) and assumes the worst explanation (he stole it through cruelty). The verse assumes a zero-sum world where land is finite, and one person's gain requires another's loss — a realistic view of ancient agrarian economies, but not necessarily true of Job's actual transactions.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'man of arm,' an idiom for someone wielding physical power or military force. The zero'a (arm) represents strength, violence, and the capacity to dominate. The Covenant Rendering captures this as 'the powerful man.'
word_study.significance: The term carries a pejorative sense in wisdom literature. The 'man of arm' is not virtuous strength but coercive power. In contrast, the wise gain authority through counsel, not force. Eliphaz is accusing Job of being someone who uses brute power to achieve his aims.

word_study.meaning: Possessive pronoun: 'to him,' 'for him,' indicating ownership or belonging. The preposition lo marks exclusive possession.
word_study.significance: The brevity of the phrase — 'to him the land' — suggests illegitimate seizure. The land 'belonged to him' not by law but by force. The possessive is aggressive, not peaceful.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'lifted of face,' meaning one who receives respect, honor, or special privilege. The image is of someone whose face is lifted above others, exalted, receiving deference.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's 'privileged one' captures the sense of unearned favor. This person dwelt in the seized land not because it was rightfully theirs, but because their social status protected them. Eliphaz suggests Job was part of an exploitative system that benefited the already-elevated.

cross_references.connection: God declares: 'The land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me.' No Israelite could own land absolutely or dispossess neighbors permanently. Eliphaz's accusation assumes violation of this fundamental principle.

Samuel appeals to his entire judgment record: 'Whose ox have I taken? or whose ass have I taken? or whom have I defrauded?' The rhetorical defense echoes Job's own implicit argument — true leaders build through integrity, not dispossession.

Isaiah pronounces woe on those who 'join field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth.' The prophecy condemns exactly the land-seizing practice Eliphaz accuses Job of.
The prophet rebukes: 'they covet fields, and take them by violence; and houses, and take them away.' Again, the seizure of land through power is precisely what prophetic tradition condemns.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient agrarian societies, land was wealth. Control of land meant control of food production, economic surplus, and political power. The mechanisms of land seizure in the ancient Near East included false legal claims, debt slavery that led to forfeiture, deliberate impoverishment through taxation, and outright force. Eliphaz's accusation assumes Job used some combination of these. The 'man of arm' phrase suggests military or enforcer violence — hiring mercenaries to intimidate neighbors, using property disputes as pretext for territorial expansion. The irony is that Eliphaz is describing real practices by real oppressive elites in Israel's history — practices that prophets repeatedly condemned. But he is attributing them to Job, who, we will learn, was the opposite: a protector of those who could be dispossessed.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon reflects deep concern with the danger of concentrated wealth and power. King Benjamin warns against priestcraft and the desire for gain (Mosiah 2:31-37). The Nephite society repeatedly falters when the wealthy become 'lifted up in pride,' the very 'nesu panim' (privileged ones) that Eliphaz describes. Alma 4:8 notes that the Church began to wax proud because of their riches, a pattern that echoes Eliphaz's world.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 56:16-17 condemns those who 'are puffed up in the pride of their hearts, and do boast in their own strength.' The language echoes 'the man of arm.' Modern revelation repeatedly warns against the spiritual danger of using power to dominate others.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant includes specific language about justice and restitution. Those who have gained through wrongdoing cannot enter into exalted covenants. The principle is that legitimate authority rests on righteousness, not coercive power.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus explicitly rejected the logic of the 'man of arm.' His temptation in the wilderness included the offer of 'all the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of them' (Matthew 4:8-9) — earthly power and privilege. He refused. His kingdom operates by entirely different principles: 'the first shall be last' (Matthew 19:30), 'blessed are the meek' (Matthew 5:5), power perfected in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). Christ's life demonstrates that legitimate leadership is purchased through service and sacrifice, not through seizing what belongs to others.
commentary.application: This verse challenges us to examine the sources of our own security and status. Do we benefit from systems that concentrate privilege among the already-powerful? Are we complicit in land seizure, wage theft, or structural dispossession? The verse also cautions against the judgment error Eliphaz commits: assuming that someone's wealth proves they obtained it illegitimately. Some people are wealthy and righteous. The test is not how much one has, but whether it was gained justly and whether it is used generously. The application: scrutinize both your own path to provision and your assumptions about others' paths. Eliphaz's error was to confuse visibility of wealth with certainty of its origins.

text_kjv: Thou hast sent widows away empty, and the arms of the fatherless have been broken.

commentary.narrative: This verse represents the climax of Eliphaz's fabricated accusations. He moves beyond general cruelty to accuse Job of victimizing the two most legally and morally protected categories in Israelite society: widows and orphans. The first charge — sending widows away empty-handed — suggests Job refused aid to women who had lost their husbands and had no male protector. The second charge — breaking the arms of orphans — uses metaphorical language (though possibly literal): to break someone's arm is to incapacitate them, to render them unable to work or defend themselves. The Hebrew phrase captures violent cruelty: Job allegedly crushed the capacity of already-vulnerable children to survive. The savage irony, which becomes apparent only when we read Job 29, is that Job was renowned precisely as the protector of widows and orphans. He was the one who gave substance to widows and 'delivered the orphan' (Job 29:12). Eliphaz's accusation is not merely wrong; it is an exact inversion of Job's true character. This verse is Eliphaz's rhetorical zenith and worst lie — and it sets up the absolute moral clarity that will come in Job's defense and in the divine verdict.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'sent away empty.' Shillachta is the 2nd person feminine singular past tense of shalaach (to send, dismiss, divorce). Reiqam means empty, without provision or hope. Together, the phrase describes dismissing someone with nothing, refusing them aid.
word_study.significance: The specific use of shalaach (send away/dismiss) rather than simply 'deny' suggests aggressive expulsion. These widows came seeking help and were driven away. The empty-handed condition emphasizes their return to destitution. The word reiqam appears in Exodus 22:16 (God will surely slay you if you afflict widows), making this specific language deeply charged in covenant context.

word_study.meaning: Plural of zero'a (arm), used both literally as the physical limb and metaphorically as strength, power, or capacity to act. In parallel structure with 'widows,' the arms of the orphans represent their capacity to survive and work.
word_study.significance: The metaphorical sense is crucial. To 'break the arms' of orphans is to incapacitate them, to remove their ability to fend for themselves. It is not just harm but systematic destruction of agency. The same zero'a (arm) that Eliphaz attributed to the 'mighty man' in verse 8 is here turned against the powerless.

word_study.meaning: Root duk means to crush, pound, or press down. The passive sense 'are crushed' or 'are broken' suggests an ongoing state of being crushed, not a single violent act but sustained oppression.
word_study.significance: The form yedukka implies that the crushing continues — the arms remain broken, the orphans remain incapacitated. This is not a single crime but a systemic condition Job allegedly maintains. The Covenant Rendering's 'crushed' captures the metaphorical totality of destruction.

cross_references.connection: God explicitly commands: 'Ye shall not afflict any widow, or fatherless child...if thou afflict them in any wise...I will surely hear their cry; and my wrath shall wax hot.' This is the legal foundation for Eliphaz's accusation — and proof that Job's actual behavior inverts it completely.

Deuteronomy emphasizes that God himself executes justice for widow and orphan, and curses anyone who 'perverts the judgment of the stranger, fatherless, and widow.' Eliphaz's charge places Job in the category of the cursed.

Job's own testimony: 'Because I delivered the poor that cried, and the fatherless, and him that had none to help him...the blessing of him that was ready to perish came upon me.' This verse directly refutes Eliphaz's accusations by describing Job's actual relationship to widows and orphans.

In his oath of innocence, Job swears: 'If I have withheld the poor from their desire, or have caused the eyes of the widow to fail...then let mine arm fall from my shoulder blade.' Job invokes the same imagery Eliphaz uses — 'breaking the arm' — as proof of his opposite character.
The New Testament echoes the Old Testament principle: 'Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction.' The standard is eternal.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern societies, widows and orphans represented the most economically vulnerable population. A widow had lost her male provider and had no legal standing to own property or conduct business in most cultures. An orphan had lost both parents and was entirely dependent on family or community charity. Israel's legal system, uniquely, provided extraordinary protections for these groups, enshrining them in law rather than leaving them to individual charity. To abuse a widow or orphan was not merely unkindness; it was a violation of the most fundamental covenant protection. Ancient Near Eastern texts show that the legitimacy of rulers rested partly on their protection of vulnerable persons. The Enuma Elish, the Hammurabi Code, Egyptian wisdom literature, and Mesopotamian royal inscriptions all emphasize the ruler's duty to 'open the ears of the widow' and protect the orphan. Eliphaz's accusation assumes Job violated the most basic standard of legitimate authority.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly emphasizes covenant obligation to the poor and afflicted. Alma 34:38-39 warns that if one will not impart of substance to the poor, one cannot participate in the Atonement's benefits. The theme is constant: a covenantal people must protect the vulnerable. Mosiah 4:26 teaches that those who do not care for the poor and afflicted are without God.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 38:30-39 emphasizes the covenant necessity of caring for the poor. Section 52:40 identifies refusal to clothe the naked, feed the hungry, or visit the sick as denial of discipleship. Modern revelation makes clear that this is not optional improvement but covenant obligation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant creates an explicit obligation to care for those in covenant (widows, orphans, the bereaved). Modern temple worship includes emphasis on caring for family members, which extends by principle to the community's vulnerable. One cannot make temple covenants while actively harming the protected classes.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ himself identified with the widow and orphan. Luke 4:18 quotes Isaiah: Christ was anointed to 'preach the gospel to the poor...set at liberty them that are bruised.' The metaphor of 'broken arms' and incapacitation appears in the healing miracles: Christ restores sight to the blind, strength to the lame, hope to the desperate. He explicitly identifies the care of widow and orphan as His own work (Luke 18:1-8). To break the arms of an orphan is to work against Christ's mission; to restore them is to do His work.
commentary.application: This verse tests our willingness to defend the vulnerable, especially those with no power to defend themselves or to reward us. Eliphaz's accusations are false, but his standard is biblical: a truly righteous person actively protects and provides for widows, orphans, the poor, and the marginalized. Modern application: Identify one vulnerable person or group in your community — a single parent, a refugee family, an elderly person without family, a child in crisis — and commit to sustained, covenantal protection. Not charity that makes you feel good about yourself, but consistent, sacrificial obligation. This is what Job actually did, and it is what the covenant requires.

text_kjv: Therefore snares are round about thee, and sudden fear troubleth thee;

commentary.narrative: With this verse, Eliphaz makes the logical leap from accusation to explanation: because Job has committed these terrible crimes (verses 6-9), his suffering is not mysterious — it is retribution. The 'therefore' (al ken in Hebrew) is the hinge of Eliphaz's entire theology. It is the word that connects sin to suffering, deed to consequence. Snares surround Job; sudden terror assails him — all because of his hidden sins. The imagery is vivid: Job is trapped, hunted, unable to escape. The word 'snares' suggests deliberate traps set by divine justice, closing in from all sides. 'Sudden fear' (pachad pit'om) emphasizes that Job cannot predict or prevent the terror — it strikes without warning, catching him helpless. This verse crystallizes the retribution theology that dominates the first cycle of speeches. The logic is seductive: suffering is explained, causation is clear, and morality is straightforward. The problem, which Job has spent the entire dialogue resisting, is that the logic is false. Job's suffering is not explained by hidden wickedness. But Eliphaz believes he has 'solved' the problem. The al ken ('therefore') is his greatest error — the false causal link that Job must break.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'upon this,' a conjunction meaning 'therefore,' 'for this reason,' or 'because of this.' It marks causal connection: one thing follows from another.
word_study.significance: This single word is the hermeneutical key to the entire speech. It assumes a direct causal link between the sins of verses 6-9 and the sufferings of verses 10-14. The 'therefore' is the foundation of retribution theology — and its falsity is Job's central protest. Job does not deny that wrongdoing brings consequences; he denies that his suffering is evidence of his wrongdoing.

word_study.meaning: Plural of pach, a trap or snare set to catch an animal or person. The image is of hidden mechanisms designed to ensnare the unwary.
word_study.significance: The snares are divine judgment — invisible, surrounding, inescapable. The metaphor emphasizes helplessness. Unlike an open threat Job could see and resist, snares work by entanglement. The plural ('snares round about') suggests multiple traps, total encirclement, no escape route.

word_study.meaning: Pachad means fear, terror, or dread; pit'om means suddenly or unexpectedly. Together, the phrase describes overwhelming terror that strikes without warning.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's 'sudden terror' captures the totality of fear. This is not rational anxiety but existential dread — the terror of being hunted, trapped, unable to anticipate or escape danger. Job's internal emotional state mirrors his external physical condition (surrounded by snares).

word_study.meaning: From bahl, meaning to terrify, confound, or overwhelm. The form suggests the fear takes over, controls, leaves one helpless.
word_study.significance: The verb form indicates that the terror is not fleeting but controlling. Job is not merely afraid; he is overwhelmed by fear, unable to function rationally. This intensifies the portrait of total wretchedness.

cross_references.connection: Job's own opening lament: 'For the thing which I greatly feared is come upon me, and that which I was afraid of is come unto me.' The same language of fear (pachad) appears — but Job attributes it not to hidden sin but to cosmic suffering.

The psalmist prays: 'Mine eyes are ever toward the LORD; for he shall pluck my feet out of the net.' The net and snare imagery is common in psalms of lament — but the psalmist expects deliverance, not the permanent entrapment Eliphaz describes.

Wisdom tradition teaches: 'Thorns and snares are in the way of the froward: but he that doth keep his soul shall be far from them.' The snares are presented as avoidable if one lives righteously — Eliphaz is claiming Job did not avoid them.

Job describes his own suffering: 'For the arrows of the Almighty are within me, the poison whereof drinketh up my spirit.' The imagery echoes Eliphaz's — but Job insists his affliction is disproportionate to any sin.

The counterpoint: 'The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?' Trust in God's justice should dispel the fear Eliphaz describes — but that presupposes the causal logic ('therefore') that Job rejects.

commentary.historical_context: The logic of retribution theology was dominant in the ancient Near East. The principle 'the gods reward the righteous and punish the wicked' appeared in Egyptian, Mesopotamian, and Israelite thought. The advantage was that it made the world morally intelligible: suffering meant you had done something wrong. The danger was that it forced a false dichotomy: if you were suffering, you must be guilty. Job's friends could not imagine innocent suffering because their entire worldview excluded it as a logical category. The 'snares' and 'fear' Eliphaz describes would have resonated with ancient readers as obvious proof of divine judgment. To modern readers, Job's refusal of this logic can seem counterintuitive, but it is precisely the refusal that makes the book revolutionary.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon warns against false confidence in retribution theology. Alma 32:39-40 teaches that trials come to all: 'For if ye are righteous ye shall not perish.' But the converse is also true — if you perish, it does not always mean you were unrighteous. The principle in Nephi's record (1 Nephi 2:21, 3:7) is that the righteous may be tested and afflicted for purposes other than punishment.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 101:2 reveals divine wisdom about suffering: 'Verily, thus saith the Lord unto you whom I love, and whom I love I also chasten that their faith may be strong.' Suffering in covenant life may come for refinement, not as retribution. Section 122:7 teaches that suffering endured covenantally is actually gain, not loss.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant teaches that mortality is a period of testing — but not all testing is punishment for sin. The covenant prepares us for trials, including unjust suffering. The endowment narrative itself includes righteous characters who suffer.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ exemplified innocent suffering. He was surrounded by opposition and danger (Matthew 23:37, John 11:53-57), experienced sudden fear in Gethsemane (Matthew 26:37-39), and was ultimately caught in the 'snares' of human injustice. Yet His suffering was not punishment for personal sin but redemptive sacrifice for others' sins. Jesus's sufferings shatter the 'therefore' logic: righteousness does not guarantee comfort; innocence does not prevent pain. This verse, in light of Christ, reveals the profound error of retribution theology applied to innocent suffering.
commentary.application: This verse tests whether you believe that suffering proves guilt. The corollary temptation is to assume that those who suffer must have done something wrong — a judgment Eliphaz makes and modernity still makes. Do you secretly judge the bereaved, the unemployed, the diseased, the marginalized as having 'brought it on themselves'? This verse shows how seductive that logic is, and Job shows how false it can be. The application: resist the 'al ken' (therefore) that connects others' suffering to their hidden sin. Instead, adopt the covenant stance: suffering is a reality for the righteous and the wicked; it requires compassion, not judgment. When you suffer, do not accept the false causal logic that your suffering proves your guilt.

text_kjv: Or darkness, that thou canst not see; and abundance of waters cover thee.

commentary.narrative: Eliphaz now shifts his imagery to describe the totality of Job's affliction. The 'or' (o) suggests these are alternative descriptions of the same reality: Job is engulfed in darkness, unable to see, drowning in an overwhelming flood. These are not two separate afflictions but metaphorical expressions of complete disorientation and inundation. Darkness traditionally represents suffering, judgment, or divine abandonment in biblical imagery (see Exodus 10:21-23, Lamentations 3:2). The inability to see suggests not merely physical blindness but spiritual/existential blindness — loss of orientation, inability to discern the way forward. The flood imagery ('abundance of waters') builds on the darkness: Job is not only blind but also engulfed, drowning, unable to breathe. Water in biblical metaphor can represent judgment (the flood), chaos (the primordial deep), or overwhelming force. Eliphaz is describing Job as completely undone, utterly helpless, swallowed by forces beyond his control. The rhetorical effect is to make Job's suffering seem obviously proportionate to enormous, hidden crimes. How else could one explain such total devastation? Yet this is precisely the assumption Job must challenge: this extreme suffering does not necessarily indicate extreme guilt.

word_study.meaning: The disjunctive conjunction 'or,' introducing an alternative possibility or expression. In Hebrew parallelism, o often introduces synonymous restatement rather than true alternatives.
word_study.significance: The 'or' suggests Eliphaz is offering multiple descriptions of the same reality. Whether expressed as darkness or flood, Job's condition is comprehensive disaster. The parallelism emphasizes totality, not options.

word_study.meaning: Darkness, obscurity, or gloom. In biblical usage, darkness often represents evil, judgment, or divine abandonment.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's emphasis on 'darkness so thick you cannot see' captures the impenetrability. This is not mere absence of light but oppressive, suffocating obscurity. Job cannot navigate, discern direction, or understand his condition.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'you cannot see,' from the root ra'ah (to see, perceive, understand). In Hebrew, seeing is often metaphorical for understanding or knowledge.
word_study.significance: The negation is absolute: complete inability to perceive. Job is not merely in darkness but is denied the capacity to understand his own condition. This compounds the terror: he suffers and cannot comprehend why.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'abundance of waters' or 'outpouring of water.' Shif'ah means abundance, overflow, or flood. Waters often represent judgment, chaos, or overwhelming force in biblical metaphor.
word_study.significance: The image is of being submerged, drowning, overwhelmed beyond capacity to resist or escape. The 'abundance' suggests the overflow is beyond proportional response — it is total inundation. Combined with darkness, it creates a picture of complete sensory and existential loss.

word_study.meaning: From kasah, meaning to cover, conceal, or hide. The form suggests the covering is complete, continuous, and total.
word_study.significance: Job is not partially wet but thoroughly covered, submerged. The covering hides him, obscures him, makes him indistinguishable from the waters. He is swallowed by the flood.

cross_references.connection: Job himself uses similar darkness imagery: 'If I say, I will forget my complaint, I will leave off my heaviness, and comfort myself: I am afraid of all my sorrows, for I know thou wilt not hold me innocent.' Like Eliphaz, Job describes his condition as total, but unlike Eliphaz, Job refuses to infer his own guilt from it.

A lament psalm: 'Save me, O God; for the waters are come in unto my soul...I sink in deep mire, where there is no standing.' The same flood imagery appears in the laments of the innocent, showing that this metaphor does not require prior guilt.
Jerusalem's lament: 'He hath led me, and brought me into darkness, but not into light.' The darkness is real, but the speaker (Jerusalem) does not thereby confess specific sins that merited it.

God promises: 'When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee.' The waters and floods are presented as real dangers — but covenant protection is offered, not as evidence of prior innocence but as divine grace.

The disciples are tossed by waves at night, in darkness, terrified — yet their suffering is not punishment for sin but a circumstance in which Christ comes to them. The application is profound: suffering in darkness does not indicate condemnation.

commentary.historical_context: Darkness and water imagery carried specific cultural resonance in the ancient Near East. The chaos of creation mythology involved dark, watery chaos (tehom) — formless, deadly, opposed to order and life. To be submerged in water or engulfed in darkness was to revert to chaos, to lose the order and safety of the created cosmos. The Exodus narrative used darkness (the plagues of darkness) as divine judgment, and the Red Sea as both judgment and deliverance. For an ancient hearer, the imagery Eliphaz uses would evoke both divine judgment and cosmic destruction. The power of the metaphor is that it makes Job's suffering cosmically proportionate — not merely pain but the dissolution of order itself. This reinforces Eliphaz's logic: only someone guilty of enormous crimes could experience suffering of such cosmic magnitude.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon uses flood and darkness imagery to describe the condition of those who reject God's word: 2 Nephi 28:28-29, Alma 41:11. However, the book also contains experiences of righteous individuals who pass through darkness: Nephi's experience with Lehi's vision (1 Nephi 8), the experience of righteous saints in times of persecution. The principle is complex: darkness can indicate rejection, but not invariably.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 95:1-2 reveals God's chastisement of the Church: 'Verily, thus saith the Lord unto the Church which I have established.' Yet the Church is still God's covenant people, not reprobate. Chastisement does not equal rejection. Section 122:7-9 teaches that tribulation — even extreme tribulation — can be refining, not necessarily destructive.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment includes passage through darkness and difficult circumstances — but these represent testing, not condemnation. The covenant promise is that even through darkness, the faithful are guided. The temple does not assume that those in darkness are guilty; it assumes they need spiritual guidance.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ experienced darkness in a literal and metaphorical sense. Matthew 27:45 records darkness covering the land at Christ's crucifixion. More profoundly, Christ experienced abandonment ('My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' — Matthew 27:46), a spiritual darkness, an inundation of judgment. Yet Christ's suffering was innocent — He bore the judgment for others. The cross refutes retribution theology: the most righteous person experienced the darkest suffering. This verse in light of Christ shows that darkness and flood do not measure guilt; they measure the depth of what one is called to bear.
commentary.application: When you face darkness — literal depression, existential confusion, loss of direction, or spiritual drought — do not accept the automatic inference that it indicates hidden sin. You may be undergoing refinement, testing, or redemptive suffering on behalf of others. You may be experiencing circumstantial hardship unrelated to your righteousness. Guard against the spiritual trap of self-incrimination when facing hardship. Instead, seek to understand what the darkness is teaching you, while maintaining trust that it is not evidence of your condemnation. If you know someone in darkness — the bereaved, the depressed, the persecuted — do not infer their guilt from their suffering. Instead, offer presence and covenant companionship.

text_kjv: Is not God in the height of heaven? and behold the height of the stars, how high they are!

commentary.narrative: With this verse, Eliphaz begins a new argument that will dominate the remainder of his speech (verses 12-20). He acknowledges God's absolute transcendence — God is in the heights of heaven, exalted above the stars. The rhetorical questions pose as agreement with a theological fact: yes, God is exalted. But this verse is a setup. Eliphaz is about to argue that some people (presumably Job) think God's exaltation means God cannot see what happens below — that divine transcendence equals divine ignorance of earthly affairs. The verse thus marks a transition from accusation to theological rebuttal. Eliphaz will argue: even though God is infinitely high and far above, He is not ignorant of human conduct. He sees everything, and therefore the retribution theology that Eliphaz has been building is not only plausible but inevitable. God must reward the righteous and punish the wicked, because He knows all and withholds nothing. The question is not whether God is exalted (that is granted); the question is whether exaltation implies indifference — and Eliphaz will answer emphatically: no.

word_study.meaning: The singular form of Elohim, meaning God or the Divine. Though Elohim is typically plural, Eloha as singular emphasizes the unified, single divine being.
word_study.significance: The choice of Eloha rather than YHWH (the covenantal name) is notable. Eliphaz is speaking not from the relational, covenantal perspective but from the perspective of universal divine power. This reinforces the philosophical argument: God as transcendent power, not as covenant partner.

word_study.meaning: Height, exaltation, or elevation. Can refer both to physical height and to status or exaltation.
word_study.significance: The repetition of govah (height) in this verse — 'height of heaven' and 'height of the stars' — emphasizes transcendence, distance, and separation from earthly reality. The more times 'height' is repeated, the more distant and separate God becomes in Eliphaz's thought.

word_study.meaning: Plural noun meaning heaven or sky. Shamayim is the realm above the earth, the dwelling place of God and celestial bodies.
word_study.significance: God is not in the heavens generally but in the 'height' of the heavens — the uttermost exaltation, utterly transcendent, separated from earthly concerns. The emphasis on height suggests separation, distance, and the difficulty of reaching or understanding the divine will.

word_study.meaning: Plural of kokhav, meaning star. Stars are among the most exalted objects in human perception — fixed, eternal, distant, and mysterious.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's 'topmost stars' emphasizes the highest visible objects. Eliphaz is using the stars as a measure: even the highest things humans can see are beneath God's height. The implication is that from such distance, can God truly know human affairs? But Eliphaz will answer that He can and does.

word_study.meaning: Imperative singular of ra'ah, meaning to see, look, or perceive. Eliphaz is directing Job's attention.
word_study.significance: The imperative 're'eh' (behold) is ironic. Eliphaz tells Job to look at the stars' height — but in the next verse, Eliphaz will argue that God sees despite (and perhaps through) this height. The direction to 'behold' introduces the philosophical problem: how can something so exalted still perceive what is below?

cross_references.connection: The psalmist contemplates the stars and asks: 'When I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers, the moon and the stars...what is man, that thou art mindful of him?' The same imagery appears, but with the opposite conclusion: exaltation does not equal indifference; God is mindful despite transcendence.

Isaiah proclaims: 'Lift up your eyes on high, and behold who hath created these things, that bringeth out their host by number.' The stars are evidence not of divine distance but of divine power and creative attention. God numbers them — knows them completely.

The psalmist praises: 'The LORD is high above all nations...Who is like unto the LORD our God, who dwelleth on high, Who humbleth himself to behold the things that are in heaven, and in the earth.' This captures the paradox Eliphaz is setting up: height and humility, transcendence and attention.
Moses warns against worshiping the stars, emphasizing that the stars are objects God has 'divided unto all nations' — they are created things, under divine dominion, not competing powers.
Job himself references the stars and constellations, attributing them to God's creative work. The stars are part of Job's recognition of divine power, not symbols of divine indifference.

commentary.historical_context: The ancient Near East included cosmologies in which the heavens were the realm of the gods and the earth the realm of human affairs. The vastness of the cosmos — the impossibly distant stars — was sometimes used to suggest that the gods were indifferent to human concerns. This reflects a real philosophical problem in ancient thought: how can a transcendent God care about the microcosmic concerns of individual humans? Eliphaz is addressing this problem by acknowledging the vastness but affirming divine omniscience. The stars' height becomes not a reason for doubt but a measure of divine greatness — and therefore divine capacity to see all. The argument is more sophisticated than simple retribution theology; it is an attempt to reconcile divine transcendence with divine justice.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly affirms divine omniscience despite divine transcendence. Alma 7:13 teaches that Christ 'knoweth according to the flesh how to succor his people according to their infirmities.' Omniscience is not indifference; knowledge is the prerequisite for perfect mercy. Alma 18:32 affirms that 'no evil can dwell with God,' suggesting that divine perception and divine holiness are linked.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 38:2 reveals: 'I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end. And ye shall have no other God before me.' The transcendent God of the Doctrine and Covenants is not distant but covenantally present. D&C 88:6-13 teaches that the light that emanates from God fills the immensity of space and penetrates all things — transcendence does not equal distance.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant assumes that God, though transcendent, is intimately concerned with individual covenantal progress. The temple narrative portrays a God who is both exalted and present, both transcendent and relational. The covenant assumes divine attention to individual lives.

commentary.christological_typology: The Incarnation is the ultimate refutation of the idea that transcendence means indifference. Christ is described as 'the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person' (Hebrews 1:3). God's transcendence and God's intimate presence are not opposed; they are unified in Christ. Christ shows that divine exaltation is compatible with divine intimacy — the highest God becomes the closest companion. Philippians 2:5-8 describes Christ emptying himself, descending from height to become human. The movement is not God remaining distant in the heavens but God crossing infinite distance to be present.
commentary.application: This verse addresses a subtle spiritual temptation: the assumption that God is too exalted to be concerned with your specific life. If you are suffering, you may think: How can the transcendent God care about my individual pain? This verse is Eliphaz's setup to his assertion that God does care — and He does. But the error would be to then assume, as Eliphaz does, that God's care means He invariably punishes the wicked and rewards the righteous within your lifetime. The truth is more paradoxical: God is transcendent AND intimately concerned; God knows all AND allows mystery to remain. The application: Do not use divine transcendence as excuse for indifference to others' suffering. If God, infinitely exalted, attends to individual lives (and He does), then you are called to the same attentiveness on a smaller scale.

text_kjv: And thou sayest, How doth God know? can he judge through the dark cloud?

commentary.narrative:
Eliphaz launches into a direct accusation, claiming Job has said that God is ignorant of human affairs—that the divine knowledge is blocked or limited by the clouds surrounding God's throne. This is a straw man argument. Job has never claimed God doesn't know what happens on earth; rather, Job has wrestled with the apparent disconnect between God's knowledge and God's justice. Eliphaz attributes to Job a kind of theological blasphemy—the denial of divine omniscience—that Job has never articulated. What Job actually questions is not God's knowledge but God's apparent indifference to injustice. Eliphaz, unable to refute Job's genuine complaint about suffering and inequality, invents a more extreme position and attributes it to Job, making his counterargument easier to demolish.

The word translated 'dark cloud' (arafel) carries deep theological weight in Hebrew scripture. This is the same thick darkness that accompanies God's presence at Sinai (Exodus 20:21, Deuteronomy 4:11)—a sign of divine mystery and majesty, not divine blindness. Eliphaz weaponizes the cloud imagery: he suggests Job thinks the very cloud that manifests God's presence actually conceals God's sight. It's an inversion of biblical theology. For Eliphaz, the cloud should represent divine inscrutability combined with perfect knowledge. For Job (as Eliphaz caricatures him), the cloud becomes a barrier to vision. The accusation is theologically loaded and deeply unfair.

word_study.meaning: What does God know / Is God aware. Yada means 'to know' in the sense of personal, relational knowledge, not mere abstract awareness. Here it questions whether God actively knows or cares about human circumstances.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering emphasizes the accusation: 'What does God know?' This is not a philosophical inquiry but a charge of divine ignorance or indifference. In Hebraic thought, yada is intimate and active knowledge; to say God does not yada human affairs is to say God is disconnected from His creation.

word_study.meaning: Thick darkness, deep cloud, or gloom. In biblical usage, arafel specifically describes the dense cloud associated with God's presence and divine revelation (Exodus 20:21, Deuteronomy 4:11, 1 Kings 8:12). It connotes mystery but also divine presence.
word_study.significance: The arafel is not separation from God but the very mode of His presence on earth. Eliphaz's accusation cleverly twists this: he suggests Job believes the arafel—God's characteristic mode of manifestation—actually prevents God from seeing. The irony is bitter: the cloud that reveals God becomes, in Eliphaz's caricature of Job's view, the cloud that blinds God.

word_study.meaning: To judge, to render judgment, to execute justice. The root shaphat encompasses both judicial decision-making and actual enforcement of consequences.
word_study.significance: Eliphaz questions whether God can judge through the darkness—combining the charge of ignorance (God doesn't know) with incapacity (God can't act justly even if He did know). This ties together two dimensions of the attack: divine blindness and divine impotence.

cross_references.connection: Moses enters the arafel (thick darkness) where God is present, establishing that darkness is the sign of divine presence, not divine absence. Eliphaz inverts this theology.
Job himself has quoted the wicked as saying 'Depart from us; for we desire not the knowledge of thy ways.' Eliphaz will echo this in verse 17, implying Job holds the wicked's blasphemy.
Darkness is no barrier to God's knowledge: 'if I say, Surely the darkness shall cover me; even the night shall be light about me.' A direct refutation of the charge Eliphaz attributes to Job.
Jacob's complaint that 'my way is hid from the LORD' is answered: 'Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard? ... the everlasting God...fainteth not.' God's knowledge transcends all barriers.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern thought, gods were often conceived as distant and detached. Mesopotamian texts sometimes portray deities as unconcerned with human suffering. The biblical tradition radically counters this: the God of Israel knows, sees, and cares (Psalm 113:5-6). Eliphaz's accusation that Job doubts God's knowledge would have been recognized as importing pagan assumptions into Israelite theology. The arafel specifically evokes the covenant moment at Sinai when God drew near in judgment and grace—not distance. Eliphaz's rhetorical move is to associate Job with pagan impiety.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 34:34-35, the Nephite apostles teach that 'now, we see but a little; wherefore we believe in Christ that he will make himself manifest unto all flesh.' This connects divine knowledge to divine manifestation through Christ. The arafel of the Old Testament prefigures the veil through which Christ will ultimately reveal Himself to all creation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:6-13 teaches that Christ is 'the light which is in all things' and that 'he giveth to all life, by whom all things are sustained.' This counters the charge that God's knowledge is obscured; rather, God's knowledge is active, sustaining presence in all creation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The innermost chamber of the temple is darkness (Holy of Holies), where God's presence is most intensely manifested. This sacred darkness recalls the arafel—not a barrier to knowledge but the precise location of divine communion. Job's wrestling, like Jacob's encounter at Peniel, takes place in a liminal space where human knowledge meets divine mystery.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ as 'the light of the world' (John 8:12) fulfills what the arafel prefigures—God's presence made visible and knowable. The charge that darkness obscures divine knowledge is ultimately answered in Christ, who is simultaneously God's complete self-revelation and the One who 'dwelleth in the light which no man can approach unto' (1 Timothy 6:16). Christ reconciles divine transcendence and immanence.
commentary.application: When we face unexplained suffering or injustice, we may be tempted to question whether God truly knows or cares—whether the divine 'cloud' obscures rather than reveals. But Eliphaz's accusation against Job warns us: attributing our doubts about God's justice to a deficiency in God's knowledge is a misunderstanding of the problem. The real issue is not whether God sees; it is whether we can trust that His seeing includes a justice and mercy we cannot yet comprehend. Like Job, we must learn to distinguish between legitimate questions about divine justice and illegitimate denial of divine knowledge.

text_kjv: Thick clouds are a covering to him, that he seeth not; and he walketh in the circuit of heaven.

commentary.narrative:
Eliphaz continues the imagined quote, deepening the caricature. He portrays Job as claiming that clouds hide God from sight, and that God moves about the dome of heaven untouched by earthly concerns. The image is one of divine remoteness and indifference. God 'walks in the circuit of heaven'—He traverses the vault of the sky like a cosmic bureaucrat making rounds, oblivious to what transpires below. This is a devastating inversion of the biblical God who 'desires mercy' (Micah 6:8), who 'goes about doing good' (Acts 10:38 in NT terms), and who hears the cries of the afflicted.

The 'circuit of heaven' (chug shamayim) refers to the circumference or vault of the sky—the visible dome that ancient cosmology imagined encircling the earth. Eliphaz accuses Job of accepting a cosmological view in which God inhabits a separate celestial realm, disconnected from terrestrial suffering. This would make God like the distant sky itself—present but unreachable, bright but cold. The charge is subtle: Eliphaz is not accusing Job of denying God's existence but of denying God's relevance. God exists, yes—but safely removed, walking His heavenly circuit, while earthly injustice continues unaddressed.

word_study.meaning: Clouds. The plural form suggests density and multiplicity—not a single cloud but a thick mass. In biblical usage, clouds often represent God's presence (e.g., 'the pillar of cloud'), but here Eliphaz weaponizes them as a barrier.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering renders this 'Clouds are a screen for him'—seter lo emphasizes concealment and obstruction, not divine presence. This Hebrew term for clouds (avim) elsewhere appears in contexts of God's manifestation; here they serve only as concealment.

word_study.meaning: Hiding-place, screen, shelter, cover. The word can mean protective covering but here means obstruction. Seter lo literally means 'a hiding-place for him'—God hides behind the clouds.
word_study.significance: The usage conveys concealment with a hint of shame or withdrawal. God is not resting in clouds as on a throne but hiding behind them. This language suggests cowardice or evasion rather than majestic transcendence.

word_study.meaning: And he does not see. Yir'eh means 'he sees' or 'he is seeing'—an active, continuous perception. The negation denies this active seeing.
word_study.significance: In Hebrew, yara (to see) encompasses both visual perception and moral perception—discernment, understanding, judgment. To say God does not yir'eh is to say He lacks discernment of human affairs, not merely physical eyesight.

word_study.term_english: walketh in the circuit of heaven
word_study.meaning: And the circle/vault of heaven he walks about. Chug is the horizon, the circumference of the sky-dome. Yithalakh means 'he walks about, he moves back and forth.'
word_study.significance: The imagery is of a deity confined to the celestial realm, pacing the boundary between heaven and earth but never truly entering into earthly affairs. The verb yithalakh (he walks) suggests restless movement without purpose or engagement with creation below.

cross_references.connection: The 'firmament' (rakia) is the dome or vault of heaven. Eliphaz's 'circuit of heaven' (chug shamayim) uses similar cosmological language but divorces it from the created order God sustains.

Though God 'is high above all nations' and 'dwelleth on high,' He 'humbleth himself to behold the things that are in heaven, and in the earth.' A direct refutation of Eliphaz's claim that God's transcendence prevents His engagement.
God says 'I dwell in the high and holy place' but also 'with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit.' God's height does not isolate Him from earthly suffering.
God 'shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust.' The wings of God descend into the earthly realm; they do not remain in the celestial vault.

commentary.historical_context: Ancient cosmologies in Mesopotamia and Egypt often depicted gods as inhabiting a separate realm, occasionally intervening but fundamentally removed from human struggle. The Babylonian Enuma Elish shows gods growing weary of creating humans to do their labor. Israel's theological revolution was the proclamation that God is actively involved: God hears prayers, God sees injustice, God acts in history. Eliphaz's accusation that Job embraces a pagan cosmology—where God is distant and uninvolved—is a way of saying Job has abandoned the unique Israelite faith. The 'circuit of heaven' language echoes Mesopotamian cosmic geography, where gods traverse fixed celestial paths.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 18:24-35 presents King Lamoni questioning whether God has power over all things. The restored understanding through Ammon teaches that God 'knoweth all things, and there is not any thing save he knows it.' The Nephite theology explicitly refutes the notion that God's height removes Him from knowledge of particulars.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:24 teaches that God's eye is 'upon all the inhabitants of the earth, and in all the reasonings in their hearts.' God's omniscience encompasses the chug shamayim (circuit of heaven) and every hidden thought on earth. The veil is not a barrier but a membrane through which divine awareness flows.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where heaven and earth meet. The inner courts ascend gradually toward the Holy of Holies, where heaven and earth are believed to touch. This architecture refutes the notion that heaven and earth are separated by an impassable distance. The righteous who enter the temple access the chug shamayim while still on earth.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ descends from 'the circuit of heaven' to enter human flesh and human suffering (Philippians 2:6-8). He breaks the barrier between the celestial realm and earthly pain. The charge that God 'walketh in the circuit of heaven' untouched by suffering is answered by the Incarnation—God entering fully into the human condition, feeling pain, weeping, dying. Christ proves that transcendence and intimate engagement are not mutually exclusive.
commentary.application: We may sometimes feel abandoned by God because He seems distant—'up there' in heaven, moving in grand cosmic patterns while we suffer 'down here' in earthly pain. Eliphaz's caricature reflects a genuine temptation. But the biblical narrative insists that God's transcendence does not prevent His immanence. The question is not whether God is aware but whether we can trust that His awareness includes purposes beyond our immediate comprehension. Modern faith must, like Job's, learn to hold both truths: God is infinitely high, and God is intimately near.

text_kjv: Hast thou marked the old way which wicked men have trodden?

commentary.narrative:
Eliphaz shifts rhetorical strategy. Having accused Job of denying divine knowledge and justice, he now confronts Job with a historical warning. He speaks of an 'old way' or 'ancient path'—a path trodden by wicked men in former times. The most natural historical reference is to the generation destroyed in Noah's flood (Genesis 6-9). Eliphaz is implying that Job, by his rebellious speech against God, is walking the same path that led previous generations to destruction. The rhetorical move is powerful: it positions Job among the antediluvian rebels, those whom God judged and obliterated.

The 'old way' (orach olam) carries weight. 'Olam' can mean 'eternity' or 'ancient time,' and 'orach' is the way, path, or manner of living. Eliphaz is invoking a path established in antiquity—not a new heresy but an ancient one, tried before the flood and already judged. This is meant to terrify Job into conformity: do you not know what happened to those who walked this way? Why would you follow it now? The accusation assumes that all who challenge God's justice are following an old pattern of rebellion. Yet the irony is that Job has never denied God judges the wicked—Job has only questioned whether God always judges the wicked proportionately, whether innocent people suffer unjustly. Eliphaz refuses to hear the distinction.

word_study.meaning: To keep, to guard, to observe, to maintain. Can mean 'to take note of' or 'to understand,' but also 'to keep to, to follow.' The sense here is deliberate adherence.
word_study.significance: The question 'Will you keep to the ancient path?' is not 'Will you study it?' but 'Will you follow it?' Eliphaz accuses Job not of intellectual inquiry but of active participation in an ancient, damned ideology.

word_study.meaning: A way or path of eternity/antiquity. Orach means 'path, way, manner'; olam means 'eternity, endless time, or antiquity.' Together, the phrase suggests a path established in the distant past and enduring.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's 'ancient path' emphasizes temporal depth—this is not a new rebellion but an old one. It carries a tone of warning: this path was tested before and condemned by God. Why would Job step into it now?

word_study.meaning: Men of wickedness, iniquity, or vanity. Aven can mean 'trouble, sorrow, wickedness, or vanity.' The plural 'metei' means 'men of' or 'people of.' This phrase emphasizes that these are not just any sinners but specifically those characterized by fundamental wickedness.
word_study.significance: By grouping Job with 'metei-aven,' Eliphaz classifies him among those whose entire existence is defined by rebellion against God. It is a harsh judgment but one Eliphaz believes Job's words merit.

word_study.meaning: They trod, they walked, they crushed. The verb darakh means to tread or walk upon but carries connotations of treading down, trampling, or marching as an army does.
word_study.significance: The imagery is of many feet treading the same path repeatedly, wearing a groove in the earth. This suggests a well-established trajectory of rebellion, not a one-time deviation.

cross_references.connection: The antediluvian generation walked in wickedness, 'and God saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth.' This is the ancient path Eliphaz references—the one that led to the flood.

The way of the wicked is described as one where men 'leave the paths of uprightness, to walk in the ways of darkness.' The contrast between the ancient way of the wicked and the path of righteousness is a Wisdom tradition.

Moses describes Israel abandoning 'the God who made him' and becoming 'vain' (aven)—the same term Eliphaz uses for the ancient wicked. The Mosaic recitation of how peoples fall into rebellion provides historical precedent.

The blessed man does not 'stand in the way of sinners' or 'sit in the seat of the scornful.' Eliphaz is essentially accusing Job of moving toward the path of sinners, abandoning the way of the righteous.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, recounting the deeds of the wicked who were punished served as a moral warning. The flood story (attested in Sumerian and Babylonian versions as well as Genesis) was a shared cultural memory of divine judgment. Eliphaz's invocation of this precedent would have carried weight: Job's rebellious speech is not new; it is part of an ancient pattern that always ends in destruction. The 'old way' is both literal (the way of antediluvian rebels) and archetypal (the way of all those who defy God). By linking Job to this history, Eliphaz is saying: you are not breaking new theological ground; you are stepping into a worn path that leads to ruin.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly warns against following the 'ways of the world.' Alma 5:37-42 describes the path of the wicked as ancient and destructive. Yet the Nephite record also shows that personal experience of divine witness can lead to repentance and turning away from the ancient path. Job has not yet made this turn—he is still questioning.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:16 speaks of those who 'have strayed from my statutes, and have not kept my commandments.' The tension between the ancient way of wickedness and the restored path of righteousness is central to Restoration theology.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple represents the way of righteousness, contrasted with the ways of the world outside. The endowment ceremony teaches the choice between following the straight and narrow path (the temple) and wandering into the ways of the wicked (Babylon). Eliphaz is essentially saying to Job: you are choosing Babylon when the temple is available.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ as 'the way, the truth, and the life' (John 14:6) offers an alternative to the ancient way of the wicked. Where the old path leads to destruction (as in the flood), Christ's way leads to redemption. The paradox is that Job's wrestling with divine justice actually puts him on a path toward deeper faith—not the ancient way of the wicked but the way of Job's maturity in faith.
commentary.application: When we suffer or witness injustice, we may feel pressure to conform to dominant explanations: 'You must have sinned; God always rewards righteousness and punishes sin.' To question this is to risk being labeled a heretic following an 'ancient way of the wicked.' But legitimate suffering and legitimate questions are not the same as rebellion. The challenge is to discern whether we are questioning God out of genuine wrestling with theodicy (which can lead to deeper faith) or out of fundamental rejection of God (which is indeed an ancient path to destruction). Job's path, though it looks dangerous to Eliphaz, leads ultimately to restoration.

text_kjv: Which were cut down out of time, whose foundation was overflown with a flood:

commentary.narrative:
Eliphaz provides the historical proof of his warning. The ancient wicked—those who walked the old path—were 'cut down out of time,' meaning they died prematurely, snatched away by divine judgment before their natural lifespan was complete. Their 'foundation was overflown with a flood.' The reference is unmistakably to the generation of Noah, upon whom God poured out the waters of judgment. This is Eliphaz's exhibit A: God does judge the wicked; He cuts them off suddenly and completely. The foundation—the basis of their existence, their families, their property, their legacy—is obliterated.

Yet here lies a critical misreading. Eliphaz is correct that God judged the antediluvian generation, and correct that the wicked do sometimes face swift punishment. But he applies this historical fact to Job with a logical error: he assumes that because the wicked sometimes suffer, all who suffer must be wicked. He inverts the logical direction. It does not follow that because evil is punished, all suffering is punishment for evil. Job has never denied that God judges the wicked; Job has questioned whether God always judges proportionately, whether innocent people suffer without cause, whether divine justice operates according to simple retributive logic. By citing the flood, Eliphaz believes he has settled the argument. In reality, he has only demonstrated that God is capable of judging—which Job never disputed.

word_study.meaning: They were snatched away / shriveled / seized, and not their time. Qummat can mean 'to seize, to pluck, to wither, or to shrivel.' Ve-lo et literally means 'and not time'—their time was not fulfilled; they died prematurely.
word_study.significance: The phrase captures the sudden, untimely death of the wicked—their lives cut short, not allowed to reach their natural span. In Hebrew thought, to die before one's time is to die under a curse or judgment.

word_study.meaning: Foundation, basis, underlying structure. Can refer literally to the foundation of a building or metaphorically to the basis of existence, family line, or property.
word_study.significance: To have one's yesod destroyed means total obliteration—not just death but the erasure of one's house, descendants, and lasting impact. It is the ultimate judgment in an ancient society where legacy mattered profoundly.

word_study.meaning: A river / flood was poured out. Nahar is a river or stream, often used metaphorically for overwhelming waters. Yutsaq means 'was poured out' or 'was shed.'
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering renders this 'a river poured over their foundations'—emphasizing the covering, engulfing nature of the judgment. The same waters that destroyed the earth in Genesis 7 are here personified as divine judgment poured out.

cross_references.connection: The historical event Eliphaz cites: the waters of the great deep burst forth and covered all the high mountains. This is the nahar (flood) that destroyed the antediluvian generation.

God 'sat upon the flood; yea, the LORD sitteth King for ever.' God's dominion over the waters of judgment emphasizes His sovereignty—which is Eliphaz's point but which does not require that all suffering is judgment.

Noah is called 'a preacher of righteousness' while God 'spared not the old world, but saved Noah... bringing in the flood upon the world of the ungodly.' The judgment Eliphaz cites is also attested in NT tradition.
Job himself will later speak of the wicked's offspring being cut off, their widows not weeping. The theme of swift judgment on the wicked is one Job acknowledges but applies differently.

commentary.historical_context: The flood narrative was deeply embedded in the ancient Near Eastern consciousness. Sumerian and Babylonian texts attest to flood stories predating or contemporary with Genesis, all emphasizing divine judgment of a wicked generation. For an ancient audience, the invocation of the flood would be immediately recognizable as the prime example of divine retribution. Eliphaz is drawing on widely shared cultural memory: when humanity becomes wicked, God responds with overwhelming force. The question is whether all human suffering is such a response or whether other factors are in play.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly cites the flood as a type of coming judgment (Helaman 8:24, 3 Nephi 23:11). But it also teaches that God's judgment is tempered with mercy for the faithful. The righteous are preserved (as Noah was) even while judgment falls on the wicked. Job's suffering does not fit the pattern of antediluvian wickedness.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 45:26-33 describes future judgment but also emphasizes God's mercy toward the faithful. The flood is cited as a type but not the only pattern. Suffering is complex and does not always correlate with sin.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The waters of baptism recall the flood—a judgment that separates the righteous from the wicked. Yet baptism is not itself destruction but regeneration. The connection between water-judgment and water-redemption is central to temple theology.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ preached to 'the spirits in prison, which sometime were disobedient, when once the longsuffering of God waited in the days of Noah' (1 Peter 3:19-20). Christ's redemptive work encompasses even those lost in the flood, suggesting that judgment is not final and that God's mercy extends beyond what earthly punishment indicates. The flood, a type of judgment, is answered by Christ's resurrection, a type of redemption.
commentary.application: When others cite historical examples of swift judgment on the wicked to convince us that our suffering must be punishment, we should accept the truth but reject the inference. Yes, God judges wickedness—sometimes swiftly, sometimes not. But the fact that judgment exists does not mean all suffering is judgment. The presence of a flood does not mean all water flows from judgment. Job must learn, and we must learn, to hold both truths: God is just, and yet suffering often defies simple explanation. To cite only examples of judgment is to tell only half the story of divine justice.

text_kjv: Which said unto God, Depart from us: and what can the Almighty do for them?

commentary.narrative:
Eliphaz's rhetorical trap now becomes explicit. He directly quotes the words of the wicked antediluvian generation—'Depart from us'—and then, with devastating cunning, he associates these words with Job's own speech from Job 21:14-15. In Job 21:14-15, Job quotes the wicked as saying to God: 'Depart from us; for we desire not the knowledge of thy ways. What is the Almighty, that we should serve him?' Eliphaz is saying: you, Job, are now speaking with the voice of the antediluvian wicked. You are quoting their blasphemy. Therefore, you are on their path. Therefore, you should expect their fate.

This is a powerful rhetorical move but a devastating misreading of Job's actual speech. When Job quoted the wicked in chapter 21, he was not endorsing their words—he was describing their condition and noting the apparent injustice that the wicked often prosper despite their defiance. Job was observing the problem, not embracing the wicked's blasphemy. Eliphaz, however, conflates observation with endorsement. He accuses Job of actually saying 'Depart from us' to God. The verbal echo—which both Job and Eliphaz quote—becomes the basis for Eliphaz to claim Job is a rebel. What Job intended as a description of the wicked's state, Eliphaz reframes as Job's own confession of faith. It is a profound misunderstanding born of Eliphaz's need to defend the traditional doctrine.

word_study.meaning: Those who say / are saying to God. The participle omerim conveys ongoing, habitual speech—it is not a one-time utterance but a characteristic stance toward God.
word_study.significance: The use of the participle makes the indictment more severe: these are people whose entire relationship to God is defined by rejection, not people who once stumbled.

word_study.meaning: Turn aside from us, depart from us, go away from us. Sur means 'to turn aside, to depart'; the preposition min means 'from.'
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering preserves the directness: 'Leave us alone!' It expresses not theological denial but practical rejection—a demand that God cease involvement in their affairs.

word_study.term_english: what can the Almighty do for them
word_study.term_original: וּמַה־יִּפְעַל שַׁדַּי לָמוֹ (u-ma yif'al Shaddai lamo)
word_study.meaning: And what can / will the Almighty do to them? The phrasing is ambiguous in Hebrew—lamo can mean 'for them' (beneficially) or 'to them' (as judgment). The question challenges the Almighty's power or relevance.
word_study.significance: The wicked are asking rhetorically: what harm can the Almighty actually inflict on us? It is a direct challenge to God's power and a statement of practical atheism. Even if God exists, the wicked imply, why fear Him?

cross_references.connection: Job's actual quotation of the wicked: 'Depart from us; for we desire not the knowledge of thy ways: What is the Almighty, that we should serve him?' Eliphaz quotes this same passage but attributes it directly to Job as his own belief.

God asks 'See now that I, even I, am he' and declares 'I lift up my hand to heaven and swear by my life forever' that He will render vengeance. The wicked's question 'what can the Almighty do?' is answered by God's affirmation of power.
Wisdom describes the wicked as those who 'called, and I refused... because I have called, and ye refused.' Like Eliphaz's wicked, they reject God's offer. But the result is judgment.

God challenges those who question His power: 'Woe unto him that striveth with his Maker!... Shall the clay say to him that fashioneth it, What makest thou?' The challenge to God's power is the ancient rebellion.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern texts, rebellion against the gods is characterized by refusal to acknowledge their power and relevance. The accusation that someone questions the gods' ability to act is among the most severe charges. To ask 'What can the gods do to us?' is to declare practical atheism—the gods may exist but are impotent or indifferent. Eliphaz, by attributing this statement to Job, is accusing Job of the most fundamental heresy in ancient religious thought.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 30:27-35 records Korihor's challenge to the Almighty: 'Can ye lay aside your garments and assume the role of a man?' and his practical denial of God's power. Like Eliphaz's wicked, Korihor is challenging God's ability to act. But Alma responds that Korihor's own blindness is evidence of God's power. Korihor is struck dumb—not by Job's wrestling but by direct judgment.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:35-36 speaks of the wicked as those who say 'We will withhold our tithings' and turn away from God. The practical denial of God's power and relevance is the core of rebellion in Restoration theology.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The taking of covenants in the temple is, in essence, Job's opposite position: 'I do fear the Almighty; I do desire knowledge of His ways; I do covenant to serve Him.' The wicked's 'Depart from us' is countered by the faithful's covenant commitment.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's temptation in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1-11) includes Satan's implicit challenge to Christ's faith: 'If thou be the Son of God, command that these stones be made bread' and 'If thou be the Son of God, cast thyself down.' Satan is asking, 'What can the Father actually do for you?' Christ's refusal—'Man shall not live by bread alone'—is the antithesis of the wicked's skepticism toward the Almighty's power. Christ trusts the Father's provision completely.
commentary.application: Eliphaz's tactic of attributing one's observations to one's own beliefs is a common rhetorical trap. When we describe the problem of the wicked prospering or innocent suffering, we may be accused of believing precisely that injustice is normal and God is powerless. But describing a reality does not require endorsing it. Job's problem is not that he believes 'What can the Almighty do?' but that he observes the Almighty apparently not doing what Job believes He should. The distinction is crucial for our own spiritual integrity. We can acknowledge hard realities—yes, the wicked sometimes prosper; yes, suffering is sometimes unjust—without abandoning faith in God's power or goodness. The question is not whether we see the problem but how we interpret it.

text_kjv: Yet he filled their houses with good things: but the counsel of the wicked is far from me.

commentary.narrative:
The final verse of Eliphaz's initial attack contains a remarkable admission followed by a self-righteous protestation. Eliphaz acknowledges—just as Job acknowledged in 21:16—that God is the source of the wicked's prosperity. 'He filled their houses with good things.' This concession is important: even Eliphaz cannot deny that the wicked often prosper materially, that God provides them with abundance. Yet having admitted this fact, Eliphaz immediately pivots to a disclaimer: 'But the counsel of the wicked is far from me!' He is distancing himself from any identification with the wicked's ideology, saying in effect: 'Yes, they prosper, but I reject their thinking.'

This verse presents a curious structure: Eliphaz quotes Job 21:16 almost verbatim, where Job himself says 'the counsel of the wicked is far from me.' Eliphaz is appropriating Job's own disclaimer and using it against him. He is saying: Look, I can say those words authentically—I truly do reject the wicked's counsel—but can you, Job? When you say those words (in chapter 21), do you mean them, or are you actually sliding into their camp? This is accusation by echo, a subtle suggestion that Job's words ring hollow, that Job's rejection of wicked counsel is performative rather than genuine. The irony is that both Job and Eliphaz claim to reject the wicked's defiance, yet they differ on its cause and cure. Eliphaz assumes the wicked prosper briefly before judgment; Job observes they sometimes prosper indefinitely.

word_study.term_english: filled their houses with good things
word_study.meaning: He filled / He will fill their houses with good / prosperity. Mille means 'to fill, to complete'; batteim is the plural 'houses'; tov is 'good, prosperity, wellbeing.'
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering emphasizes the completeness of God's provision: 'it was God who filled their houses with good things.' This is not incidental or temporary blessing but full, abundant provision.

word_study.meaning: Counsel, advice, purpose, plan, scheme. Often refers to deliberation or a course of action chosen after reflection.
word_study.significance: To distance oneself from the wicked's 'counsel' is not just to reject their theology but to refuse to adopt their way of living, their strategic approach to prosperity and power.

word_study.meaning: It is far from me, it is distant from me. Rachaqa means 'to go far, to be distant, to recede'; menni means 'from me.'
word_study.significance: The language is emphatic and personal. Eliphaz is not merely saying the wicked's counsel is wrong; he is saying it is foreign to him, unthinkable, completely at odds with his identity.
