They 'thrive in the open' (yirbu va-bar, literally 'increase in the wilderness/open field'). The open field is where the young develop their strength independently, away from maternal protection. And then comes the crucial point: 'they go forth, and do not return to them' (yatse'u velo shavu lamo). The young animals leave and never come back. They do not visit their mothers. They do not maintain family ties. They do not ask permission or bid farewell. The separation is absolute and natural.

This verse articulates a principle of natural order that Job has clearly violated: the necessity and appropriateness of separation between parent and child, the building of independence, the letting go of the young by the parent and the leaving of the young from the parent. In the context of the book of Job, this principle undercuts any claim Job might make about his children or about what is owed to him by those he has brought into the world. The wild animals demonstrate that there is a natural, divinely ordained cycle: birth, nursing, weaning, strengthening, departure, and separation. To cling to one's young beyond this natural cycle, or to demand that they return, is to violate the order God has written into creation itself. The theological move is subtle: by presenting the natural history of wild animal young, God suggests to Job that the loss of children (which is Job's most devastating loss — see 1:19) is part of a natural order that extends beyond human preference or claim.

word_study.meaning: To be healthy, strong, vigorous, robust. The verb chalam is related to health and vitality. In verse 4, yachlemu describes the young animals becoming strong and robust. The word conveys physical development and well-being. The Covenant Rendering's 'grow strong' captures the sense better than the KJV's more obscure 'are in good liking.'
word_study.significance: The verb choice emphasizes that the young animals are not merely alive but thriving, growing robust, developing the strength they will need for independent survival. This is presented as a natural and positive development. For Job, the implication is that children are meant to grow strong and leave, not to remain dependent or to return seeking parental support.

word_study.transliteration: rabah (to multiply, to increase, to grow)
word_study.meaning: To increase, to multiply, to grow in number or size. The verb rabah is used throughout Scripture for multiplication and growth (Genesis 1:22, 'Be fruitful and multiply'), for the increase of flocks and herds, for the growth of populations. In verse 4, yirbu va-bar ('they increase in the open field') describes the young animals' development in the wilderness, away from human or maternal protection.
word_study.significance: The verb rabah emphasizes organic, natural growth. The young grow without being formally 'raised' in the sense of being monitored or managed. They develop in the open, in the wilderness, in the condition of freedom and wildness. Their growth happens according to natural processes, not according to parental planning or control.

word_study.meaning: Field, wilderness, open country. The word bar refers to open terrain not domesticated by human cultivation. It appears frequently in descriptions of wild spaces where animals roam free (Psalm 80:13, 'The boar from the forest destroys it' [min-yaar]). In verse 4, bar refers to the open field where the young animals grow and develop independently.
word_study.significance: The choice of bar ('open field, wilderness') rather than gina ('enclosed garden') or sa'deh ('cultivated field') emphasizes the wildness and freedom of the young animals' development. They are not contained; they are not domesticated; they develop in open, untamed space. This is not presented as deprivation but as the natural and proper environment for wild creatures.

word_study.transliteration: yatsa' (to go out, to go forth, to depart)
word_study.meaning: To go out, to depart, to emerge, to exit. The verb yatsa' is one of the most frequent verbs in Hebrew, used for any kind of going forth or departure (Genesis 2:10, 'A river flowed out of Eden'; Exodus 3:10, 'Come, I will send you to Pharaoh'). In verse 4, yatse'u describes the young animals leaving their parents.
word_study.significance: The verb yatsa' is neutral and natural. The young animals do not 'flee' (nutzach) or 'escape' (malat); they 'go forth.' This is not presented as an emergency or a tragedy but as a normal, natural movement. The separation is not traumatic; it is biological.

word_study.transliteration: shuv (to return, to turn back, to come back)
word_study.meaning: To return, to come back, to turn back. The verb shuv is fundamental to biblical repentance (teshuva, 'returning' to God). In verse 4, the negative form 'velo shavu lamo' ('and they did not return to them') emphasizes the permanent nature of the separation. The young do not come back.
word_study.significance: The use of shuv ('to return') creates a stark theological implication: just as the animals do not return to their parents after going forth, so too there is a point beyond which certain separations are permanent and irreversible. For Job, the loss of his children is not a temporary separation but a permanent severance. The animals' young demonstrate that such permanent separation is part of the natural order ordained by God.

word_study.meaning: To them, for them. The suffix lahem is the third masculine plural indirect object pronoun, referring back to the animal parents (the wild goats and hinds of verses 1-2). The young animals do not return 'to them' — to their mothers and fathers.
word_study.significance: The personal pronoun emphasizes the emotional dimension: the parents lose their young. This is not merely a biological fact but a relational one. The parents do not see their young again. This is presented not as a tragedy but as an inherent feature of wild animal life. Job, who has lost his children, is confronted with the reality that such loss is part of creation's design.

cross_references.connection: God's first blessing is 'Be fruitful and multiply,' establishing reproduction and growth as divinely ordained. Verse 4's description of young animals growing strong illustrates the fulfillment of this original blessing.

'Therefore a man leaves his father and his mother and cleaves to his wife,' establishing the principle that children naturally leave their parents — a principle illustrated in the animal world in verse 4.
The psalmist mentions 'the boar from the forest destroys it,' using the language of wildness and the open field (bar/forest) similar to verse 4's description of young animals thriving in the open.

The narrative summary of Job's losses: 'your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother's house, when suddenly a great wind swept across the desert and struck the four corners of the house.' Job's lost children are the implicit context for understanding God's question about animal young who depart and never return.

'Train up a child in the way he should go; even when old, he will not depart from it,' establishing the cultural ideal that children are raised to independence, which verse 4 shows happens naturally in the animal world.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern pastoral and agricultural societies, the weaning and independence of young animals were observable, predictable processes. Young cattle, goats, and sheep would be nursed, would develop strength on open pasture, and would eventually be separated from their mothers — through sale, slaughter, or simply natural drift into independent herds. The biblical audience would have witnessed this cycle repeatedly. The observation that young animals 'go forth and do not return' would have been empirically true and culturally familiar. However, its theological application — the suggestion that separation between parent and child is natural and irreversible — would have carried weight. In cultures with strong family bonds and expectations of filial duty, the assertion that nature itself ordains separation and non-return is a pointed challenge to assumptions about permanence and obligation in family relationships.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 2 Nephi 31:19-20, Nephi describes the path of discipleship as one of pressing forward 'with steadfastness in Christ, having a perfect brightness of hope, and a love of God and of all men.' The language of 'going forth' appears frequently in the Book of Mormon (Mosiah 7:14, 'they went forth into the wilderness'). The principle of leaving parents and establishing independent covenant relationships is central to Book of Mormon theology: one enters the covenant of baptism as an individual, not as an extension of parental faith.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 58:26-29 establishes the principle of agency and stewardship: 'Verily I say, the Lord willeth that the inhabitants of the earth shall know that there is a God; and that he is God, and to bring about his infinite designs, he worketh not among the children of men upon the same principle by which he worketh among other creations... if you love me you will keep my commandments; and the blessings which I promise unto you are not of temporal but of spiritual blessings.' Parents are stewards of children, not possessors. The young must go forth to establish their own covenants.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Temple theology teaches that each individual stands before God in covenant, not as an extension of parental covenant. Children are 'given' to parents in mortality but belong ultimately to God and must make their own covenants at the age of accountability. Verse 4's principle — that young go forth and do not return — illustrates the necessity of this independent relationship with God.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus leaves His earthly family (Matthew 12:46-50: 'Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?'), establishing a new covenant family not based on biological descent but on discipleship. Jesus also teaches that disciples must 'leave father and mother' to follow Him (Matthew 19:29). The animals' young in verse 4, going forth and not returning, prefigure the pattern of separation and new covenant relationship that Jesus establishes. Yet Jesus also promises 'You will be filled with joy and gladness' rather than loss (John 16:22), suggesting that the separation serves the good of those who depart.
commentary.application: This verse speaks directly to parents who must release their children into adulthood and independence. The natural world demonstrates that such release is not failure but fulfillment. Children are meant to grow strong, leave their parents, and establish their own lives. The sadness of this separation is natural, but clinging to children beyond the season of dependence is a violation of natural order. For adult children, the verse offers permission to depart fully, to 'not return' in the sense of not remaining psychologically dependent or obligated to parents' expectations. The young animals illustrate a principle: there is a proper time and way for separation. For those who have lost children (as Job has), the verse offers the grim acknowledgment that such separation, when it occurs through death, is indeed permanent and absolute. This is not comforting language, but it is honest language about the nature of loss in a world governed by natural laws that even God does not override.

text_kjv: Who hath sent out the wild ass free? or who hath loosed the bands of the wild ass?

commentary.narrative:
With verse 5, God shifts from goats and deer to the wild donkey (pere, onager), and the question shifts from reproductive processes to freedom itself. 'Who sent out the wild donkey free? Who untied the bonds of the wild donkey?' This is no longer a question about knowledge God possesses and humans lack; it is a question about a deliberate divine decision. God made the wild donkey free. God untied the ropes binding it. The theological implication is revolutionary: God created at least one creature whose entire being is organized around freedom, and God delighted in that freedom even though the creature is useless to human purposes.

The word chofshi ('free') is the legal term for a freed slave (Exodus 21:2, 'If you buy a Hebrew slave, he shall serve six years, and in the seventh he shall go out for nothing, for free [chofshi]'). The wild donkey is 'emancipated' — not by accident, not as a deficit, but as a divine declaration. It was never enslaved because God chose it for freedom before it existed. The parallel image of 'bands' or 'moserot' ('fetters, bonds, restraints') being loosened emphasizes that someone had to actively remove constraints that might otherwise bind the creature. The rhetorical question 'Who did this?' contains its answer: God and God alone. No human sent the wild donkey out free; no human loosed its bonds. God did. And God did it deliberately, knowing that this creature would be wild, untamable, and useless for human purposes. The theological challenge to Job is profound: If God delights in the freedom of a useless wild donkey, why does Job assume that everything in creation exists to serve human purposes? Why does Job assume that God owes him an explanation of cosmic order in terms Job can understand or judge?

word_study.meaning: Wild donkey, onager. The pere is the untamed counterpart to the domesticated donkey (chamor). The pere inhabits arid steppes and deserts across the ancient Near East. Unlike the domesticated donkey, which responds to training and serves human purposes, the pere is fundamentally untamable. It is mentioned throughout Scripture as a symbol of wildness and uncontrollable independence (Genesis 16:12, where Ishmael is prophesied to be 'a wild donkey of a man'; Isaiah 32:14, where abandoned cities become habitat for wild donkeys; Jeremiah 2:24, 'a young she-ass accustomed to the wilderness'; Hosea 8:9, 'Ephraim has hired himself out to lovers, ephraim shall become like an oestral wild ass').
word_study.significance: The choice of the pere (wild donkey) rather than any other creature is deliberate. The pere is not just wild; it is wild in a way that humans recognize and understand, because the domesticated version exists. The wild donkey represents what the domesticated donkey might have been but is not — free, untamed, self-directed. By asking 'Who set the pere free?' God is asking Job to consider a creature that embodies the principle of freedom and to recognize that God created and sustains this principle even when it serves no human advantage.

word_study.transliteration: shalach (to send, to send out, to release)
word_study.meaning: To send, to send out, to dispatch, to release. The verb shalach appears frequently in the context of sending people or objects away (Genesis 37:14, 'So he said, "Go now, see if it is well with your brothers and the flocks, and bring me word." So he sent him out of the valley of Hebron'; Exodus 12:39, 'So the people took their dough before the yeast was added, and carried it on their shoulders in kneading-bowls wrapped in clothing'). In verse 5, the theological sense is of divine release or emancipation: God 'sent out' the wild donkey as a deliberate act.
word_study.significance: The verb shalach emphasizes agency and decision. This was not an accident or an oversight. God intentionally 'sent out' the pere (wild donkey). God released it into the world as a creature of freedom. The verb choice suggests purposefulness: God knew what He was creating, and He created it freely.

word_study.meaning: Free, liberated, exempt from service or obligation. The adjective chofshi is derived from chofesh ('freedom, liberty'). In legal texts, a slave declared chofshi is legally free, released from all obligation to serve. In verse 5, the wild donkey is described as chofshi — not enslaved, not domesticated, not obligated to serve anyone. It exists in a state of absolute freedom.
word_study.significance: By using the legal term chofshi ('free'), God elevates the wild donkey's freedom to the status of a divinely ordained legal condition. The animal is not merely wild by accident; it is free by divine decree. This is theologically significant: God values freedom as a created good, not merely as an absence of constraint. The wild donkey's freedom is not a deficit or a problem to be solved; it is a positive aspect of creation.

word_study.transliteration: moserah (pl. moserot), from the root asar (to bind)
word_study.meaning: Bonds, fetters, cords, restraints. The word moserot refers to any kind of binding device — chains, ropes, cords used to restrain animals or prisoners. The root asar ('to bind') appears throughout Scripture in contexts of constraint: Samson bound with moserot (Judges 15:14), Jeremiah bound in moserot (Jeremiah 40:1). In verse 5, the rhetorical question assumes that someone might have bound the wild donkey with moserot, and then someone (God) removed those bonds.
word_study.significance: The image of 'loosed bonds' reinforces that freedom was actively granted, not accidentally achieved. Someone had to untie the ropes. The question 'Who loosed them?' assumes an answer: God and God alone. The theological point is that freedom is not a default state but a deliberate divine gift.

word_study.meaning: Wild donkey, onager. A synonym for pere (wild donkey), used for variety in poetic parallelism. The arod emphasizes the same creature — the untamed, semi-wild equine of the ancient Near Eastern deserts.
word_study.significance: The parallelism between pere and arod ('wild donkey... onager') creates poetic emphasis: the same creature is addressed from two different angles (freedom and bondage), suggesting that the creature's identity is thoroughly wrapped up in these two poles. It is the freed creature; it is the one from whom bonds have been loosened.

cross_references.connection: Ishmael is prophesied to be 'a wild donkey of a man [pere adam],' using the same pere to describe a human being whose essential nature is untamable freedom and resistance to constraint.

The law establishes that a Hebrew slave shall serve 'six years, and in the seventh he shall go out for nothing, for free [chofshi],' using the identical word chofshi ('free') that describes the wild donkey in verse 5.

The prophet describes judgment: 'The fortress is abandoned, the city is deserted; the hill and the watchtower become permanent dens and joys of wild donkeys [pere],' connecting the pere to desolation and divine judgment.

'A wild ass accustomed to the wilderness, in her heat sniffing the wind! Who can restrain her lust? None who seek her need tire themselves; in her month they will find her,' using the pere (wild donkey, female) as a metaphor for Israel's unfaithfulness.

God's previous questions about the lion seeking its prey and the raven crying out for food establish a pattern of God valuing wild creatures' independence and autonomy, which continues in the pere (wild donkey) of verse 5.

commentary.historical_context: The pere (wild donkey, onager) was endemic to the steppe regions of the ancient Near East, particularly the arid regions east of the Jordan and south of the Dead Sea. Unlike the domesticated donkey (chamor), which had been tamed and used for transportation and burden-bearing since at least the 3rd millennium BCE, the pere resisted domestication. Ancient Near Eastern texts and iconography celebrate the pere as a symbol of wildness and untamed vigor. The ancient audience would have understood the contrast: humans had successfully domesticated one equine species (the donkey) but could not domesticate its wild cousin. The pere represented a boundary of human power — there were things in creation that humans could not master or control. By asking 'Who sent the pere out free?', God is asking Job to acknowledge a dimension of creation that exceeds human purpose and human power.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon emphasizes agency — the ability and responsibility of humans to choose. In 2 Nephi 2:26-27, Lehi teaches 'Wherefore, men are free according to the flesh... and they are free to choose liberty and eternal life... or to choose captivity and death... they are free to act for themselves and not to be acted upon.' The pere (wild donkey) in verse 5 embodies this principle of freedom to act for oneself, to refuse constraint, to follow one's own path. Yet the Book of Mormon emphasizes that this freedom is most fully realized when aligned with God's will.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 29:39 states 'I am the Lord thy God, and I gave unto you the lesser law, until the fulness should be revealed,' suggesting that God grants creatures (and humans) different measures of law and liberty. The pere (wild donkey) is given the law of wildness and freedom. Humans are given higher law that includes covenant and restraint. Each is appropriate to the creature.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Temple theology teaches that freedom and covenant are not opposites but complements: humans enter covenants freely, and their freedom is most fully realized within those covenants. The pere (wild donkey) represents a different kind of creature — one whose freedom is expressed in absolute independence. Humans are invited to a higher order: freely chosen covenant relationship with God.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus teaches 'If the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed' (John 8:36), emphasizing that true freedom comes from relationship with Christ, not from the absence of constraint. Yet Jesus also voluntarily submits to constraint: 'Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will' (Matthew 26:39). Jesus does not embody the pere's (wild donkey's) freedom of absolute independence; rather, He exemplifies the freedom of willing submission to the Father's will. The contrast between the pere's freedom and Christ's freedom is instructive: the pere is free to act according to its nature (wildness, independence). Christ is free to choose the Father's will perfectly, which involves voluntary constraint.
commentary.application: In contemporary culture, this verse strikes against the assumption that freedom means the absence of all constraint or obligation. The wild donkey is presented as genuinely free, yet its freedom is expressed within the boundaries of its nature: it lives in deserts, eats desert plants, runs in herds, responds to the seasons. Its freedom is not chaos; it is the expression of its nature. For modern readers, the verse invites a reconsideration of what freedom means. Is freedom the ability to act without any constraint (the pere's kind of freedom)? Or is freedom the ability to act according to one's deepest nature and values, even if that nature includes voluntary constraints (the kind of freedom the gospel offers)? The verse also challenges any assumption that God demands utility from creation. The pere serves no human purpose. It is not domesticated, it cannot be ridden, it will not plow. Yet God celebrates its freedom. This suggests that some of God's creative delight is expressed in things that serve no human end — wildness, freedom, beauty that no one harnesses or masters.

text_kjv: Whose house I have made the wilderness, and the barren land his dwellings.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 6 completes the description of the wild donkey by describing its habitat. God did not merely set the pere (wild donkey) free; God also gave it a home — but what a home it is: the wilderness, the salt flats, the places no sane person would choose to live. The Covenant Rendering's rendering captures the starkness: 'I made the wasteland its home and the salt flats its dwelling.' The aravah ('desert plain, steppe, wilderness') is not a garden; it is a place of scarcity, heat, and desolation. The melechah ('salt-crusted terrain, salt flats') is even more barren — salt-encrusted land where nothing grows, where the earth itself is toxic to most life. Yet this is what God gave to the wild donkey. This is its house. This is its dwelling place.

The theology here is subtle but profound. God could have made the wild donkey beautiful and noble, fit to live in green valleys and fertile lowlands where humans also dwell. Instead, God made it to thrive in places humans have abandoned or never attempted to settle. The pere's home is the anti-city, the anti-garden, the anti-civilization. Its habitat is defined by its hostility to human habitation and use. This is deliberate. God assigned the pere its place, and that place is precisely where the human-ordered world cannot reach. The question is implicit: If this is how God cares for the pere — by giving it a home in the wilderness, a dwelling in the salt flats — then why does Job insist that everything God creates must serve human purposes? Why does Job assume that God's attention and care is limited to what humans can understand, control, or benefit from? The wild donkey's home in the wilderness suggests that God's care extends to the useless, the untamed, the uncontrollable, the places beyond civilization.

word_study.meaning: House, home, dwelling place, household. The word bayit is foundational to Hebrew vocabulary for human habitation and family structure. In verse 6, God uses this domestic, familial term — 'house' — to describe the wild donkey's habitat. This is surprising: a house is typically a structure humans build; here God is calling the wilderness a 'house.' The paradox is theological: what is a 'house' or 'home' is not what humans would choose, yet it is genuine home to the creature.
word_study.significance: By using the term beito ('its house'), God personifies the wild donkey's relationship to the wilderness: the wilderness is as much the pere's home as a human's house is the human's home. This is not deprivation or exile; this is genuine dwelling. The theological implication is that God provides homes appropriate to each creature's nature, and the wildness of the pere's home is not a problem but a perfection.

word_study.transliteration: sim / sum (to put, to place, to set, to make)
word_study.meaning: To put, to place, to set, to establish. The verb sim is the first-person singular perfect 'I made/set.' In verse 6, God uses the first person: 'I made [samti] the wasteland its home.' This is a divine claim of ownership and assignment: God is the one who designated the wilderness as the pere's habitat.
word_study.significance: The choice of first person ('I made') emphasizes God's personal involvement in the assignment of habitats. God did not leave these things to chance; God deliberately set the pere in the wilderness. This is an act of divine creativity and sovereignty. The same verb (sim) is used when God 'sets' or 'places' humans in the Garden (Genesis 2:8, 'And the Lord God planted a garden in Eden, in the east; and there he put [sim] the man whom he had formed'). The wild donkey's placement in the wilderness is as deliberate as humanity's placement in Eden.

word_study.meaning: Desert plain, steppe, wilderness, arid region. The aravah specifically refers to the valley regions that are dry, relatively level, and largely uninhabited. The term is used particularly for the Jordan Valley and the regions south of the Dead Sea. The aravah is not absolute desert (like the Negev or the Syrian desert to the east) but a semi-arid steppe where little grows and human settlement is sparse.
word_study.significance: The choice of aravah rather than midbar ('wilderness, desert') is significant. The aravah is not the worst possible environment; it is livable for those adapted to it (like the pere), but it is clearly a marginal, demanding environment for humans. God chose this place as the pere's home — a place where the creature would thrive but humans would struggle.

word_study.meaning: Salt, salt-encrusted terrain, salt flats. The melechah is terrain so saturated with salt that vegetation cannot grow. The Covenant Rendering's 'salt flats' captures the environmental reality: these are places where salt has accumulated to the point of toxicity. Such places exist in the ancient Near East, particularly around the Dead Sea and other arid regions where water evaporates and leaves salt deposits behind. The Psalmist uses similar language to describe desolation: 'I became a monster to you; yet I do not hide from you. I am like a wasteland, like a barren [salt-strewn?] place' (Psalm 88:8-9).
word_study.significance: The choice of melechah ('salt flats') emphasizes extreme barrenness. Salt flats are not merely poor soil; they are anti-soil, places where the earth itself is hostile to life. Yet this is the dwelling God assigned to the pere. The theological implication is stark: God cares for creatures even in the harshest environments. God is not limited to beautiful or productive creation; God extends care to the marginal, the harsh, the apparently useless.

word_study.meaning: Dwelling place, habitation, tent. The word mishkan is related to the verb shakan ('to dwell, to tabernacle'). In verse 6, mishkenotav ('its dwellings') refers to the places where the pere dwells. The plural 'dwellings' (mishkenot) suggests multiple dwelling places — the pere does not stay in one location but moves through various habitats within the wilderness and salt-flat regions. Interestingly, mishkan is also the term used for the 'Tabernacle' in the Torah — God's dwelling place among Israel. The parallel is subtle but present: the pere has its mishkenot (dwellings) in the wilderness just as God has His mishkan (tabernacle) among the people.
word_study.significance: The word choice mishkenot ('dwellings, habitations') elevates the pere's habitat from mere survival space to genuine home. These are not temporary refuges but established dwellings, places the creature knows and inhabits. The plural form suggests that the pere knows many such places, moves among them, and considers them all home. This is not exile or deprivation; this is genuine dwelling.

cross_references.connection: God 'planted a garden in Eden, in the east; and there he put [sim] the man whom he had formed,' using the same verb samti ('I made/set') as verse 6, establishing the parallel that both humans and the pere are deliberately placed in appropriate habitats.

The psalmist celebrates that God 'sends springs into the valleys; they flow among the hills... By them the birds of the heavens have their habitation,' extending the principle that God provides habitats for all creatures, not just humans.

'For the palace will be forsaken, the populous city deserted; the hill and the watchtower will become dens forever, a joy of wild donkeys [pere], pasture of flocks,' describing the wild donkey inhabiting the ruins and wasteland that humans have abandoned.

The psalmist describes himself as 'like a wasteland, like a barren place,' using similar language of desolation and salt-encrusted terrain to describe spiritual abandonment, creating a contrast with God's deliberate care for the pere.

Jesus teaches that God provides for the birds and the lilies of the field; verse 6 illustrates this principle concretely by showing that God provides appropriate habitat even for creatures in barren places.

commentary.historical_context: The aravah and the melechah regions were well-known to the biblical audience as places of extreme environmental challenge. The aravah (the valley of the Jordan and the regions south of the Dead Sea) was sparsely populated and considered marginal for human habitation. The melechah ('salt flats') were particularly inhospitable, with high salinity making traditional agriculture impossible. Yet the pere (wild donkey) was known to thrive in these very regions. Archaeological evidence and ancient Near Eastern texts confirm that the wild donkey was endemic to the arid steppes and semi-desert regions of the Levant and Mesopotamia. It was not an animal humans could hunt or herd effectively; it was wild, swift, and adapted to marginal lands. By asking Job to consider the pere's home in the wilderness and salt flats, God is using an empirically true observation: there are creatures that belong in places where humans do not flourish, and these creatures are provided for and sustained by God.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon emphasizes that God provides for His people even in wilderness conditions. Nephi says 'And we did sojourn for the space of many years in the wilderness... and we did perform all manner of labor, and we did make all manner of tools' (1 Nephi 17:7-8). The wilderness is a place of trial but also of divine care. Similarly, the pere's wilderness home is a place of challenge but also of God's sustaining care. The principle is that God's care is not limited to comfortable or civilized places.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 88:62-65 teaches 'And again, I say unto you, he hath given a law unto all things, by which they move in their times and their seasons; And their courses are fixed, even the courses of the heavens and the earth, which comprehend the earth and all the planets; And they give light to each other in their times and in their seasons, in their glory, according to their creation.' The pere in its wilderness home operates according to the law given to it by God. Its courses are fixed, its seasons are appointed. It thrives in the salt flats because God has given it the nature and law suited to that place.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Temple theology teaches that God has ordered all things in their places and degrees of glory. The pere, dwelling in the wilderness and salt flats, occupies its appointed place in creation, which is glorious and appropriate to its nature. Humans have a different place — the cultivated garden, eventually the celestial kingdom. Each creature has its proper sphere, and God sustains each in its place.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus taught 'Foxes have holes and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head' (Matthew 8:20). Jesus does not have a permanent home; He dwells in the wilderness with the outcasts and the poor, much as the pere dwells in the salt flats. Yet Jesus's homelessness is voluntary and redemptive — it is the condition of His ministry. The pere's wilderness home is not voluntary but suited to its nature. The contrast illuminates both: the pere accepts its place as natural; Jesus voluntarily accepts a place of displacement for the sake of redemption.
commentary.application: Verse 6 challenges contemporary assumptions about progress and civilization. We tend to view civilization, agriculture, and urbanization as improvements on 'mere' wilderness. The verse suggests a different perspective: the wilderness is not inferior to the city; it is simply different, suited to different creatures and different ways of life. For those who feel displaced or marginal — those whose gifts do not fit neatly into civilization's demands, whose nature leads them to wilderness experiences or countercultural paths — verse 6 offers theological dignity. God assigns habitats. God's care is not limited to the cultivated and controlled; it extends to the wild and the marginal. For those struggling with their place in the world, the verse suggests: perhaps you, like the pere, are suited to places and circumstances others would avoid. That is not a failure; that is your appointed dwelling. God knew what He was making when He made you; God assigned you your place; God sustains you there.

text_kjv: He scorneth the multitude of the city, neither regardeth he the crying of the driver.

commentary.narrative: God's rhetorical question pivots from the wonders of natural birth and animal instinct to the question of human control over creation. The wild donkey—utterly indifferent to human civilization—becomes the first example of a creature that refuses to be domesticated or dominated. The verb "scorneth" (yischaq) carries the sense of mocking laughter; the donkey does not merely ignore the city's noise; it actively finds human society absurd and contemptible. The translator notes reveal that the Hebrew sachaq expresses a kind of contempt rooted in fundamental incompatibility. The wild donkey lives according to its own nature, not human expectation.
commentary.narrative_continued: The second half of the verse introduces the "driver" (noges), the same Hebrew term used for Egyptian slave-drivers in Exodus. This is not accidental word choice. God is drawing a deliberate parallel: just as Pharaoh's taskmasters could not ultimately control the Hebrew people, no driver or taskmaster can compel the wild donkey. The creature is constitutionally immune to coercion. This moves the discourse beyond mere animal husbandry into the realm of freedom and divine design. The wild donkey embodies a principle: God creates some beings with an inviolable freedom that no system of domination—no whip, no fence, no shout—can suppress.
commentary.significance: For Job, who has been arguing about justice and divine obligation, this is a startling revelation. The universe contains creatures that are radically free, that neither owe service to humans nor answer to human calls. This does not suggest chaos; rather, it suggests that creation operates on principles beyond human utility and control. Some things God made for their own sake, not for ours. The wild donkey's laughter at the city is the laughter of a being who knows something the taskmaster does not: that there are ways of being in the world that transcend the master-servant relationship entirely.
commentary.application: Modern readers often assume that God's purpose in creation is human utility—that animals exist for our use, that nature should be managed and controlled, that all beings should ultimately serve human ends. Job 39:7 disrupts this assumption. The wild donkey teaches that some creatures exist for their own sake, according to their own nature, indifferent to human projects and expectations. This has implications for how we approach creation: not everything can or should be domesticated. Some wildness, some refusal to be tamed, reflects divine design. In personal spiritual life, this verse invites humility: not everything in God's creation is about you. Some things exist according to their own nature, and your role is to recognize that beauty and freedom rather than assume you can control it.
commentary.christological_typology: The wild donkey's radical freedom and contempt for human systems of control foreshadows the Savior's freedom from worldly authority. Christ refused to be bound by the political, religious, or social expectations imposed upon Him. He laughed (metaphorically) at the Pharisees' systems of control and power. Yet unlike the wild donkey, Christ chose submission—not because He had to, but because love and covenant required it. The contrast highlights Christ's voluntary nature of His sacrifice.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 17:33, Nephi speaks of how the Lord made the waters to divide so that the Israelites could cross on dry ground. Just as the wild donkey was made free by its nature, the waters obey God's command. Yet Nephi's point is about divine power and human obedience. Job's point is the inverse: God made some creatures with a nature that resists all human command. The Book of Mormon generally emphasizes human agency and responsibility; Job 39 introduces the reality that not all creatures share human moral accountability.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 38:1 identifies God as the one who made all things, and D&C 104:14-18 teaches that 'all things are the Lord's, and he hath made man steward over them.' Yet Job 39 presents creatures that cannot be stewarded—the wild ox and wild donkey exist outside the stewardship model. This suggests that divine creation includes a sphere of radical freedom that no human stewardship can encompass. Some things God made for their own glorification, not for human use.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple worship, initiates learn about divine order, obedience to covenant, and human exaltation. The wild donkey and wild ox in Job 39 present a counterpoint: they are God's creations who live in perfect alignment with their nature without covenant obligation or temple ordinance. They teach that not all of creation is oriented toward human salvation or exaltation. Their freedom is not rebellion but a different kind of divine ordering.

commentary.historical_context: The wild donkey (Hebrew pere) inhabited the semi-arid regions of the ancient Near East, particularly the deserts and mountain ranges surrounding Mesopotamia and Palestine. Unlike domesticated donkeys, which were essential beasts of burden in ancient agriculture and trade, the wild donkey remained untamable and roamed in herds. Ancient Near Eastern texts (including Sumerian and Akkadian literature) describe wild asses as creatures of the steppe that could not be captured or controlled. Archaeological evidence suggests they were occasionally hunted for food but never successfully domesticated. The contrast between the city (representing human civilization, order, and control) and the wild donkey's mountain habitat reflects the ancient perception of these zones as fundamentally opposed ecological and social spaces. For an ancient Israelite, the city was the center of law, governance, and labor systems; the wilderness was the realm of freedom and divine presence (as seen in the wilderness accounts throughout Scripture).

cross_references.connection: God hears the cry of His enslaved people and remembers the noges (taskmasters) oppressing them. The wild donkey's freedom from the noges mirrors the divine concern for liberation from oppression.
The Lord laughs (yischaq) at His enemies who defy Him. The wild donkey's laughter at human civilization parallels divine laughter at human presumption.
Nephi describes how men scorn (sachaq) the words of the prophets, showing that mocking laughter is the typical response to what opposes human desires—as the wild donkey mocks the city's expectations.

The Lord tells the Saints that the earth is sanctified and that all things are for the use of man in the Lord's time. Yet the wild donkey shows that some creatures exist for their own sake, beyond human dominion.

word_study.meaning: to laugh, to mock, to deride. The root sachaq appears throughout Scripture to denote laughter that expresses contempt or scorn (e.g., Genesis 21:6, Psalm 2:4). Here it is the laughter of derision—the wild donkey finds human civilization beneath notice.
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering ('it laughs') better captures the active derision than the KJV's 'scorneth.' The wild donkey is not passively ignoring; it is actively mocking. This suggests a consciousness, a judgment about the absurdity of human social structures from the perspective of a free creature.

word_study.meaning: tumult, noise, crowd, multitude. The word carries connotations of disorder, commotion, and the chaotic sound of many voices or activity. In Job 39:7, it is the cacophony of the city.
word_study.significance: The wild donkey's environment—open mountains—is quiet. The city's hamon is foreign to its nature. The contrast between the mountain's silence and the city's noise frames the donkey's world as one of natural peace, opposed to human bustle.

word_study.meaning: one who drives, a taskmaster, an oppressor. The same word appears in Exodus 3:7, 5:6, and other passages describing Egyptian slavedrivers who imposed forced labor on the Hebrews.
word_study.significance: The deliberate use of the Exodus term elevates the wild donkey's refusal to a covenantal significance. Just as God freed His people from Pharaoh's taskmasters, the wild donkey is constitutionally free from any human noges. This suggests that freedom from oppression is woven into creation itself.

word_study.meaning: cries, shouts, calls. The plural form emphasizes the repeated, insistent calls of the driver trying to command the animal.
word_study.significance: The donkey simply does not hear—not because it is deaf, but because the driver's authority holds no sway over it. The verbal command, the fundamental tool of mastery, is rendered powerless.

text_kjv: The range of the mountains is his pasture, and he searcheth after every green thing.

commentary.narrative: Having established that the wild donkey refuses human civilization and control, God now describes its habitat and sustenance. The verse presents a complete picture of radical self-sufficiency: the entire mountain range is its pasture. There is no owner, no fence, no boundary marker defining what the donkey can and cannot graze. The mountains themselves become the measure of the creature's domain—vast, open, and wholly free. This is not subsistence living constrained by scarcity; it is abundance accessed through freedom. The wild donkey does not ask permission; it does not negotiate with shepherds or farmers. It simply goes where it wishes and finds what it needs.
commentary.narrative_continued: The second clause introduces a profound theological resonance: the donkey "searches after every green thing" using the verb darash, the identical Hebrew word used throughout Scripture for seeking God (e.g., Psalm 24:6, Isaiah 55:6). The translator notes make this connection explicit. The same intensity of desire, the same yearning quality that characterizes a worshipper's pursuit of the divine, characterizes the donkey's search for food. This is not mere animal foraging; it is a quest, a seeking. The donkey's entire existence is a kind of worship—not worship of God, but worship of its own nature and its own survival. It seeks with the wholeness that human beings are called to seek God.
commentary.significance: This verse completes the portrait: the wild donkey is free from the city (verse 7), roaming an unbounded territory, and sustained by its own seeking. It depends on God (green things grow by divine provision), yet it owes nothing to human systems. For Job, this is radical. It means that a creature can be entirely dependent on God's provision without being subject to human authority. It means that freedom and divine sustenance are not mutually exclusive. It means that the world contains beings who live in perfect alignment with their nature without hierarchy, without masters, without the social structures Job has been arguing about throughout the book.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse disrupts any assumption that spiritual seeking should be settled, passive, or occasional. The wild donkey's constant search (yidrosh) for green things—using the same verb applied to seeking God—models a spiritual intensity that should characterize our discipleship. We are called to 'seek' with the wholeness of our being, constantly, through all the mountains and valleys of our lives. Yet like the donkey, our seeking should be rooted in freedom, not fear; in trust, not anxiety. The creature does not fear that green things will not be found; it simply seeks, knowing that the world is provision. What would it mean to seek God—through prayer, scripture, temple, service—with the unreserved intensity and confidence of the wild donkey seeking verdure?
commentary.christological_typology: Christ, like the wild donkey, withdrew to mountains and wilderness spaces for prayer, seeking communion with the Father (Matthew 4:1-4, Luke 5:16). His sustenance came not from the systems of the world but from 'every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God' (Matthew 4:4). The Savior's constant seeking of His Father's will mirrors the donkey's constant search—both represent perfect alignment with the source of sustenance. Yet Christ was eventually bound, sacrificed, brought to the city He had mocked (metaphorically) through His teaching. Unlike the wild donkey who escapes all bindings, Christ allowed Himself to be bound out of love.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 17:8-9, Nephi describes how the Lord led his family through the wilderness, and 'we did take our journey in the wilderness with our children.' Like the wild donkey, Nephi's family roamed lands as their pasture, depending on God's provision rather than stored agriculture. The Book of Mormon repeatedly portrays the wilderness journey as a space where dependence on God becomes immediate and unavoidable. The wild donkey in Job 39 represents an entire way of being that the Book of Mormon narratively explores: radical freedom from human systems paired with total dependence on divine sustenance.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:24-25 describes how God gave the earth to man, but D&C 59:17-19 teaches that the beasts of the field and the birds of the air 'belong to the Lord' and should be used 'with judgment, not for sport.' The wild donkey's freedom to roam mountains and search for sustenance represents a use of creation that honors the creature's own nature rather than subordinating it entirely to human utility. This aligns with the Restoration's teaching that stewardship implies care for the creature's wellbeing, not merely its exploitation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, the initiate learns about moving through different kingdoms and states of being. The wild donkey's constant roaming through mountains—seeking, moving, never settling—prefigures the temple journey itself, a constant seeking for sustenance and light, moving through different realms of understanding. The mountains themselves, in temple theology, often represent exaltation and high places of divine encounter.

commentary.historical_context: The wild donkey's habitat in the ancient Near East was the semi-arid steppe and mountain regions—areas with seasonal water sources and vegetation dependent on rainfall. Archaeological and textual evidence suggests that these regions (including the Negev, the Syrian Desert, and areas of Mesopotamia) supported herds of wild asses that migrated seasonally in search of water and vegetation. Unlike the settled agricultural zones where domesticated animals were herded in fixed territories, the wild donkey's habitat was inherently unstable and required constant movement. The vegetation (yaroq) would have been sparse and scattered, requiring the animal's intelligence and persistence to locate. Ancient Semitic cultures understood the wild donkey as emblematic of the steppe—a creature of the liminal space between civilization and true wilderness. The image of seeking in mountains would have resonated strongly with ancient readers for whom mountains were understood as places where God dwelt and where sustenance came directly from divine provision rather than human labor.

cross_references.connection: Moses calls Israel to 'seek the LORD thy God' with the same verb (darash). The wild donkey seeks green things as Israel is called to seek God—with the whole heart, constantly, throughout life.
The psalmist describes 'the generation of them that seek him, that seek thy face, O Jacob' using darash. The wild donkey's search parallels the spiritual seeking that characterizes the righteous.

Isaiah exhorts: 'Seek ye the LORD while he may be found, call ye upon him while he is near.' The wild donkey's constant seeking reflects the spiritual principle of seeking the divine source of all sustenance.
Alma teaches that prayer should be constant and heartfelt. The wild donkey's constant search for green things mirrors the spiritual discipline of constant seeking and prayer.

The Lord teaches that 'light cleaveth unto light' and that seekers find what they seek. The wild donkey seeks green life and finds it because it is oriented toward seeking; this principle applies to spiritual seeking as well.

word_study.meaning: to range, to roam, to wander. The root tur suggests movement without fixed direction, wandering through territory freely.
word_study.significance: Unlike the domesticated animal that stays in one pasture, the wild donkey's movement is characterized by yetur—constant roaming, exploring, claiming vast spaces through its movement. This is not confinement; this is the freedom of exploration.

word_study.meaning: pasture, grazing land. Mir'eh refers to both the place of feeding and the act of grazing. The possessive 'hu' ('his') emphasizes that the pasture belongs to the donkey—or rather, the donkey belongs to the pasture in a reciprocal relationship.
word_study.significance: In ancient pastoral culture, pasture was precious and contested. To claim the mountains as one's pasture is to claim absolute freedom of movement and feeding. No shepherd guards this pasture; no owner disputes the donkey's right to it.

word_study.meaning: to seek, to search for, to inquire. The verb darash is used for seeking God (Deuteronomy 4:29), seeking wisdom (Proverbs 8:17), and seeking righteousness (Isaiah 51:1). It implies intentional, purposeful seeking with longing.
word_study.significance: The TCR translator notes the profound connection: the donkey searches for green things with the same intensity a worshipper searches for God. This elevates the donkey's survival quest to a spiritual dimension—not metaphorically, but in the structure of its being. The wild donkey's existence is a kind of seeking, a constant orientation toward what sustains it.

word_study.meaning: green, verdant, vegetation. Yaroq emphasizes growth, life, freshness—the signs of water and fertility in an arid landscape.
word_study.significance: The wild donkey seeks not mere sustenance but life itself—the green signs of water and growth. This adds a dimension of spiritual hunger to the physical act of grazing. The donkey is drawn to life, to vitality, to the signs of divine provision.

text_kjv: Will the unicorn be willing to serve thee, or abide by thy crib?

commentary.narrative: The discourse shifts from the wild donkey (a creature of the steppe, smaller and more elusive) to the wild ox or aurochs (re'em)—a creature of immense physical power that dwarfs the donkey in scale and strength. The KJV's "unicorn" is a translation based on the Septuagint's monoceros, but modern scholarship recognizes the re'em as the aurochs (Bos primigenius), an extinct wild bovine that stood approximately six feet at the shoulder and possessed massive, dangerous horns. The Hebrew emphasizes this creature's power through the verb "avah" (to be willing, to consent), which frames the question as a matter of the animal's choice or willingness. This is not a question about capability but about will: Will this powerful creature choose to consent to service?
commentary.narrative_continued: The double question structure—will it serve you, or will it lodge by your crib—progressively narrows the scope from active labor to mere dwelling. Even simple cohabitation, the verse implies, is beyond Job's power to command. The wild ox will not consent (avah) to any arrangement with humans. The term "crib" (abus) refers to a feeding trough where domesticated animals are fed and controlled. The juxtaposition is stark: the wild ox, with strength that exceeds human capacity, refuses both labor and the comfortable servitude of the domesticated animal. It will not be persuaded. The phrase "be willing" (hayo'veh) suggests that the animal has a will that is active and contrary. This creature is not helpless or hesitant; it is actively unwilling.
commentary.theological_weight: For Job, whose entire ordeal has been framed around questions of divine justice and human obligation, this verse introduces a creature whose will cannot be violated or overridden. The wild ox has a fundamental freedom that is absolute. No amount of human rhetoric, force, or persuasion will change what the creature by its nature refuses. This moves beyond mere physical strength into the realm of moral or spiritual autonomy. The creature's resistance is not rebellion (it was made that way); it is constitution. God has made a being whose unwillingness is its defining characteristic. For a man who has been arguing about what he owes God and what God owes him, the encounter with a creature that owes nothing and will accept nothing is a profound disruption.
commentary.application: The wild ox's unwillingness teaches an uncomfortable lesson about the limits of control. In modern life, we often assume that if we have enough information, power, resources, or rhetoric, we can persuade any being (human or animal) to serve our purposes. The wild ox announces that this is not true. Some beings—particularly those with strong wills, deep nature, or inherent power—will refuse regardless of what we offer. This applies most acutely to human relationships: you cannot make another person serve your purposes if they have decided to refuse. The gift of agency means that refusal is always possible. For believers, this is liberating: God honors your refusal, just as He respects the wild ox's. You have a will that cannot be overridden. Yet this also means you must honor others' refusal and cannot force the world to bend to your purposes. This is humbling for those accustomed to control.
commentary.christological_typology: The wild ox represents a kind of power and refusal that Christ could have embodied but rejected. In the wilderness, Christ was tempted with power—to turn stones to bread, to leap from the temple, to receive all kingdoms (Matthew 4:1-11). His divine power exceeded the re'em's strength infinitely. Yet Christ chose submission over wild power. Unlike the aurochs that refuses service because it is wild, Christ embraced service because He loved. His power was infinite but His will was subordinated to the Father's (Matthew 26:39). This makes Christ's voluntary service infinitely more profound than the wild ox's refusal.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon emphasizes that all beings possess agency. In 2 Nephi 2:26-27, Lehi teaches that all creatures were granted moral agency—'the Lord God gave unto man that he should act for himself.' The wild ox's refusal to serve reflects an agency that is built into creation. Yet humans, uniquely, are called to covenant and service—to willingly choose submission to God's will. The wild ox's unwillingness illuminates, by contrast, the great gift and burden of human choice to serve or refuse.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:35 teaches that all creatures 'have dominion, and the dominion thereof is given unto the children of men.' Yet Job 39 suggests that this dominion has limits—some creatures have been made with a constitution of freedom that no dominion can overcome. D&C 104:7-8 clarifies that God is 'the owner of all things,' and that humans are merely stewards. The wild ox reminds us that stewardship does not mean unlimited control; it means recognizing and respecting the nature God has given to creatures.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple covenants, the initiate promises obedience and service. The wild ox, by contrast, demonstrates absolute refusal to enter into such a covenant. This contrast underscores the sacred nature of human choice in covenant-making. We are not the wild ox; we possess the capacity to covenant and the responsibility to honor those covenants. Our service differs fundamentally from the creature's refusal because our service is chosen, not instinctual.

commentary.historical_context: The aurochs (re'em) was the wild ancestor of domesticated cattle, standing six feet at the shoulder with massive horns that could span five feet or more. It inhabited the forested and grassland regions of the ancient Near East and survived in Europe until 1627 when the last individual was killed in Poland. Ancient Mesopotamian and Egyptian records describe the aurochs as a dangerous, powerful animal that was occasionally hunted but never successfully domesticated. Unlike wild donkeys, which could sometimes be captured and trained as beasts of burden, the aurochs's temperament and strength made domestication impossible. Ancient Near Eastern hunting texts and artwork depict the aurochs as a quarry for kings and heroes—its defeat symbolized great power. The animal's absolute refusal to be domesticated would have been well-known to ancient Israelites through cultural memory and trade relationships. In the context of Job, the aurochs represented the limits of human power: here was a creature so strong that it could not be forced into service, so wild that it would not consent to it. For an ancient audience, the re'em was the ultimate symbol of power beyond human reach.

cross_references.connection: Balaam declares of Israel: 'God brought them out of Egypt; he hath as it were the strength of an unicorn.' The re'em symbolizes Israel's divinely given power that cannot be cursed or broken by human opposition.

Moses blesses Joseph with the horns of the re'em—'with them he shall push the people together to the ends of the earth.' The re'em's strength is a blessing, but it remains wild and oriented toward its own purposes, not human ones.
The psalmist prays: 'Save me from the lion's mouth: for thou hast heard me from the horns of the unicorns.' The re'em's horns are instruments of danger; the creature is hazardous even in proximity.
Adam is placed in the garden to 'dress it and to keep it'—to serve a divine purpose within creation. The wild ox's refusal to serve contrasts with humanity's created role to tend and steward.

Alma teaches that 'a man is saved no faster than he gains knowledge' and that faith is a voluntary act of will. The wild ox's unwillingness mirrors the principle that no creature can be forced into submission; the will must be engaged.

word_study.meaning: to be willing, to consent, to agree. The verb avah expresses the will of the subject—it is about what the creature chooses or refuses, not what it is forced to do.
word_study.significance: The emphasis on willingness is crucial. God is not asking whether Job can overpower the wild ox (he cannot), but whether it will voluntarily choose to serve. The answer is built into the creature's nature: it will not. This frames servitude as a matter of voluntary consent, not compulsion. The wild ox's refusal is a kind of moral statement.

word_study.meaning: wild ox, aurochs (Bos primigenius). The creature is described elsewhere in Scripture as a symbol of overwhelming strength and power (Numbers 23:22, Deuteronomy 33:17, Psalm 22:21). It was a massive, dangerous bovine, now extinct, which inhabited the ancient Near East.
word_study.significance: The re'em appears consistently in Scripture as a symbol of power that cannot be broken. Its inclusion here emphasizes that raw power, combined with an unwilling nature, is beyond all human dominion. This is not a weak or timid creature. This is strength united with refusal.

word_study.meaning: to serve, to work, to be enslaved. The verb avad describes both free service and forced servitude. In this context, it encompasses any form of labor or service to humans.
word_study.significance: The wild ox will not accept even willing service. The creature's freedom is absolute; it will not enter into any relationship of service or subordination, whether voluntary or forced. This contrasts sharply with humanity's created role in Genesis 2:15 to 'dress and keep' the garden—to serve a purpose within creation.

word_study.meaning: a manger, feeding trough, or crib. The abus is the place where domesticated animals are fed and where they settle, contentedly, under human care.
word_study.significance: The crib represents domestication, comfort, security, and settled life within a human household. The wild ox refuses even this: it will not lodge by the crib, will not accept the role of the settled domestic animal. Its freedom precludes even the comfort of domestication.

text_kjv: Canst thou bind the unicorn with his band in the furrow? or will he harrow the valleys after thee?

commentary.narrative: God presses deeper into the question of usefulness. Even if the wild ox possessed the strength that would make it invaluable to agriculture (which it does), could Job make practical use of it? The verse moves from the question of consent (verse 9) to the question of control—can you bind it? Can you harness it? The Hebrew word telem (furrow) refers to the straight line plowed by a plow drawn by yoked animals. To bind the wild ox to a furrow would be to make it walk in a straight line, obedient to the plow, breaking the soil according to human design. This requires not just strength but submission to direction. The second question—will it harrow the valleys after you—envisions the creature following behind Job, continuing the work, serving as a multiplier of human labor. Both images are agricultural fantasies: the wild ox will do neither.
commentary.theological_implication: The contrast between what the wild ox could do (if broken) and what it will do (nothing) highlights the gap between potential utility and actual refusal. This is the human condition in miniature. Job might have wanted servants who possessed the strength of the re'em but the obedience of a domestic ox. The natural world does not comply with our desires. The creature that would be most useful is precisely the creature that refuses. By introducing the labor fantasy (the ox breaking furrows in straight lines, harrow following), God shows Job the pattern of human hope: we want power without the inconvenience of the creature's will. We want the ox's strength in service to our plan. We will not accept the ox's strength expressed in its refusal.
commentary.the_deeper_reality: Notice that nowhere in these verses does God suggest that the wild ox is disobedient or that breaking it is impossible. Job could, theoretically, break the wild ox's spirit—ancient peoples knew how to do this. But such breaking would destroy the very thing that makes the creature magnificent: its wildness, its power, its authentic nature. God seems to be suggesting that there is something sacred in allowing creatures to be themselves, even when (or especially when) their selves refuse to serve us. This is a profound statement about the nature of creation. It is not all oriented toward human use. Some of it exists to be admired in its refusal.
commentary.application: Modern readers often labor under the illusion that if we can find or create the right systems, structures, or incentives, we can harness any resource (human or animal) to our purposes. The wild ox announces that this is false. There are limits to what can be controlled or directed according to human will. More importantly, this verse invites reflection on what we lose when we insist on harnessing everything to our use. The wild ox's refusal preserves something precious: its authentic nature, untouched by human purpose. In our modern world, where everything tends toward instrumentalization (the viewing of all things, including people, as means to human ends), the wild ox teaches a counter-intuition: some things are most beautiful when left unharnessed, their power expressing itself according to their own nature rather than our designs. What would it mean to honor the 'wildness' of people and creatures around us—their refusal to serve our purposes—not as a frustration but as a form of integrity worth preserving?
commentary.christological_typology: Christ was the ox that could have refused the plow—He possessed divine power that could have rejected the cross. Yet He chose to be bound, willingly accepting the yoke of the atoning sacrifice (Isaiah 53:4-6). Unlike the wild ox that refuses the furrow, Christ walked the hard path laid out for Him, submitting His infinite power to the Father's design. His binding was voluntary; His plowing was redemptive. This contrast—between the ox that refuses all binding and the Savior who embraced binding—illuminates the nature of sacrifice and covenant.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 30:12-16, Korihor argues that humans should not be bound by commandments—that they should be free like the wild creatures. The wild ox in Job 39 seems to support Korihor's point: here is a creature that refuses all binding, all direction, all service. Yet the Book of Mormon consistently teaches that human beings are different: we possess not just the power to refuse, but the capacity to covenant. Our binding—to God, to law, to righteousness—is not slavery but the condition of true freedom (Alma 12:34-37). The wild ox's refusal is freedom without meaning; human covenant is freedom elevated through chosen submission.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 58:26-29 teaches that the 'earth is full of the abundance of the Lord,' but that this abundance is given through law: 'all things have their seasons...and in their seasons all things return unto the bosom of the earth.' The wild ox operates outside of human law and purpose; it follows creation's law, not human agriculture. D&C 82:10 teaches that 'I, the Lord, am bound when ye do what I say; but when ye do not what I say, ye have no promise.' The wild ox shows the inverse: it is not bound by what we say, and it gives us no promise except the promise of refusal.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple celebrates human capacity to enter into binding covenants with God. The wild ox, unable to covenant, represents the limitation of creatures who lack this capacity. Yet the ox's freedom (in its refusal) also reflects a truth: not all of God's creation is oriented toward the covenant structure. Some creatures exist for their own sake, according to their own nature, within the larger cosmic order but not subject to the covenants of the exalted.

commentary.historical_context: Agricultural life in the ancient Near East depended entirely on yoked animals—primarily oxen and donkeys—to break and work the soil. The invention of the plow, drawn by oxen, was transformative for civilization, allowing the expansion of cultivable land and food production. Domesticated oxen were among the most valuable possessions of a family or estate. The ability to harness powerful animals to human purposes was literally the foundation of ancient agricultural prosperity. The wild ox's refusal would have been deeply meaningful to an ancient audience: here was a creature with power that would be incredibly valuable if it would only submit, but it simply will not. The practical reality of ancient agriculture was that this fantasy—the wild ox serving human purpose—was impossible. Wild aurochs were occasionally hunted, but harnessing them was never feasible. The animal's temperament, strength, and refusal to be broken made domestication futile. Archaeological evidence shows no evidence of wild aurochs being yoked or used in agriculture. For an ancient Israelite, the wild ox represented the outer boundary of human dominion: the point where human will meets absolute refusal and cannot proceed.

cross_references.connection: After the Fall, God tells Adam: 'In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread.' Job's desire to harness the wild ox to do his agricultural labor is an attempt to escape the curse of toil—to have power work for him instead of working in sweat himself.

The law prescribes the use of a heifer that has 'never been wrought with.' The wild ox, by contrast, will never be wrought with because it refuses the yoke. Some creatures are constitutionally unsuitable for human service.

Isaiah recalls how God 'which maketh a way in the sea, and a path in the mighty waters...bringeth forth the chariot and horse.' God exercises sovereignty over creation by controlling its movement. The wild ox shows that this sovereignty has limits—not all creatures will follow the path God's people wish for them.

The proverb teaches: 'A whip for the horse, a bridle for the ass: but a rod for the fool's back.' The implication is that different creatures require different governance. The wild ox requires something beyond whips and bridles—it requires the creature's own refusal to bend.

Lehi teaches that all creatures 'have dominion, and the dominion thereof is given unto the children of men, and by the power thereof, and the faith thereof,' they are sustained. Yet the wild ox's dominion over itself—its refusal—is a form of power beyond human faith.

word_study.meaning: to bind, to tie, to fasten. The verb qashar refers to securing something firmly, making it unable to move or escape. The wild ox would need to be bound—restrained—in order to be harnessed.
word_study.significance: Binding implies coercion. The question is not whether binding is theoretically possible, but whether it is practically feasible and whether the result would be worthwhile. To bind the wild ox would require force; the result would be a creature broken rather than willing.

word_study.meaning: a furrow, the line created by a plow. The telem represents the planned, ordered path of agricultural work—the human design imposed on the earth.
word_study.significance: The furrow is the opposite of the wild donkey's unbounded roaming. It represents constraint, order, and submission to a predetermined path. The wild ox will not accept the furrow because the furrow embodies human control over direction and purpose.

word_study.meaning: to break up, to make smooth, to harrow. The verb shadad refers to the breaking and smoothing of soil after plowing, preparing it for planting.
word_study.significance: Harrowing is a continuation of human labor, a deepening of the soil's submission to human will. The wild ox will not follow; it will not continue the work. It will not become an extension of human purposes even through the seemingly minimal task of harrow following.

word_study.meaning: behind you, after you. The preposition indicates position relative to Job—the ox following, submitting to his lead.
word_study.significance: The image of the ox following 'after' Job is the image of subordination, of a creature whose will is subordinated to the human's direction. This is the ultimate fantasy: not just strength, but willing attendance and continuation of human purpose.

text_kjv: Wilt thou trust him, because his strength is great? or wilt thou leave thy labour to him?

commentary.narrative: God narrows the question further: even if Job could not harness the wild ox for labor, could he trust it as a tool? Could he rely on its immense strength for his purposes? The Hebrew verb bitach (to trust, to have confidence) moves the focus from control to reliance. The verse asks whether Job would dare depend on a creature whose power is undeniable but whose reliability is non-existent. The second clause deepens the question: would Job entrust his ygi'a (toil, labor, the fruit of his labor) to the wild ox? This is not asking whether the ox could carry his goods; it is asking whether Job would stake his livelihood—the accumulated result of his sweat—on an animal that owes him nothing and answers to no one.
commentary.the_trap_of_power: Here is a subtle trap that God sets. The wild ox does have strength—tremendous strength. There is a seductive logic that says: "Surely such power must be useful. Surely I can find a way to leverage it for my benefit." But strength without obedience, power without reliability, and capability without submission are worse than useless—they are dangerous. To trust the wild ox with one's labor would be to place one's survival in the hands of a creature that respects no master and answers to no authority. The ox might break free at any moment, scattering Job's possessions, refusing to continue, abandoning the work midway. To rely on it would be folly.
commentary.theological_center: For Job, who has been trusting God despite catastrophic loss, this verse presents a moral paradox. Job has suffered because (from his perspective) God is powerful but seemingly unreliable—great in strength but apparently indifferent to Job's suffering and confusion. God seems to be asking: "Would you rather trust a creature that is strong and refuses you, or trust Me, who am both strong and faithful?" The wild ox embodies the futility of relying on power without relationship. Trust, in Scripture, always requires both power and character—the ability to help and the commitment to do so. Power alone is not trustworthy. This is why Job's complaints about divine injustice, though understandable, are insufficient. The answer is not to find a more reliable power source, but to trust the One whose power is inseparable from His character.
commentary.application: In modern life, we often look for 'strong' resources, people, or systems to rely on—powerful companies, charismatic leaders, impressive institutions—and assume that power implies trustworthiness. The wild ox teaches an essential distinction: strength without character is dangerous. Before placing your labor, your time, your trust in another person or institution, ask not merely whether they are strong, but whether their strength is committed to your welfare. Are they reliably good? Do they have a track record of keeping commitments? Are they answerable to something beyond themselves? In personal relationships, this means discerning not just charisma or capability, but integrity and consistency. In organizational life, this means understanding not just efficiency or power, but whether those running the organization are accountable to values beyond profit. Most importantly, it means understanding why trust in God is different from trust in any earthly power: because God's strength is eternally and essentially committed to our welfare, and this is the only foundation for genuine trust.
commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the answer to the question posed by the wild ox. Christ possesses infinite strength (all power was given unto Him in Matthew 28:18), yet His strength is inseparable from His love and commitment (John 13:1, 'having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end'). Unlike the wild ox, Christ's power can be fully trusted because it is exercised for others' welfare and redemption. The Atonement is the ultimate answer: power placed at the service of love.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 2 Nephi 4:34, Nephi declares: 'O then, if I have seen so great things, if the Lord in his condescension unto the children of men hath visited men in so much mercy, why should my heart weep and my flesh lapse into carnal sensibilities?' Nephi has learned that trust in God is justified not merely by God's strength but by God's 'condescension'—His willingness to commit His strength to the welfare of His people. The wild ox teaches the inverse: great strength that is indifferent to one's welfare is not trustworthy. Alma 32:21 teaches that faith is 'a perfect brightness of hope' and that it must be grounded in relationship, not merely in perception of power.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:5-6 teaches of God: 'Great and marvelous are thy works, O Lord God Almighty!...Thy patience and thy long-suffering are everlasting toward the children of men.' God's strength is paired with patience and commitment. This is why God is trustworthy in a way the wild ox is not. D&C 29:11 teaches that 'all things are subject unto me,' but the context makes clear this is because all things are made for God's children and for God's glory—power is exercised in love.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple covenants, the initiate enters into relationship with God based on His power and His commitment to care for those who covenant with Him. The temple teaches trust in a Being whose strength is inseparable from His love and character. The wild ox, which shows strength without character, represents the antithesis of the temple's promise of divine relationship.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient agricultural societies, animals represented capital investment and crucial infrastructure.
